[tnikolai2]: I found, this prroblem happens when I add --closure 1 in addition to -O3 . But it reduces resulting .js size from 99kb to 53kb.

[bvibber]: Ok, concentrating on the `FS` / `__syscall3` issue... `__syscall3` appears as an import on the intermediate wasm file I see using `EMCC_DEBUG=1` but isn't called anywhere, nor does it appear in the function table, just in the `asmLibraryArg` object.

```js
  try {
    var d = ra.f(), e = qa(), f = qa();
    return (void 0).read(d, H, e, f);
  } catch (g) {
    return x(g), -g.c;
```

Under 1.39.6 it's explicitly turning `FS` into `(void 0)` which is a synonym for `undefined` IIRC.

Oh, looks like upstream Closure has fixed a bug there (`undefined.read()` is not useful, so better catch it at compile time). I think the real issue is that we should get that syscall3 DCEd out before it even reaches closure, or gate the FS object with NO_FILESYSTEM if it does need to be there.

---

[kripken]: Thanks for the testcase! I think this is another case of `NO_FILESYSTEM` causing issues when the code contains some syscalls that use FS. We've fixed a few, but we should just do something more general - I opened #10427 now which hopefully fixes all such issues (verified as fixing this testcase).

title: WASM=2 and symbol maps
body:
Using `WASM=2` along with `--emit-symbol-map` option results in
- Unsrtripped WASM binary
- Not minified asm.js file.

Looks like this happens, because of passing `--emit-symbol-map` sets the `intermediate_debug_info` to true, which is later passed to `shared.Building.wasm2js` as a `debug_info` parameter.
comments:
[kripken]: Thanks @crsib !

The wasm not being stripped should be fixed in #10633 

By `not minified asm.js file` do you mean the `.wasm.js` file? The compiled code inside it looks minified (which is almost all the file). It is true the non-compiled code is not minified, but I think that's the same with or without symbol files?

---

[crsib]: Hi, @kripken !

title: getTypeName is not defined when calling C function
body:
I recently tried to update my emscripten build of game-music-emu to latest with the help of _embind_ and when calling the function like this:

```
var payload = new Uint8Array(this.response);
var ref = Module.allocate(1, "i32", Module.ALLOC_STACK);
var samplerate = 44100;
if (Module.gme_open_data(payload, payload.length, ref, samplerate) != 0)
    console.error("could not load data", payload);
```

I get the following error:

```
Uncaught ReferenceError: getTypeName is not defined
```

Which happens during construction of the error message passed to a _UnboundTypeError_. So even if the original problem would disappear, there would still be an exception thrown.

For reference, I used to call this function in my old (~2 years ago maybe) emscripten build via:

```
Module.ccall("gme_open_data", "number",
             ["array", "number", "number", "number"],
             [payload, payload.length, ref, samplerate]) 
```

The _embind_ C++ code looks like this:

```
#include <emscripten/bind.h>
#include "gme.h"

using namespace emscripten;

EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS(Gme) {
    function("gme_open_data", &gme_open_data, emscripten::allow_raw_pointers());
    ....
}
```

And the _gme_open_data_ prototype looks like this:

```
gme_err_t gme_open_data( void const* data, long size, Music_Emu** out, int sample_rate );
```

Where _Music_Emu_ is an opaque type (actually a C++ class, but the API is C), and _gme_err_t_ is a _const char *_.

I built this (https://bitbucket.org/mpyne/game-music-emu) with:

```
~/bin/emsdk_portable/emscripten/master/em++ -O0 --bind -std=c++11 -o out.js *.cpp
```

In the _gme_ sub-directory of the git-repo, where I added my _Emscripten.cpp_ file with the _EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS_ declaration.

emscripten version is:

```
emcc (Emscripten GCC-like replacement) 1.32.0
    (commit b3efd9328f940034e1cab45af23bf29541e0d8ff
        (HEAD -> master, tag: 1.32.0, origin/master, origin/HEAD))
```

We could emit code like `flatten()` in the js optimizer does,

```
var moar = true;
if (x == 0) {
  ...
  moar = false;
}
if (moar && x == 1) {
  ...
  moar = false;
}
...
```

Or it could have chunks each of which is a switch, to decrease the linear time cost. How does that sound?

---

[juj]: Would it be feasible to top-down binary bisect the switch-case into if()-else() halves until the number of cases is small enough to retain a switch-case internally. Something like:

```
switch(foo) {
    cases 1-40000: ...; break;
    default: /*defaultblock*/; break;
}
```

would be first halved to

```
var default = false;
if (foo <= 20000) {
    switch(foo) {
        cases 1-20000: ...; break;
        default: default = true; break;
    }
} else {
    switch(foo) {
        cases 20001-40000: ...; break;
        default: default = true; break;
    }    
}
if (default) {
    /*defaultblock*/;
}
```

which would then get recursively subdivided by halving the cases, until each switch-case contains fewer cases than some fixed limit for the size of a switch-case. If there is no `default:` block, then emitting the code for default handling could be omitted, and when doing multiple nested levels, there would not be need to recursively add such default handling variable to each level, but just the top level.

To me this kind of subdivision scheme sounds like the most performant (logN growth), and the call stack in parsers (I am not expert on parsers, so this is an assumption), would then grow only logarithmically, so 100k-ish cases in a switch should be easily achievable. CC @bnjbvr for a more technically expert opinion?

---

[bnjbvr]: I am compiling a browser to make some experiments with respect to parsing thread stack sizes and long chains of if/else vs switches, but in the meanwhile, here is some information I've compiled with respect to compilation time.

On my machine, with the test files @juj provided to me, with a recently Nightly on which these test cases compile, total compilation time is ~30 seconds, with two functions compiled slowly, namely the two functions that contain the big chains of if/else.
So I decided to make an experiment to see how compilation time was behaving with respect to the number of "else if" or the number of "case" statements within a switch statement. Here are the results:

```
Time of compilation, in ms (switch (number of cases) / if (number of "else if"))

1: 0 / 0
10: 0 / 0
100: 0 / 0
200: 2 / 4
400: 18 / 37
800: 218 / 240
1000: 510 / 761
1100: 656
1200: 952 / 1257
1300: 1340 / 1495
1400: 1647 / 1800
1500: 2507 / 2273
1600: 2999 / 2774
1700: 3383 / 5533 (!)
1800: 4567 / 4517
1900: 5378 / 6499 (!)
2000: 7126 / 6367
3000: 29057 / 29855
```

For instance, the line `1600: 2999 / 2774` reads as:
- for a switch statement with 1600 cases + default, compilation took 2999ms
- for a chain of if/else with 1600 `else if`, compilation took 2774ms

That shows two things;
- choosing `switch` over `else if` chains (almost) doesn't impact compilation time
- the more cases, the longer the compilation

So, in terms of compilation time, the approach suggested by @juj makes sense to me, with a low number of switch cases.

I'll try to get some numbers for the same experiment, with respect to stack size this time.

---

[bnjbvr]: Actually, with these compilation times in mind (which have been measured on the really powerful dev machine I have), it seems that compilation time would be a no-go anyways on low-end platforms like phones (before we have a baseline compiler for asm.js on Firefox, at least). So we have a strong argument in favor of splitting switch here and by doing so, we wouldn't encounter the stack size issues anyways. As a matter of fact, the series of experiments I was planning to do seems to be of lesser value, so I won't do them right now.

---

[kripken]: Wow, 30 seconds for 3,000 cases in a switch? Am I reading that right?

---

[bnjbvr]: Yes, that is the number on my machine (haswell processor with 8 cores 2.6Ghz, 16 GB of RAM). I wonder if we should limit the number of cases at asm.js validation? Or at least emit a warning telling to avoid this pattern and recompile with a more recent version of emscripten (when that's fixed in emscripten of course), to not break existing code? @lukewagner, wdyt?

---

[lukewagner]: Hmm, probably a good idea to first file a bug to see if there is some accidental O(n^2) algorithm in the backend or generally what the reason is.

---

[bnjbvr]: And that would be https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1174230

---

[kripken]: I have a patch that bisects switches similar to what @juj suggested earlier. This really doesn't solve the problem, though:
- Odin AOT times are still bad. A switch with 20,000 cases is broken up into many smaller ones, and there might be some improvement, but there is also extra control flow code to move around. Total code size is enormous, and still contains lots of smaller switches instead of one big one.
- LLVM opt times on such a switch are slow, as are our js opt times. This makes for very slow compilation times.

Overall then it is still painful even with split up switches. Perhaps the `moar` option I mentioned would avoid this, by having no switches whatsoever, but that would increase code size even more.It seems like it is not a good thing for code generators to emit switches with 20,000 cases. @juj, the only testcase I am aware of is the one you refer to - can their codegen avoid doing this, or is it necessary?

---

[kripken]: Some numbers on a 20,000 case switch

| max switch size | AOT time (ms) | Code Size |
| --- | :-: | :-: |
| none | 5913 | 849483 |
| 8192 | 5806 | 849447 |
| 4096 | 5924 | 849429 |
| 2048 | 5905 | 849992 |
| 1024 | 6077 | 851130 |
| 512 | 6096 | 853257 |
| 256 | 6090 | 857563 |
| 128 | 5915 | 866261 |
| 64 | 6473 | 884033 |
| 32 | 7031 | 918062 |

The smaller numbers are not that interesting (max switch size of 32 is pretty ridiculous), but just to show the trend. AOT time is extremely high regardless of bisecting switches. It's basically **linear in the number of switch cases**, instead of polynomial in the max switch size.

Due to that, my patch seems only useful to avoid "too much recursion" in the browser, but not AOT times.

However, I don't see a "too much recursion" error even with a switch with 20,000 case statements, so I am not sure what value to use in the switch bisector. @juj , on what size did you see it?

---

[kripken]: I opened pull requests for the splitter and the test updates. Splitter is at https://github.com/kripken/emscripten-fastcomp/pull/102

---

[juj]: Tested the PR locally on Windows computer, and I can see it works as intended, and no more `too much recursion` error. Discussed on IRC with @kripken , and I think the new bisecting switch-cases behavior is superior to the old if-else emitting. AOT times are not improved (but not really hurt either), and there should never be a danger of recursing to kill the call stack after this (this happened in Firefox, LLVM and IE11 on the partner's test case), so it's just great. Nice job!

---

[kripken]: Ok, I merged those two.

title: USE_PTHREADS freezes Firefox Nightly 42.0a1
body:
Hi. I'm trying to make simple threads example to work with Emscripten's `-s USE_PTHREADS=1` option but unfortunately it doesn't work with latest stable Emscripten and Firefox Nightly. Probably I'm doing something stupidly wrong, sorry for that.

Here is simple pthread example:

``` c
$ cat 1.c 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>

void *thread_fn(void *arg) {
    printf("Thread done\n");
    return NULL;
}

int main(void)
{
    pthread_t thread1, thread2;
    pthread_create(&thread1, NULL, thread_fn, NULL);
    pthread_create(&thread2, NULL, thread_fn, NULL);
    pthread_join(thread1, NULL);
    pthread_join(thread2, NULL);
    printf("Done\n");
    return 0;
}
```

I'm compiling it with the following options to `index.html`:

```
$ emcc -s USE_PTHREADS=1 1.c -o index.html
```

body:
Now this is a rather odd situation. Running locally the tests

```
browser.test_gl_ps, error=2 (allowed slack was=1)
browser.test_gl_ps_packed, error=2 (allowed slack was=1)
browser.test_gl_ps_strides, error=1 (allowed slack was=0)

browser.test_sdl_fog_density, error=1 (allowed slack was=0)
browser.test_sdl_fog_linear, error=2 (allowed slack was=1)
browser.test_sdl_ogl, error=2 (allowed slack was=1)
browser.test_sdl_ogl_defaultmatrixmode, error=2 (allowed slack was=1)
browser.test_sdl_ogl_p, error=2 (allowed slack was=1)
browser.test_sdl_ogl_proc_alias, error=2 (allowed slack was=1)
browser.test_sdl_rotozoom, error=6 (allowed slack was=3)
```

on my brand new Windows 8.1 64bit with Core i7 5960X and a MSI GTX 980 4G Gaming with latest Geforce Driver 355.82 (also occurred on an older driver version), each of the above tests fail the per pixel reftest by a very small margin. Looking closer, the failures are due to the image brightness being just so slightly different on the tests (hand-examined test_sdl_rotozoom and test_gl_ps to check). This is really odd, since for one, any display gamma settings should not affect the generated pixel values (gamma is applied at the end of the pipeline in the hdmi output circuitry), and since the recent emunittest reftests do work correctly. Things tested so far:
- Verified that it is not any display driver setting by attempting to tune the different brightness/contrast/gamma knobs in the control panel, that did not change anything. 
- In addition to FF 40, tried old Firefox version from 2012, and current FF Nightly 2015-09-15, the issue persists in each.
- The failure occurs also on Chrome (45) on the same computer.
- The failure does _not_ occur on IE11.
- Running the same Emscripten compiled test page of test_sdl_rotozoom on a Mac OS X computer passes the test, so it is not Emscripten compilation time specific.
- Another Windows computer with Windows 7 and nVidia Geforce GTX 980 passes the tests.

Since IE11 passes the test, I don't think this should be specific to the display driver. I haven't run the browser suite on this computer before, so I don't think the tests have ever passed, so this is not likely a regression. Perhaps it is something to do with ANGLE shader compiler specifically against the MSI GTX 980.. Not sure yet how to fix.

title: Using std::cout before main has been entered
comments:
[kripken]: Very strange. LLVM emits

```
@llvm.global_ctors = appending global [2 x { i32, void ()*, i8* }] [{ i32, void ()*, i8* } { i32 65535, void ()* @_GLOBAL__sub_I_a.cpp, i8* null }, { i32, void ()*, i8* } { i32 65535, void ()* @_GLOBAL__sub_I_iostream.cpp, i8* null }]
```

And [langref](http://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#the-llvm-global-ctors-global-variable) says "The order of functions with the same priority is not defined." Which means that the iostream constructor can happen after A's constructor, which is why this is broken.

@sunfishcode, is LLVM doing the right thing here? Is this undefined behavior perhaps?

---

[kripken]: Or perhaps does libc++ need to raise the priority of it's global constructors?

---

[sunfishcode]: I don't remember if cout is guaranteed to be initialized before static constructors that use it, and the language in the C++ standard is eluding me at the moment. However the standard does at least have the footnote "If it is possible for them to do so, implementations are encouraged to initialize the objects [cout etc] earlier than required." so if it's not difficult to raise the priority of these global constructors, it would be good to do so.

---

[kripken]: Thanks, I'll find out how to do that.

---

[kripken]: Fixed on incoming.

---

[kripken]: I suppose the reason we see this is that natively, libcxx is normally linked as a library, and the system makes sure to run linked library global constructors first, while for us, we merge all the code as bitcode first, so libcxx constructors are in no special position.

---

[ldionne]: Hi. Libc++ maintainer here. I want to fix this issue, but I don't know how to test it -- I can't reproduce the issue on mac os. Any idea about how I could reproduce this on non-emscripten? What's special about static constructors in emscripten that make this fail?

---

[kripken]: @ldionne Thanks! There might not be anything to fix in libc++, though, I'm not sure. We fixed this locally with https://github.com/emscripten-core/emscripten/commit/25ddbe8694824de514230b4386097909e7714877 which adjusts the priority of the constructor. That includes a testcase that failed before but passes with the fix.

I'm not sure why that isn't necessary on other platforms, but one big difference is emscripten links in libc++ statically, and it's treated as just normal code that is linked in at that point. So it "competes" with all other global ctors, and without a special priority it can "lose" and run too late. Perhaps normally the dynamic linker on a native system would initialize libraries before user code that uses the library, which would avoid this being an issue. Maybe static linking on mac os, or static + LTO, could reproduce the issue.

---

title: Gzip and Lazy Filesystem
body:
Hi,

I'm not sure whether this issue as been discussed before, I didn't find it using the github search:

Problem: 
Lazy loaded files which are served by the webserver using gzip are truncated.

Reason: 
https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/blob/master/src/library_fs.js#L1577
content-length is the compressed length, not the data length

Suggested Fix:
-check if gzip is used in this line.
-if not, continue as right know
-if it is use, download the whole file and get the true length

Sideeffect:
Getting the length of a compressed file will cause the download. BUT: It is better to download the file than to report a WRONG lenght.

Are there any opinions on this issue?

Fixing this issue would make manuels.github.io/texlive.js/ (which is listed as an example of using emscripten) work again. Right know it fails because github is compressing .map files which causes the bug to truncate it and pdftex will complain about missing fonts..

-Felix
comments:
[kripken]: Perhaps instead of downloading the whole file, it could throw an error, saying that gzip compression is not compatible with lazy-loaded files? Might be better for people to just not use a lazy-loaded file if they serve it compressed. I don't feel strongly about this though.

---

[fzimmermann89]: My goal is to not have it fail - after reconsidering it might be the best solution to have it in three stages:
If uncompressed continue as right know
If compressed, look for an additional header telling the uncompressed length (if the user has the ability to add one), else diwnload the whole file.

The description of lazyloading doesn't imply that it has to use chunks.
Throwing an exception would mean that certain files cannot be lazx loaded from github pages, etc. Not using chunks seems to me the "smallest surprise" for the developer. We might throw a warning - but lazy loading has more benefits than just junks:
For texlive.js a whole texlive installation is lazy loaded - a lot of rather small text files. Using gzip is actually better than chunking those files (and gh pages doesn't allow you to turn gzip off)

-Felix

//Edit:formatting

---

[kripken]: Sounds good. We should warn in the console if we are forced to download the whole file.

title: Error: WebGL: drawBuffers: invalid <buffers> (buffers must not be empty)
comments:
[juj]: Ugh, reading the GLES3 spec at https://www.khronos.org/registry/gles/specs/3.0/es_spec_3.0.0.pdf (section 4.2.1), it has the following two statements: 
- If the GL is bound to the default framebuffer, then n must be 1 and the constant must be BACK or NONE.
- In both cases [GL is bound to default framebuffer, or GL is bound to a framebuffer object], the draw buffers being defined correspond in order to the respective fragment colors. The draw buffer for fragment colors beyond n is set to NONE.

Therefore one can conclude that passing `n=0` is only valid in native `glDrawBuffers` when a FBO is bound, and that would translate to `gl.drawBuffers` accepting an empty array only if a FBO is set. One can experiment with the following code:

```
<html><body>
<canvas id="c" width="64" height="64"></canvas>
<script>
var gl = document.getElementById('c').getContext('webgl2');
gl.drawBuffers([]); // Empty array when no FBO, should not be accepted.

var fb = gl.createFramebuffer();
gl.bindFramebuffer(gl.FRAMEBUFFER, fb);
gl.drawBuffers([]); // Empty array when with FBO, should be accepted.
</script>
</body>
</html>
```

should generate one error only, but in FF Nightly, it generates an error in both cases. The WebGL 2 specification does not have a special wording regarding this. Given that the GLES3 spec is so obtuse here, it's probably best to validate and enforce this directly in Emscripten.

---

[erunehtar]: Thanks @juj ! Perhaps we should file a bug to mozilla so that we don't have to keep this work-around forever?

---

[juj]: A more precise test:

```
<html><body>
<canvas id="c" width="64" height="64"></canvas>
<script>
console.log('case no fbo:');
var gl = document.getElementById('c').getContext('webgl2');
while(gl.getError() != 0) gl.getError(); // flush
gl.drawBuffers([]); // Empty array when no FBO, should not be accepted.
console.log('gl error: ' + gl.getError()); // Should have an error


console.log('case yes fbo:');
var fb = gl.createFramebuffer();
gl.bindFramebuffer(gl.FRAMEBUFFER, fb);
while(gl.getError() != 0) gl.getError(); // flush
gl.drawBuffers([]); // Empty array when with FBO, should be accepted.
console.log('gl error: ' + gl.getError()); // Should not have an error
</script>
</body>
</html>
```

---

---

[erunehtar]: Thanks!

title: Exclude zero-initialized values from .mem file
body:
Consider this small C program:

``` c
#include <stdio.h>

int buf[1048576];

int main() {
  printf("hello, world! %d\n", buf[123456]);
  return 0;
}
```

When I build this file with `emcc -O2`, it produces a large (4MB) `.mem` file:

```
$ emcc -O2 hello.c -o hello.js
$ ls -l hello*
      111 hello.c
   185535 hello.js
  4198443 hello.js.mem
```

This file is almost entirely zeros, as evidenced by how well it gzips:

```
$ gzip -c hello.js.mem | wc -c
    5302
```

When I build the same binary with `gcc`, I get a much smaller output:

```
$ gcc -O2 hello.c -o hello
$ ls -l hello
8464 hello
```

So evidently `gcc` is smarter about not writing zero-initialized values to disk.

I realize that, since this file compresses so well, it may not seem like an issue in practice. But not everyone's web server is configured to do this properly. It feels like an unnecessary risk to have such a large file lying around and it feels like a bug when you first use Emscripten. If it's not necessary, why include all those zeros?

See also #3815 and [this discussion](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/emscripten-discuss/nZz2tjepBPY) on emscripten-discuss.
comments:
[kripken]: Pushed an optimization to incoming. If you get a chance to measure this on your app I'd be interested to hear the results.

---

[danvk]: Brilliant! Thanks for the quick fix.

Before (emcc 1.34.12):

```
    346353 out.js
   2076549 out.js.mem
```

After (emcc 1.35.9):

```
    347675 out.js
      6177 out.js.mem
```

---

[kripken]: Great, thanks for the confirmation.

---

[juj]: Do we have a real zero section in Emscripten? I.e. all global data that have their initializer value initialized to zero would lie in subsequent memory addresses, and the memory initializer could omit all of the zeroes? I suppose that is what the staticBump is about?

---

[kripken]: Yes. Typed arrays are zero-initialized anyhow, so all we need is to bump the top of static memory, to leave space for them. The optimization just sorts them all to the end, and does not emit them into the memory init file.

title: Race condition can cause redundant IDBFS store sync operations.
body:
It looks like if one uses the following code pattern

```
for(x times)
{
    create file in idbfs mount;
    FS.syncfs(false); // persist created file to IDBFS.
}
```

then it can happen that a quadratic number of file sync operations are performed, when at each iteration, all of the created files are stored again to IndexedDB, instead of just the previously created file. This seems to be timing specific, and e.g. if one creates a very small file, the issue doesn't occur, but when the synced files are relatively large (seen with ~8MB), then there are `O(x^2)` stores that occur.

To reproduce, add some debugging to indexedDB storage where the IDB put operations are performed: https://github.com/juj/emscripten/commit/8ad9f6a3aab5ed2e732e60b7058a4a86c8e7e740

and try the following code:

```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <emscripten.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <string.h>

int main()
{
  // Create a IDBFS mount.
  EM_ASM(
    FS.mkdir('/idbfs');
    FS.mount(IDBFS, {}, '/idbfs');
  );

  // Incrementally create 10 ~8MB files.
  for(int i = 0; i < 10; ++i)
  {
    char filename[256];
    sprintf(filename, "/idbfs/file%d.txt", i);
    FILE *handle = fopen(filename, "w");
    for(int j = 0; j < 500000; ++j)
      fputs(filename, handle);
    fclose(handle);

    // Sync each file after creation.
    EM_ASM( FS.syncfs(false, function(err) { console.log('syncfs finished: err: ' + err); }); );
  }

  emscripten_exit_with_live_runtime();

  return 0;
}
```

We should probably store the timestamp of a new file immediately somewhere before starting the asynchronous IDBFS persist store operation, so that subsequent syncs won't start syncing the same file again if the previous sync on that file hasn't yet finished, but I'm unsure yet what would be the best way to store this information.
comments:
[kripken]: I'm not sure we can do better here - we need to fire a full sync, as previous ones might fail.

The proper solution is for the app to do a single sync at the end of a batch of operations. If we land #3867 then we'll have a warning that can point people to this problem in their code.

---

[juj]: Do you mean that there could be a case where one syncs file A twice back-to-back, and first sync fails, but second sync succeeds? What would be an example of such a scenario? Even if that could happen, couldn't we detect the previous failure?

---

[kripken]: We could detect it, yes, but it adds complexity. There would be a queue of operations, and we'd need to diff in between, etc. I'd really like to avoid that.

I think warning on too many calls is a good start. Another option is to provide an API, `syncLater()` that will call a sync at the next "convenient time", which would be after all current syncs are done (plus maybe another delay, to reduce the # of syncs). How does that sound?

---

[juj]: Such a function `syncLater` would not have sequential consistency if one happens to modify the file later but would not like the later changes to persist (they might accidentally piggy-back into the future sync). It feels like it should be possible to be absolutely bombproof here, but indeed it can be complex, since it might require some copy-on-write semantics to file write syscalls. Let me think about this more.

title: Chrome Canary breaks regexes run on function toString()
body:
In Chrome Canary 50.0.2654.0, function toString() now includes the function name. This breaks zlib-asm, and while investigating it (reported as crbug.com/587818) I found that asm.js code appears to run a regex on the result of function toString(), and since it doesn't expect the name to be there it fails to match and then throws when it tries to slice the result.

The workaround is to find this regex:

```
/^function\s*\(([^)]*)\)\s*{\s*([^*]*?)[\s;]*(?:return\s*(.*?)[;\s]*)?}$/
```

and (my hack, feel free to improve) add a [A-Za-z0-9]\* to optionally match the function name if emitted:

```
/^function\s*[A-Za-z0-9]*\(([^)]*)\)\s*{\s*([^*]*?)[\s;]*(?:return\s*(.*?)[;\s]*)?}$/
```

Then this works in both current and Canary versions of Chrome. The Chrome bug will allow Google to determine the web compat impact, but this might need fixing in Emscripten anyway.
comments:
[rossberg]: Note that Chrome's new behaviour conforms to the current ES.next proposal for standardising toString:

http://tc39.github.io/Function-prototype-toString-revision/

It basically amounts to "return the original source code", modulo white space changes. This was agreed upon at the last TC39 meeting, and is currently at stage 2.

---

[kripken]: Thanks for the report and the info. Fixed on incoming.

The reason we need this is that for `ccall` we want to emit fast code, and we figure out what code to emit using a regex on a minified function (otherwise minification will mix us up). If you build with `NO_DYNAMIC_EXECUTION = 0` then we go through a slow path that avoids this, btw.

---

[AshleyScirra]: FWIW, this only happens in Canary with "experimental javascript" enabled, and it looks like a V8 patch is on the way to correct it as well. However I would guess the change ought to be made anyway for robustness.

---

[kripken]: Yes, agreed.

---

[rodneyrehm]: Unless I'm missing something, `[a-zA-Z]*\s*`is not going to match all possible function names.

``` js
String(function _(a, b){ return a + b; })
String(function ಠ_ಠ(a, b){ return a + b; })
```

If I didn't miss anything, I'd suggest matching for `[^(]*` instead (anything but opening parens)

---

[kripken]: You're right, but this is only run a very specific set of methods, that we provide.

Although, come to think of it, you're right, the minified name might not fall in that subset. But I'm worried about matching anything but `(` as it might allow non-function things.

Reopening, we should improve this.

---

[kripken]: I pushed a commit that makes it support all the values we can have as minified outputs. There is a risk of another minifier being used, however - but AFAIK none use unicode tricks.

---

[rodneyrehm]: In such a case I would've added a comment to the source explaining why we're limiting function names to the given set, but LGTM. :)

title: window.id conflict when compiling with --closure 1
body:
This is a tricky one. 
When handling focus/blur events on window with Emscripten (with `emscripten_set_focus_callback`), I'm getting an error `Uncaught TypeError: a.charCodeAt is not a function` in the emscripten code of the event handling, more precisely in `registerFocusEventCallback` in library_html5.js, when calling `writeStringToMemory(id, ...)`. 

When compiling with  `--closure 1`, all classes and functions in the global scope get renamed to window.a, window.b, window.c, ... window.aa, window.ab, window.ac, ... and there is also one that takes window.id...
As a result, when trying to write window.id in the memory, instead of writing a String like it would normally do, it tries to write a window.id which in this case will be an object, and fails on window.id.charCodeAt.

What options do I have if I don't want to give up `--closure 1` and can't listen to focus events anywhere else than on window ?

Some way to fix this in emscripten would be to replace this line 

`var id = e.target.id ? e.target.id : '';`

with this 

`var id = e.target.id && (typeof e.target.id) == 'string' ? e.target.id : '';`

```

#include <math.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#if PREVENT_CONSTANT_FOLDING
#define NO_FOLD volatile
#else
#define NO_FOLD
#endif
int main() {

 NO_FOLD int finetune = 0;

 return 0;
}

returned: 6.349605

manx@idefix ~/tmp $ node a.out.js
expected: 6.349605
returned: 6.441961

manx@idefix ~/tmp $ 
```

---

[manxorist]: Results on Firefox44/32bit/Windows, Firefox45.0/x86-64/Ubuntu14.04 and nodejs-4.1.1/x86-64/Ubuntu14.04 are all the same for me. To me, this does not look like a browser problem.

---

[kripken]: I can confirm it's not a browser problem. Also that `PRECISE_F32` fixes it.

And looks like with `-DPREVENT_CONSTANT_FOLDING=1`, LLVM can't optimize away the computation at compile time, so it hides the problem that `PRECISE_F32` fixes.

As to why the problem is so large, `exp2f` from musl must be sensitive to float/double differences on these inputs. We'd need to debug it to find out why.

---

[manxorist]: Getting the whole calculation before `pow()` completely out of the picture:

```
manx@idefix ~/tmp $ cat test2.c
#include <math.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
int main() {
 uint32_t bits = 0x402aaaab; // 2.666667f
 float exp_ = 0.0f;
 memcpy(&exp_, &bits, 4);
 volatile float exp = exp_;

 printf("expected: %f\n", d);

 return 0;
}

manx@idefix ~/tmp $ node a.out.js
2.666667 (0x402aaaab)
expected: 6.349605
returned: 6.441961
```

---

[BartmanAbyss]: I was having the same problem. I investigated a bit more into @manxorist 's test case.
It seems, if you compile it with `-O0`, the resulting JS indeed uses `Math.pow`, but starting from `-O1` it's using `_exp2`/`_ext2f`, which compiled from native C code. Digging into their implementations seems a bit tedious, so I'm not sure what exactly is going on there

I have attached the `-O1`output of both functions for further investigation by someone more capable. (`exp2f` is the imprecise one, `exp2` is the working one)
[exp2f.txt](https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/files/265038/exp2f.txt)
[exp2.txt](https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/files/265039/exp2.txt)

---

[kripken]: Probably in `-O1` LLVM thinks it can do better than the generic pow method, as it knows it's a power of 2.

What goes wrong in those compiled methods is that they are sensitive to float precision, I believe. Perhaps they could be rewritten, but it wouldn't be easy ;)

Overall, the solution is just to use `PRECISE_F32` to get the proper precision. I wish we could have it on by default, but browser limitations prevent it. However, it will be on in WebAssembly, so things will improve here.

---

[BartmanAbyss]: The problem with `PRECISE_F32` is, that our code runs about 3x slower with it enabled.
So my current workaround is to just `#define powf pow`. Seems to be working quite okay.

---

[kripken]: That 3x slowdown is in chrome, I guess? Yeah, they are [the reason](https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/wiki/Chrome-Perf-Issues#float32) we can't turn this on by default.

(If it's another browser, that might be an unknown issue that needs to be filed for that browser.)

---

[BartmanAbyss]: Yes, this is in both Node.js and Chome 50.

---

[manxorist]: I can reproduce this problem with emscripten 1.36.0 on node.js 4.1.1.
I cannot reproduce this problem with emscripten 1.37.9.
I cannot reproduce this problem with emscripten 1.37.36 on node.js 8.9.1.
I cannot reproduce this problem with emscripten 1.38.8 (with -s WASM=0) on node.js 8.10.0
I cannot reproduce with emscripten 1.38.8 (default native-wasm mode) on node.js 8.10.0 either.

I have not checked any other versions in-between.
I am also not sure if *all* problems that previously required PRECISE_F32=1 to work-around now do work or whether this is specific to the reduced test case.

---

title: FS.createPreloadedFile throws Uncaught ReferenceError: Browser is not defined
body: I believe https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/blob/master/src/library_browser.js isn't getting pulled in appropriately.
comments:
[lambdabaa]: This is with emcc version 1.36.0 fyi

---

[kripken]: Do you have a testcase showing the problem?

---

[BugraBarin]: @kripken I am having this exact issue in our code base after upgrading to sdk-tag-1.36.14-64bit. As a test case, I just created a simple main.cpp:

```
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  std::cout << "Hello world" << std::endl;
  return 0;
}

```

and built it as follows:
emcc main.cpp -o main.html

I cannot see any of the library_browser.js code in the generated main.js.

In our code we call FS.createPreloadedFile and it fails due to missing object "Browser". I wonder if I'm doing something wrong.

---

[kripken]: Yes, we don't include `Browser` if it isn't used. However, if you preload files, then it should be included, so the question is why it isn't. Are you perhaps using the file packager separately/standalone?

Even so, though, `Browser` is included if you use e.g. `emscripten_set_main_loop` or `emscripten_async_call` etc. Are you not using any of those apis either?

---

[BugraBarin]: We don't use the file packager separately. We embed some static files using --embed-file. We make FS.createPreloadedFile calls to load some localized content on-the-fly.

We don't use emscripten_set_main_loop as it was causing a constant redraw loop even when there were no user input. We never needed emscripten_async_call either.

Do we have to explicitly call something from Browser to get it included?

Thanks!

---

[BugraBarin]: Adding a dummy call to emscripten_async_call did the trick. Though I wonder if a call to FS.createPreloadedFile should also trigger the inclusion of Browser.

Though I realize we are probably an unusual case here since we don't call emscripten_set_main_loop.

Thanks for your help Alon!

---

[kripken]: Hmm, I think this is a bug that wasn't noticed since apps tend to use the `emscripten_` APIs that bring in `Browser`.

The problem is that `FS.createPreloadedFile` is in JS, where the compiler can't see it. We don't scan user-supplied JS, as it's not practical to statically analyze.

Not sure what the better solution is here. Another workaround is to build with `-s DEFAULT_LIBRARY_FUNCS_TO_INCLUDE=$Browser`, which will force-include it.

---

[BugraBarin]: That's a great workaround, thanks a lot! I will give it a try soon.

Btw, I am doing this toolset upgrade to experiment with WebAssembly using Binaryen and the results are super impressive. We see great performance improvements in CPU-bound operations with WASM (in the order of 40-70%). The app load performance is pretty terrible but I'm assuming that'll get better in time as wasm support matures in Browsers. Very exciting!

---

[kripken]: Nice, good to hear!

---

title: 1.36.12: error in mkdirTree, invalid argument
comments:
[juj]: It looks like `FS.mkdir(d, mode);` is failing with the "Invalid argument" error. Are you able to reproducibly raise the error? Can you try printing out `d` and `mode` params that go to `FS.mkdir`:

```
...
console.log('d: ' + d + ', mode: ' + mode);
FS.mkdir(d, mode);
...
```

perhaps one of these two is the bad argument.

---

[erunehtar]: Got this output:

```
d: /data, mode: undefined
```

---

[erunehtar]: yeah...

``` js
      function() { // preFinish
        // if the destination directory does not yet exist, create it
        FS.mkdirTree(destinationDirectory);
      }
```

---

[erunehtar]: Perhaps do like `mkdir` and do the following in case `mode` is undefined?

``` js
      mode = mode !== undefined ? mode : 511 /* 0777 */;
      mode &= {{{ cDefine('S_IRWXUGO') }}} | {{{ cDefine('S_ISVTX') }}};
      mode |= {{{ cDefine('S_IFDIR') }}};
```

---

[erunehtar]: nope that didn't work :(

---

[erunehtar]: Ok I think I understand the issue better now, it fails in `mknod` here:

``` js
      if (!name || name === '.' || name === '..') {
        throw new FS.ErrnoError(ERRNO_CODES.EINVAL);
      }
```

printing the directory inside the `mkdirTree` function, we find that the very first directory it tries to create is `/.` which is not valid.

We are not trying to create any folders with such a path, and the only place it ends up calling `mkdirTree` would be from `emscripten_async_wget`. Somehow that function is passing dots to `mkdirTree`. I'll keep digging.

---

[erunehtar]: Found it, in `emscripten_async_wget`:

``` js
var destinationDirectory = PATH.dirname(_file);
```

passing a file name without folder here, such as `test.txt` will return `.` as the destinationDirectory.

---

[erunehtar]: Previously we were able to pass file names without having to put a `/` in front, should that still work with the mkdirTree change?

---

[juj]: Thanks for debugging this. Looks like `emscripten_async_wget()` needs to be able to take in destination path names that are relative to cwd? Added PR #4649 which adds testing for this and implements support for relative path names for the destination directory. Does that look like what you'd expect?

---

[erunehtar]: Fix merged, we can close this.

title: Browser.requestFullsreen stack overflow
body:
Trying to set fullscreen from GLFW seems to run in infinite recursion. Looking at the code this probably affects all window APIs, since the problem comes from the fact that everywhere we calls `Browser.setCanvasSize`, the third parameter (`noUpdates`) is not set, which if set to `true` would prevent calling `Browser.updateResizeListeners` and stop the recursion. Happened in this commit: https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/commit/99810617

How do you suggest we fix this issue? Add `true` to most places, or use a default value on the function?
comments:
[kripken]: If we call this in a place that is called when updating, then yes, we need to fix that. I hope that's only in glfw, though, and in the others we call it from safe locations (that require updates to be sent). We should have tests for at least some of the others, showing it's ok.

---

comments:
[ahixon]: Probably the same problem, but if not I'll open another issue:

Weirdly, if you replace the call of `gethostbyname` to `gethostbyname2` in the above code, you get:

[kripken]: Thanks for filing. Ok, first issue is fixed on incoming. The problem is that much of our sockets code is in JS, so it can easily connect to the browser's networking APIs - so the relevant code is mostly in `library.js` instead of musl. So we need to map out the dependencies between libc and JS both ways, and the libc->JS way is not automatic, and we were missing an entry.

Second issue is that we don't have support for gethostbyname2. Looks like it's a gnu extension from the manpage? It would be nice to support it, I'm not sure offhand how easy that would be.

---

title: Fetch: failed cache store errors in successful XHR are not reported
body:
In the case of a cache store failure in the context of a successful XHR, for instance when using `EMSCRIPTEN_FETCH_LOAD_TO_MEMORY|EMSCRIPTEN_FETCH_PERSIST_FILE` attributes. It is perfectly valid that this `emscripten_fetch` call end up calling the `onsuccess` callback when the XHR is successful, but if the cache store failed, the `status` and `statusText` should be updated to reflect the real status of the fetch operation.

This happen frequently in browsers that have restrictions in IndexedDB entries size. Without this error propagated, there's no way to detect if the cache store failed when the XHR is successful.

body:
The full command is pretty long, but in short I'm trying to create an async emterpreter with wasm. It works fine with asm.js, but fails with `-s WASM=1`. I've tried applying https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/pull/5017 just on the off-chance with no success. I'm on incoming and have tested with both ayzim and the normal emscripten optimizer with identical behaviour.

The problem comes from `js-optimizer.js`, the `throw 'bad';` in [these lines](https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/blob/142adaf/tools/js-optimizer.js#L7509-L7514):
```
        switch (asmData.ret) {
          case ASM_INT: ret = srcToExp('HEAP32[EMTSTACKTOP >> 2]'); break;
          case ASM_FLOAT:
          case ASM_DOUBLE: ret = srcToExp('HEAPF64[EMTSTACKTOP >> 3]'); break;
          default: throw 'bad';
        }
```

Modifying the `default` line to read `default: { console.log('going bad'); console.log(asmData.ret); console.log(func); console.log('gone bad'); throw 'bad'; }`, I get the following output:

```
going bad
12
[ 'defun',
  '_combine_soft_light_c',
  [ 'f1', 'f3', 'f4', 'f5' ],
  [ [ 'if', [Object], [Object] ], [ 'stat', [Object] ] ] ]
gone bad
```

Note that 12 corresponds to the `ASM_NONE` type.

Some thoughts: when creating ayzim, I was able to remove `ASM_NONE` and make the type of `asmData.ret` be an `Option<AsmType>`, i.e. `ASM_NONE` is more accurately expressed as the absence of a type. Making an educated guess based on this knowledge, I changed `if (asmData.ret !== undefined) {` to `if (asmData.ret !== undefined && asmData.ret !== ASM_NONE) {` a couple of lines above this switch (as well as a similar check [elsewhere](https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/blob/142adaf/tools/js-optimizer.js#L2193)), which then allowed the emterpreter step to complete. Sadly, it later failed in the asm2wasm step so I guess my changes may have just been putting off the inevitable crash:

```
DEBUG:root:check tells us to use asm.js backend
DEBUG:root:using binaryen, with method: native-wasm
DEBUG:root:asm2wasm (asm.js => WebAssembly): /myhome/.emscripten_ports/binaryen/binaryen-version_30/bin/asm2wasm out/wesnoth.temp.asm.js --total-memory=1073741824 --emit-jsified-potential-traps -O3 --mem-init=out/wesnoth.html.mem --mem-base=1024 -o out/wesnoth.wasm
asm2wasm: /myhome/.emscripten_ports/binaryen/binaryen-version_30/src/wasm/wasm-binary.cpp:320: uint32_t wasm::WasmBinaryWriter::getFunctionIndex(wasm::Name): Assertion `mappedFunctions.count(name)' failed.
```
comments:
[aidanhs]: Oh but hang on, does a wasm module need to be fully linked? I.e. is it unable to handle
```
warning: unresolved symbol: posix_spawn_file_actions_init
warning: unresolved symbol: BZ2_bzDecompressInit
warning: unresolved symbol: posix_spawn_file_actions_destroy
warning: unresolved symbol: BZ2_bzDecompressEnd
warning: unresolved symbol: BZ2_bzCompress
warning: unresolved symbol: BZ2_bzCompressInit
warning: unresolved symbol: sendfile
warning: unresolved symbol: BZ2_bzDecompress
warning: unresolved symbol: BZ2_bzCompressEnd
warning: unresolved symbol: posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2
```
?

If so, I guess the two errors are unrelated.

---

[kripken]: Yeah, the errors seem to be unrelated, as best I can guess.

As to the first error, that's odd. We do set `asmData.ret` to undefined, and only set it to anything else if we find a return statement with a value (looking at all sites with `.ret = ` in that file). So `asmData.ret` should never be `ASM_NONE`. That's worth investigating - it's an unknown bug, not detected by the test suite nor fuzzing.

Also interesting that wasm influences things here. It actually shouldn't at this stage, this should be the same asm.js as when building the same file to asm.js.

Anyhow, maybe if you just add some debug logging after the one place we do `.ret = ` in that file (check for assigning `ASM_NONE` which is invalid, and printing the function), the problem might be come obvious. If not, maybe send me the bitcode + build command.

---

[aidanhs]: My link command involves 100MB across 15 different bitcode files, so might be a little inconvenient to send - I'll have a go at it :)

[aidanhs]: Ah but i can combine files if necessary, so that's a possibility.

[aidanhs]: Got it. See #5046.

[aidanhs]: > Oh but hang on, does a wasm module need to be fully linked?

Now I've got a successful wasm build, the answer appears to be a definite no - it works fine. So it seems that the second problem was resolved by something else, possibly updating incoming, possibly the PR above. Not important any more.

---

[aidanhs]: Aha, got the binaryen assertion again. With debugging:
```
count _emscripten_glFrustum
asm2wasm: /myhome/.emscripten_ports/binaryen/binaryen-version_31/src/wasm/wasm-binary.cpp:324: uint32_t wasm::WasmBinaryWriter::getFunctionIndex(wasm::Name): Assertion `mappedFunctions.count(name)' failed.
```
i.e. the function it can't find is `_emscripten_glFrustum`. Grepping the file for that:
```
$ grep emscripten_glFrustum out/wesnoth.temp.asm.js
```

After updating and wiping my cache, I now can't reproduce again. I did have a number of PRs ongoing branched off from different points that could have messed things up, so I'll close this issue since everything I was originally complaining about now :)

title: RuntimeError: indirect call signature mismatch
body:
This may not be too helpful, but I got `RuntimeError: indirect call signature mismatch` when I tried to run the result of compiling our app to wasm with release 1.37.5 in Firefox. The generated asm.js code appears to work fine. Is this a known issue? Is it a bug in our code? Or emscripten? Or Firefox?

The call stack wasn't helpful, even with `-g`:

```
wasm-function[1100]
wasm-function[790]
wasm-function[720]
wasm-function[2076]
wasm-function[5905]
wasm-function[4348]
wasm-function[4525]
wasm-function[3142]
wasm-function[8401]
wasm-function[2418]
wasm-function[6527]
wasm-function[5565]
```
comments:
[kripken]: It's possible it's an unknown emscripten bug. First thing I would verify what happens in another browser, like chrome canary or safari nightly. Also I'd verify it's latest incoming, as we did fix a bug like that (had to do with imports), but it was a while ago, so probably not the same.

---

[evanw]: **Chrome stable** doesn't support WebAssembly yet and so is able to run the asm.js build fine. This says to me that our code is likely correct.

**Chrome Canary** tries to load the WebAssembly build but gives `failed to compile wasm module: RangeError: WebAssembly.Module(): synchronous compilation disallowed due to module size limit set by embedder` and falls back to asm.js instead, which works fine. No idea how to bypass this.

**Safari Nightly** also tries to load the WebAssembly but the generated code throws an abort somewhere when run. It's impossible to tell where because there's no WebAssembly debugging support yet.

Our build system isn't set up to use incoming so I started trying to use the SDK script, but it's taking forever to download. I'm guessing my internet isn't fast enough to download it all at the moment. I'll have to try that again later.

I can also try building with previous emscripten releases. 1.37.1 was working fine when I tried it but 1.37.2 fails to build for [unrelated reasons](https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/issues/4934). I can try building with 1.37.3 and 1.37.4 sometime too and maybe that would give more information.

---

[kripken]: The synchronous compilation issue is a chrome limitation at the moment. Using latest incoming will default to async compilation, avoiding that (or you can set `BINARYEN_ASYNC_COMPILATION`, in a recent version).

---

[evanw]: I got our app building with incoming. I tried enabling `BINARYEN_ASYNC_COMPILATION` but then I get `WARNING:root:BINARYEN_ASYNC_COMPILATION requested, but disabled since not in wasm-only mode`. Firefox still throws `RuntimeError: indirect call signature mismatch`. Chrome Canary still shows `failed to compile wasm module: RangeError: WebAssembly.Module(): synchronous compilation disallowed due to module size limit set by embedder`.

The thing that worked was disabling the `asmjs` target. Using wasm-only mode gets rid of the warning about `BINARYEN_ASYNC_COMPILATION` and makes both Firefox and Chrome Canary work.

Is the combined wasm and asm.js mode fully supported (i.e. are you interested in fixing that)? What information would be useful for you to be able to fix it?

---

[kripken]: Interesting. So the wasm part of the wasm+asmjs build failed, but the wasm by itself build worked? And asm.js of the wasm+asm.js build also worked? Then it seems like somehow wasm is miscompiling the asm.js-friendly asm.js. Weird...

Definitely worth fixing. If you have a runnable bitcode testcase you can share I can debug that. If not, here's how I would debug it: build with `-s DETERMINISTIC=1`, and also do `EMCC_AUTODEBUG=1` in the env. It will then print out lots of logging. You can then get a log from the asm.js and wasm versions of the shared asm.js+wasm build, and diffing them shows where wasm diverges.

---

[xor2k]: When I tried to get web assembly side modules running, I stumbled upon a similar, maybe the same bug and created a gist: https://gist.github.com/xor2k/6fae4abcb4d8c4b4f456dad39256f9a3

Here, both libc as well as libcxx seem to be included properly, but as soon as std::cout related functions are called, a`RuntimeError: indirect call signature mismatch` is created.

---

[kripken]: @xor2k - which version is that with? it works for me on current incoming, using latest binaryen master.

---

[xor2k]: Yes, I verified that I am using the current emscripten incoming and the latest binaryen master. I'm using Ubuntu 16.4 and the current node.js v8.2.1 from https://nodejs.org/en/download/package-manager. When I try the bundled node-v4.1.1 or node.js v7.10.1 to run `node main.js` it says `no native wasm support detected`. I updated the gist so that now the error pops up by default and there is no need to modify the `main.cc` anymore. Also, I switched from `-O2` to `-O0 -fno-exceptions`. If `-fno-exceptions` is removed, it yields yet another error. So that gist is acutally a whole error family ;)

---

[kripken]: Maybe it's a node.js bug? I ran it in the spidermonkey shell. Can you test it in firefox and chrome, those should be the best-supported?

---

[xor2k]: I also double checked that. Indeed, the bug does not occur with Firefox (v54), but with Chrome (v59) and Chromium (v59). Compare updated gist: https://gist.github.com/xor2k/6fae4abcb4d8c4b4f456dad39256f9a3

---

[kripken]: Interesting, sounds like a v8-specific bug then. Can you please [file a bug for them](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/v8/issues/list) and link to it here?

---

[xor2k]: This one here looks promising, I've added another comment: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/v8/issues/detail?id=5913

---

[xor2k]: Good news! At least the error I have reported seems to be fixed in Node 8.3, Google Chrome v60 and Chromium v60.

---

title: glfwGetKey() stuck key state, GLFW_PRESS persists after onblur - should clear key state on window losing focus
body:
glfwGetKey() continues to return `GLFW_PRESS` even after the user has switched to another window and released the key, causing keyboard-based controls to act as if they are "stuck".

Consequently, if a user is interacting with a game, for example by pressing WASD to move around, then they switch out of it to somewhere else, they'll keep interacting (moving, jumping, etc.) while outside of the game, and even when they switch back to it.

---

Example demo for testing:

* https://satoshinm.github.io/emglfwbugs/test_glfw_get_key_stuck/test_glfw_get_key_stuck.html
* Source: https://github.com/satoshinm/emglfwbugs/blob/gh-pages/test_glfw_get_key_stuck/test_glfw_get_key_stuck.c

This calls glfwGetKey() in a loop and reports when it changes, and also updates the canvas color (red=pressed, green=released).

Hold down the spacebar, then switch out of the browser (used Cmd-Tab) and switch back.

The key will behave as if it is stuck, until you press and release it again (canvas stays red) and logs:

```
glfwGetKey says space pressed? 0
glfwGetKey says space pressed? 1
blur
```

Proposed fix: I added `emscripten_set_blur_callback()` to demonstrate an idea how this problem could be fixed in emscripten. If it reset all input states (keyboard, mouse, anything else) when receiving the onblur event, then keys should no longer stick.

emscripten 1.37.9, same behavior on Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. The problem does not occur with native glfw 3.2.1, which lets you Cmd-Tab out of the window and glfwGetKey() stops returning pressed.

---

Workaround: the user can press and release the key to unstick it -- iff they know what key that was stuck.  Sometimes this is obvious, if they are moving left then tap and release 'A', for the classic WASD controls, and so on, but depending on the application, what key got stuck is not always apparent. Especially if modifier keys are stuck, then many normal game controls no longer function. I haven't found an application-level workaround for this yet (listen for onblur, set a global blurred=1, and replace glfwGetKey() with !blurred && glfwGetKey()? I think this would be better resolved within emscripten's glfw port, or deeper down the stack.)

title: Cannot access packaged files after memory growth
comments: [kripken]: Yes, that's correct, it does avoid copies, but looks like we didn't realize that doesn't mix well with memory growth. It's possible that building with `--no-heap-copy` would make this work, in which case, we might want to just auto-enable that for memory growth. --- [olafmaas]: Just ran into the same problem. Building with ```--no-heap-copy``` solved the problem for me. Chrome will output ```Cannot perform TypedArrayCreate on a detached ArrayBuffer``` (Just mentioning this to make searching a bit more easy for other Chrome users with the same problem. :stuck_out_tongue: ) --- [nstoddard]: I just ran into this, and adding --no-heap-copy fixes it for me. Any chance this can be enabled by default when memory growth is enabled? --- [juj]: Very good find. I'm a bit surprised as to why I haven't run into this before, even though I've used these in conjunction a lot. Though I think I may have been passing a maximum size always, which probably reserves the address space up front and does not end up detaching the buffer, so this issue is avoided then. Proposed fix in above PR to use --no-heap-copy in that scenario. --- [ztl8702]: I encountered a situation where even with `--no-heap-copy` enabled this error can still happen. I was trying to port [`librime`](https://github.com/rime/librime), a C++ library to WebAssembly. In my particular use case, because the code was never optimised for the browser, it used a lot of memory (> 128MB). I initially compiled it with `-s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1` and observed the memory size grew 4 times, from 16MB to 256MB, doubling each time. `TypeError: attempting to access detached ArrayBuffer` occurred after the last growth. The codebase made use of `Boost.Interprocess`, and around the time that `TypeError` was thrown it was attempting to create a file mapping using Boost. The related code is: ``` file_.reset(new boost::interprocess::file_mapping(file_name.c_str(), file_mapping_mode)); region_.reset(new boost::interprocess::mapped_region(*file_, file_mapping_mode)); ``` ref: https://github.com/rime/librime/blob/8d8d2e6c2725041552bb17c787978cf319460d44/src/rime/dict/mapped_file.cc#L54 Below is part of the logs when the error happened. _I am looking for ways to reproduce this with in simpler codebase._ ![screenshot from 2018-03-18 03-16-50](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2714446/37557592-e155c1e8-2a5a-11e8-8f11-75596fe3dc9f.png) **Interestingly**, everything works fine when I added `-s TOTAL_MEMORY=256MB` to the compile options. So I think it likely has to do with memory growth. Software versions: ``` em++ 1.37.35 Firefox 59.0 (64-bit) Ubuntu 17.10 64-bit ``` --- [meldron]: Hey guys, so I had the same problem as @ztl8702 with opus/speedexdsp. The third memory growth failed: ``` enlarged memory arrays from 16777216 to 33554432, took 26 ms (has ArrayBuffer.transfer? false) enlarged memory arrays from 33554432 to 67108864, took 67 ms (has ArrayBuffer.transfer? false) OpusEncoderWorker.js:1 Uncaught TypeError: Cannot perform %TypedArray%.prototype.set on a detached ArrayBuffer ``` Software Versions. ``` emcc 1.37.33 & 1.37.39 Chrome 66.0.3359.139 Ubuntu 16.04 ``` So if I used `-s TOTAL_MEMORY=256MB`, everything works fine. Are there any drawbacks for using such a big `TOTAL_MEMORY`? --- [donthomasitos]: Same problem here. title: Usage of sigsetjmp/siglongjmp leads to undefined symbol references
body:
Currently, one may successfully compile a C source that references `sigsetjmp`/`siglongjmp` since they are defined in `include/libc/setjmp.h`:

```c
#if defined(_POSIX_SOURCE) || defined(_POSIX_C_SOURCE) \
 || defined(_XOPEN_SOURCE) || defined(_GNU_SOURCE) \
 || defined(_BSD_SOURCE)
typedef jmp_buf sigjmp_buf;
int sigsetjmp (sigjmp_buf, int);
_Noreturn void siglongjmp (sigjmp_buf, int);
#endif
```

But it leads to references to undefined symbols that crash program at run time:
```c
#include <setjmp.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    sigjmp_buf env;
    if(sigsetjmp(env, 1) == 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Jumping...\n");
        siglongjmp(env, 1);
    } else {
        fprintf(stderr, "Jumped.\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```
```
$ emcc test.c -o test.js
warning: unresolved symbol: siglongjmp
warning: unresolved symbol: sigsetjmp
$ node test.js
missing function: sigsetjmp
-1
-1
exception thrown: abort(-1) at Error
    at jsStackTrace (/tmp/bug/test.js:1125:13)
    at stackTrace (/tmp/bug/test.js:1142:12)
    at abort (/tmp/bug/test.js:9410:44)
    at _sigsetjmp (/tmp/bug/test.js:1775:54)
    at _main (/tmp/bug/test.js:1983:11)
    at Object.asm._main (/tmp/bug/test.js:9062:19)
    at Object.callMain (/tmp/bug/test.js:9284:30)
    at doRun (/tmp/bug/test.js:9348:60)
    at run (/tmp/bug/test.js:9362:5)
    at Object.<anonymous> (/tmp/bug/test.js:9436:1)

/tmp/bug/test.js:110
      throw ex;
      ^
abort(-1) at Error
    at jsStackTrace (/tmp/bug/test.js:1125:13)
    at stackTrace (/tmp/bug/test.js:1142:12)
    at abort (/tmp/bug/test.js:9410:44)
    at _sigsetjmp (/tmp/bug/test.js:1775:54)
    at _main (/tmp/bug/test.js:1983:11)
    at Object.asm._main (/tmp/bug/test.js:9062:19)
    at Object.callMain (/tmp/bug/test.js:9284:30)
    at doRun (/tmp/bug/test.js:9348:60)
    at run (/tmp/bug/test.js:9362:5)
    at Object.<anonymous> (/tmp/bug/test.js:9436:1)
```

According to `sigsetjmp`/`siglongjmp` man pages, they only differ from non-`sig` versions in predictable behavior considering signal masks. It looks like Emscripten currently does not support signals anyway, so they may be made just aliases to the non-`sig` versions.

I want to submit a PR and I think that since `setjmp` is some very low-level function that may be known to compiler, it may be worth just `#define`ing `sigsetjmp` to it somewhere in the headers (and adding test that `sizeof jmp_buf == sizeof sigjmp_buf`), but where is the right place: directly in the musl libc source code or somewhere in Emscripten-specific patches?
comments:
[kripken]: I worry a little that defining these could be confusing because we don't support signals. But I do see the point that it makes sense to implement them too. So probably fine to do this if it's useful.

If there is a good way to do it in the musl headers, that might be best. The optimal thing is if it could be done in our extra files for emscripten inside the musl headers. If it requires changes to core musl headers, if it's small enough maybe that's ok. Otherwise, another option is in fastcomp's setjmp handling pass to also detect sigsetjmp there, should be just a few lines.

---

[juj]: We do already implement deferred pthread cancellation. The same architecture could be used to implement support for deferred signal handling, i.e. cooperatively dispatch signals on the already defined thread cancellation points. I think this would be quite good enough for porting most signal using applications. This is not currently on the roadmap, but if you do want to submit PRs with implementation and tests towards this, those would be most welcome.

---

[atrosinenko]: Oh, I have probably incorrectly explained. Implementing signals was not on my roadmap too :) I just talked about implementing kind of no-op (with respect to signals) stub for `sigsetjmp` like stubs we currently have for `kill`, etc. Another option will probably be to **completely remove** definitions of unimplemented `sigsetjmp`/`siglongjmp` so configure script can detect their absence with more probability. And this should be much less confusing considering signal support.

---

[atrosinenko]: Implemented trivial stubs in #5295. I hope they will not confuse anyone since they should be explicitly enabled via `-D_EMSCRIPTEN_SIGLONGJMP_STUB`.

---

[atrosinenko]: I close this issue because although signals are still not implemented, the original issue was fixed in #5295 . The `multithreading` label can probably be dropped.

---

[juj]: Makes sense, thanks for the PR! I'll keep the multithreading label since they are often useful when I search for discussions that have related to a particular feature, so good to keep the label around.

title: 64-bit code generation
body:
https://github.com/WebAssembly/binaryen/issues/964#issuecomment-293648385 says that native 64-bit operations are possible when using the default (asm2wasm) backend. However, when generating standalone modules, function calls such as `getTempRet0` and `___muldi3` are emitted.

```
	emcc src/native/all.c \
	    --llvm-opts 3 \
	    -O3 \
	    -g4 \
	    -s "BINARYEN_TRAP_MODE='allow'" \
	    -s WASM=1 -s SIDE_MODULE=1 -o build/out.wasm
```

```c
int64_t test64(int64_t x, int64_t y)
{
    return x * y;
}
```

```
  (func $_test64 (type $t9) (param $p0 i32) (param $p1 i32) (param $p2 i32) (param $p3 i32) (result i32)
    (block $B0 (result i32)
      (set_local $p0
        (call $___muldi3
          (get_local $p2)
          (get_local $p3)
          (get_local $p0)
          (get_local $p1)))
      (set_local $p1
        (call $getTempRet0))
      (call $setTempRet0
        (get_local $p1))
      (get_local $p0)))
```

This is using `sdk-incoming-64bit` from emsdk.

title: llvm.round.f32/f64, libc round() and rint() rounding mode errors
body:
It looks like our implementation of rounding modes for each of `llvm.round.f32`, `llvm.round.f64`, libc `round()` family of functions and libc `rint()` family of functions are incorrect. Found out about this during LLVM 4.0.1 merge, which adds the `llvm.rint.f32/f64` intrinsic, and compilation began to route to using that one instead of musl `rint.c`. As a sidenote, musl `rint.c` implementation operates on non-canonical NaNs and it never worked properly either.

Searching through the specs, here's the official wordings:
 - `llvm.round.f32` & `llvm.round.f64`: https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#id508: `"This function returns the same values as the libm round functions would, and handles error conditions in the same way."

I was not able to find documentation of libm round functions, but I did find the following: [The GNU C Library (libc)](http://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Rounding-Functions.html): `"These functions are similar to rint, but they round halfway cases away from zero instead of to the nearest integer (or other current rounding mode). "`

 - `round`, `roundf`, `roundl`: [cplusplus.com](http://en.cppreference.com/w/c/numeric/math/round): `"1-3) Computes the nearest integer value to arg (in floating-point format), rounding halfway cases away from zero, regardless of the current rounding mode."`

so these implementations align with `llvm.round.f32/f64`.

 - Then, looking at `rint` at [cplusplus.com](http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/rint/): `"Rounds x to an integral value, using the rounding direction specified by fegetround."`, i.e. `rint` family is identical to `round` family, but this takes rounding mode into account. We don't have rounding modes implemented, so I want to make `rint()` behave according to what is the default musl rounding mode, which is `FE_TONEAREST`, or round-to-even (or banker's rounding).

The above is fixed in the LLVM 4.0.1 merge branch (#5400), which changes the LLVM intrinsic and `round` to operate away from zero, and fixes `rint` to round-to-even; however after that the one mode that remains is the emterpreter case, which is failing in test `asm2i.test_rounding`. @kripken: does emterpreter implement its math `round` intrinsic somehow differently?
comments:
[kripken]: The emterpreter doesn't have any special code for rounding. It should just do a normal call into a js library method for `_round` or such. Or do we now implement those in asm.js? If so then in theory this could have uncovered an emterpreter bug where it mistranslates the implementation code of rounding.

title: BREAKING EM_ASM API change
body:
See: https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/pull/6163

So there's no way to support EM_ASM in the LLVM wasm backend without compromising on one of the following:

1. No EM_ASM-specific knowledge in upstream LLVM
2. C support
3. No API changes

We're thinking of going with option 3. Specifically one of the following APIs:
A. `EM_ASM_idd(return $0 + $1 * $2, a, b, c)`
B. `EM_ASM(idd, return $0 + $1 * $2, a, b, c)`
C. `EM_ASM(return $0 + $1 * $2, idd, a, b, c)`
Additionally, we'll need to limit the number of arguments to a given call to EM_ASM to somewhere in the 4-6 range.

Asm.js and asm2wasm users should be unaffected. We can define the new APIs to convert to the existing EM_ASM APIs for users who use both backends (also our test suite).
But, the wasm backend will become the default backend, and at that time this will be a breaking change.

Questions:
Which API is best? (I have a slight preference for B.)
Should this wait for [EM_JS](https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/issues/6147) as a potential upgrade path? (Probably not, it's a sufficiently large restructuring that I'm not sure users will want to do it, unless you have too many arguments and need to)
comments:
[kripken]: Another option we maybe didn't look enough into is using the native inline asm functionality, which emscripten used to use but stopped because of escaping issues. Ignoring the escaping, this does keep all the important information in the bitcode, I believe, e.g.
```
int main() {
  int a = 10, b, c = 123;
  asm ("waka waka;"
       : "=r"(b)        /* output */
       : "r"(a), "r"(c) /* input */
       : "%eax"         /* clobbered register */
       );  
  return b;
}
``` => ```
define i32 @main() local_unnamed_addr #0 {
entry:
  %0 = tail call i32 asm "waka waka;", "=r,r,r,~{eax},~{dirflag},~{fpsr},~{flags}"(i32 10, i32 123) #1, !srcloc !2
  ret i32 %0
}
```
By wrapping `asm` with a macro, this might be about as good as EM_ASM is.

(One possible concern about this approach is I've heard people want to use `asm()` for literal inline wasm. I'm not sure how that could work exactly or why, but maybe there's a way to do both if we really want that.)

---

[juj]: > So there's no way to support EM_ASM in the LLVM wasm backend without compromising on one of the following:

Hmm, sorry if I missed the core idea on the other thread, but can you expand a bit on the root issue? In fastcomp backend we can neither support integer vs double input parameters, but all input parameters get casted to doubles/Numbers. So this means that `EM_ASM_VOID` is always of signature `vd*` (`*` here with the meaning of zero or more), `EM_ASM_INT` is a `id*`, and `EM_ASM_DOUBLE` is a signature `dd*`.

> `EM_ASM_idd(return $0 + $1 * $2, a, b, c)`

In here, can you touch a bit on what `idd` refers to - the usual convention has been that in these kind of signature strings, the first param would denote the return value, and the subsequent ones are the input parameters, but in this example I wonder if it was meant that `a` is an integer and `b` and `c` are doubles? Or was this intended to be a `iddd`, i.e. the three inputs are doubles, and the return is an integer that the computation would get casted to?

Since in fastcomp we are not able to support denoting the types of the input parameters either, but they're all elevated to doubles, I think we don't need to do that in wasm backend either for `EM_ASM`(?). The `_VOID`, `_INT` and `_DOUBLE` suffixes are able to label the return type of the macro, so that's the only bit of the signature we are able to specify.

Or is it the variadicity of the input arguments that is the problem, i.e. it's proving tricky to identify how many input parameters are coming in to the macro?

---

[jgravelle-google]: The problems are:
* We don't have any special handling for EM_ASM in the wasm backend, at all. (We would like to keep it that way, but that's one of the axes we can consider compromising on)
* The `em_asm_const_*` functions are called with the non-vararg calling convention, but the function prototype is variadic. With special backend handling this isn't a problem, but without that we lower the call into a variadic call, and stuff the parameters into a vararg buffer
* Once in a vararg buffer, by the time we see the code in binaryen we have lost all information about the arguments, so we can't do anything there.
* We also haven't converted the arguments to doubles, so they are either ints or floats, and we don't know which. C has no way to say "give me a vararg buffer of only doubles", so we need to inject that logic somewhere, only for EM_ASM.

The fundamental problem is that EM_ASM is nearly inexpressible in C, and relies on compiler magic to work. It's doable by using macros and templates to extract the type information in the frontend and preserve it in the runtime, but that has something near a 10x performance overhead. (https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/pull/6163) Which is another option to compromise on:
D. No API changes, 10x slowdown, don't use EM_ASM in tight loops

---

[curiousdannii]: I'd go with whichever option is simplest to implement. Library functions are always an option if performance matters.

---

[jgravelle-google]: > Library functions are always an option if performance matters.

Yeah I'm thinking that's the way to go. So for now the simplest then is to just land https://github.com/kripken/emscripten/pull/6163, and accept the performance hit. If that becomes a problem we can always break the API later.

Closing this for now.

```
$ wasm-dis 1.wasm | grep export
```

[dschuff]: What's the current difference between using `EMSCRIPTEN_KEEPALIVE` in the source vs exporting the function from the command line?

[kripken]: No difference, both export the function and keep it alive (the two concepts are not really differentiated, there was a proposal a while back to allow keeping something alive without exporting it, but it didn't get traction).

[Kagami]: WebAssembly studio [uses](https://github.com/wasdk/WebAssemblyStudio/blob/master/templates/empty_c/src/main.c)

Users can export functions either using the EXPORTED_FUNCTIONS commandline option, or EMSCRIPTEN_KEEPALIVE in the source; in both cases the user is expressing a request to export the function so the user can call it later. $ wasm2wat 1.wasm | grep export

[sbc100]: Ah yes, that is an artifact of how `.a` archives work.  Symbols that live in `.a` archives are only included if some symbol from the object file is needed by the linker, otherwise the entire `.o` file will not be included.

So in this case you would either need to:

a. Include the object file in question by referencing a symbol from it in your build
b. Use `--whole-archive`/ `--no-whole-archive` around the library to force the linker to include all objects.

But in that case there is no attribute that would help since the object file not being read at all (and therefore no symbol attributes are read).  The only solution that problem is to use something like `-Wl,--whole-archive`.. or to explicitly export the symbol on the command line.

If you are sure that `retain` did indeed have this effect then my only guess would be that something is happening in LTO maybe?  Where you using lto object files when you saw this effect?

[kg]: I'll do some more experimenting and see if I can figure out what's going on here if retain shouldn't be working and let you know if I figure it out, thanks.
