comments:
[Coolnesss]: After testing on GPU, if I set the batch size low enough it runs very fast, but anything over 2 and it runs out of memory (8gb GPU). How would I go about debugging the memory usage?

---

[soumith]: the backward pass of an unfold will involved a lot of atomicAdd CUDA instructions in the unfolded dimension. That is what slows down the backward a lot.

---

[Coolnesss]: Hey @soumith, thanks for your reply.

I notice that on GPU the backward pass runs fast but runs out of memory quickly. Do you have any tips on how to check what exactly is being allocated during the backward pass? `nvprof` hangs indefinitely if I run it with `--track-memory-allocations on`.

---

[t-vi]: > Do you have any tips on how to check what exactly is being allocated during the backward pass

I'd look at the [source](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/autograd/templates/Functions.cpp#L640-L652).

I think a better strategy could be to formulate the backward in terms of "source locations", so you'd take a pixel location in the forward's input and sum the gradient entries of the stencil locations where the that input has been mapped to. That should be both relatively efficient in terms of computation (because there won't be conflicting adds) and not need any memory. As a bonus you remove the non-determinism that atomicAdd brings. The disadvantage is that you can't just use unfold to get the indices to add from but have to calculate them yourself, but in 1d that should not be too hard.

---

[Coolnesss]: Hey Thomas, thanks for your reply. 

> The disadvantage is that you can't just use unfold to get the indices to add from but have to calculate them yourself, but in 1d that should not be too hard.

I suppose to calculate the indices one can't just use a for loop in the gradient function, as that wouldn't run on GPU?

---

[t-vi]: Well, if you work out the for loop that iterates over "all output entries y that input entry x will map to in unfold", it's easy to write that for loop in a CUDA kernel and run it in parallel on all your input coordinates.
Let's think about that a moment: So you have at most `ceil(size / step)` entries that any input entry maps to. The first (if any) is at `y = x//step`. Now you have to check `y = x//step ... x//step + ceil(size / step)` whether `y*step <= x < y*step+size`, if it is, add the `gradient_out` at position `y` to the input at `x`. Parallelize using the usual `for (x = threadIdx.x+blockIdx.x ; x < size ; x+= blocksize.x + gridsize.x)` (or so, I forget), and there is the cuda kernel for the backward.
You'd need to double check the above for correctness. Also, I haven't thought about the double backward, through with a bit of luck it's unfold again.

---

[Coolnesss]: @t-vi I could try to make a PR out of this. Do you guys have a guide or some example on how to build PT with the improved backward pass? I've built an extension that uses CUDA using the extensions API, but I guess the process is different for actual internal code.

---

[t-vi]: Thanks!
For general info, there is the [CONTRIBUTING document](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).
My suggestion would be:
- You'd have to write a new ATen function `unfold_backward`, actually `unfold_backward_cpu` and `unfold_backward_cuda`, probably. You can test those in an extension (that's what I usually do).
Also, I'd write two autogradFunctions `UnfoldFn` and `UnfoldBackwardFn` to see if gradcheck and gradgradcheck (use `UnfoldBackwardFn.apply` and `UnfoldFn.apply` in the backwards) work.
- Maybe `aten/src/ATen/native/TensorTransformations.cpp` and `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/TensorTransformations.cu` are good places for the function. Then add it to `native_functions.yaml` and edit `tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml` (and remove the old backward from `tools/autograd/templates/Functions.cpp`).
- See if you want new tests for it (e.g. test against the current torch_unfold ported back to Python in test/test_torch.py).

Does that make sense, approximately? Don't hesitate to post here if you need feedback or help (link to your git branch if you want to show code).

---

[Coolnesss]: Thanks for the pointers! I'll get to it by first making an extension and testing if it works against the current implementation.

---

[Coolnesss]: Hey, I've made some progress. I have some questions about how to proceed.

What I've done:
* Implemented the new CPU version in C++ for the case where the input is 1D. I've compared it to the existing version and it yields the same results in my tests.
* The algorithm is roughly 
   * Find the first occurence of the input element at index `i` in the output
   * Use some rules to find the next index `j` at which the element appears
   * Add the incoming gradient at index `j` to the outgoing gradient at index `i`

I plan to still:
* Get rid of division and modulo in the algorithm to make it faster
* Implement it in CUDA.

Questions:
* As far as I could tell, I need to know the dimensions of the data at compile time to be able to use accessors. I could create some sort of large if statement for the different input sizes, but it seems like a bad solution. Is there another way, or will I have to deal with strides, etc by using `.data()`?
* I'm a bit confused about the double backward part. Is there something specific that needs to be done in order to support it? Shouldn't it "just work" by calling backward twice?

Thanks for the help so far! Here is the code https://github.com/Coolnesss/unfold-backward/blob/master/unfold.cpp

---

[ezyang]: @Coolnesss awesome!

> As far as I could tell, I need to know the dimensions of the data at compile time to be able to use accessors. I could create some sort of large if statement for the different input sizes, but it seems like a bad solution. Is there another way, or will I have to deal with strides, etc by using .data()?

I'm not 100% familiar with the kernel you're writing. But if you're in a situation where you only care about indexing into, e.g., the last N dimensions (where N is constant), you can just reshape the tensor to have a fixed number of dimensions and then use accessor. Otherwise, you'll have to use one of our classes specifically for arbitrary dimension indexing (but I cannot remember the name right now)

> I'm a bit confused about the double backward part. Is there something specific that needs to be done in order to support it? Shouldn't it "just work" by calling backward twice?

If all operations in backwards are differentiable, it will just work. Otherwise, you'll need to write a derivative for the `unfold_backward` function you wrote.

---

[Coolnesss]: @t-vi, Now that I think about it, doesn't your method of calculating the indices by hand also involve atomicAdds when actually doing the addition? It occured to me that even if one calculates the indices by hand, there's a race condition when adding them since multiple indices of `grad` may point to a single index of `grad_input`. How does one deal with this, or have I misunderstood something?

---

[t-vi]: No, my proposal was to have all writes to one grad_input entry happen in the same thread. Then you don't need atomicAdd. So you'd parallelize the loop over `i` in your code and dimensions `!= dim` (which don't interact). Regarding the problem of Tesor-accessing the right thing: I guess you could either make the thing 3d (`reshape(everything_before_dim, dim, everything_after_dim)`) or do some offset manipulation for the other dimensions and just instantiate a 1-d tensor afterwards.

---

[Coolnesss]: I've made progress yet again. I have the CPU and CUDA implementations done, with the caveat that everything is for the 1D input case only. He's some preliminary benchmarks (on a single RTX 2070)

With the (arbitrarily chosen) parameters
```
input elements = 1e5
dim = 0
size = 10004
step = 3
```

Old backward:
20.4 ms ± 12.9 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
Peak memory usage 3.60 gb

New backward:
13.6 ms ± 15.4 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
Peak memory usage 1.20 gb

Next up:
* I believe I will need some help in handling the N-D input case. In the actual CUDA kernel I will have to deal with strides etc myself so what is the best way of implementing this? Actually I'm not too sure how to calculate the gradient in this case.
* The double backward needs to be written. I guess I have to write another kernel, but do I also write another `torch.autograd.function`? How does this work in terms of the extension?

---

[t-vi]: Good job!
- For the N-D case in cuda, one thing you can do is to mimic what [OffsetCalculator](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/cuda/detail/OffsetCalculator.cuh) does. Not in the sense of the actual computation, but pass in strides and sizes as arrays as fixed-size array (MAX_DIMS is 25 for OffsetCalculator). Then you can just multiply up the position from a linear index. (You could see if you can use OffsetCalculator itself for the initial offset. If not, the division-avoiding computation probably isn't as important.)
- I think you need to differentiate between 32 and 64 bit arithmetic. See e.g. batch norm for how to do that with ATen's utility function.
- I think the double backward is just fold again. To check this, define an `UnfoldBackwardFunction` and use that in the `FoldFunction` backward instead of calling unfold_backward directly. Then in the forward of the `UnfoldBackwardFunction` use the `unfold_backward` you have and in the backward use FoldFunction.apply again. Doing this consistently (i.e. making all indexing, looping use an `typename index_t` template parameter and specializing to int64_t or int32_t) might also give you a speed up in the 32bit case over mixing 32 and 64 bit indexing.

Later, you should probably change the checking etc to the C++ style of ATen.

---

[dangpzanco]: any update on this issue?

---

[ezyang]: paging @albanD who has been doing a lot of work on unfold recently

---

[nikitaved]: Any update? I could have a look at this one...

---

[albanD]: I don't think anyone is looking into this.
It most likely requires to write a specialized cuda kernel to replace the current implementation that call many different kernels.

---

[paplhjak]: I for one would appreciate it, as it would help tremendously with speed of training networks with spatially variant convolution kernels.

---

[nikitaved]: OK, them I will look into it as soon as I get time. Meanwhile, if someone interested, please, feel free to assign yourself!

---

[ngimel]: @paplhjak is it for cpu or gpu? Also it would be helpful if you provided some representative parameters for benchmarking.

---

[nikitaved]: All right, it seems like we have at most `floor((size - 1) / step)` overlaps in each slice with the right/left neighbor slice . Hence it is easy to tell whether a CUDA index might have a potential overlap with any other index in any slice of size `size`, call it a "problematic" index if there is an overlap. My plan of attack is to leave everything to operate over 1D tensors, as it is right now before `index_add`, but replace `index_add` with a kernel which performs a simple assignment for "good" indices, and an atomic add for "problematic" indices.

body:
## 🐛 Bug

On my computer (with GTX1080Ti, CUDA 10) and with today's master, I'm getting extremely slow (60 sec?) startup times. `sudo perf top` (thanks, @soumith) indicates that this is due ptx-jitting. Using NCCL seems to produce sm_30 assembly in the libcaffe2_gpu.so, which I don't get when not using NCCL.

Setting TORCH_CUDA_ARCH=6.1 doesn't help.

## To Reproduce

Compile from source on GTX1080Ti with CUDA 10. With USE_NCCL=1 vs with USE_NCCL=0.
Then initialize any cuda tensor.

title: Pytorch performance bug 18853

## 🐛 Bug

**Editorial note:** Make sure that you are not holding on to tensors via an exception object (which contains the stack trace and will retain tensors). Do not bring the exception object into scope, or do error recovery outside of the catch block.

Catching a RuntimeError on a CUDA OOM should allow one to gracefully recover, for example by lowering the batchsize. This is particularly important when using DistributedDataParallel, where workers must sync on backward, and so it's important that we be able to perform a "dummy batch" after an OOM in order to stay in sync with other workers.

Observed behavior during a CUDA out of memory event is inconsistent across nondistributed/dataparallel/distributeddataparallel. Expected behavior is that all modes should be able to recover easily.

It appears to be a leak in the autograd engine -- note that if you remove the `loss.backward()` line in @stephenroller's test case all the tests pass (except for ddp_multi which has a different error that also should be fixed).

Basically, if you're lucky and the OOM happens during forward it's recoverable. If it happens during backward() it leaks memory and is effectively unrecoverable. Unclear if this is a regression or also a bug in older versions of PyTorch.

I would suspect that some tasks live on in some of the Engine state. (Are the ready_queues empty after an error?)

#!/usr/bin/env python

#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --job-name=distributed_example
#SBATCH --partition=dev
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --time=0:10:00
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=10

import os
import argparse
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.distributed as td
import torch.nn.parallel as tp

START_BS = 8 * 1024

# these don't matter, just constants meant to be a "big" model
INPUT_SIZE = 8192
HID_SIZE = 4096
LAYERS = 8
OUT_CLASSES = 4


def wrap_dp(model):
    return tp.DataParallel(model)


def wrap_ddp_multi(model):
    td.init_process_group(
        backend='nccl',
        init_method='tcp://localhost:61337',
        rank=0,
        world_size=1
    )
    model = tp.DistributedDataParallel(
        model,
        device_ids=None,
        broadcast_buffers=False,
    )
    return model


def wrap_ddp_single(model):
    td.init_process_group(
        backend='nccl',
        init_method='tcp://localhost:61337',
        rank=0,
        world_size=1
    )
    model = tp.DistributedDataParallel(
        model,
        device_ids=[0],
        broadcast_buffers=False,
    )
    return model


def create_model(args):
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(INPUT_SIZE, HID_SIZE),
        nn.ReLU(),
    )
    for i in range(LAYERS):
        model.add_module('hidd' + str(i), nn.Linear(HID_SIZE, HID_SIZE))
        model.add_module('relu' + str(i), nn.ReLU())
    model.add_module('output', nn.Linear(HID_SIZE, OUT_CLASSES))
    return model


def fwbw(model, bs):
    print('  Forward with bs  = {:-6d}'.format(bs))
    X = torch.randn(bs, INPUT_SIZE).cuda()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    yhat = model(X)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    loss = yhat.sum()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print('  Backward with bs = {:-6d}'.format(bs))
    loss.backward()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    model.zero_grad()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()


def run_trial(args):
    print('Conda PREFIX:', os.environ['CONDA_PREFIX'])
    print('Torch version:', torch.version.__version__)
    print('CUDA version:', torch.version.cuda)

    model = create_model(args).cuda()
    if args.mode == 'dp':
        print('Wrapping in DataParallel')
        model = wrap_dp(model)
    elif args.mode == 'ddp_multi':
        print('Wrapping in DistributedDataParallel (equiv to 1 proc per node)')
        model = wrap_ddp_multi(model)
    elif args.mode == 'ddp_single':
        print('Using a single GPU in distributed (equiv to 1 proc per gpu)')
        torch.cuda.set_device(0)
        model = wrap_ddp_single(model)
    elif args.mode == 'single':
        print('Using a single GPU')
        pass
    else:
        raise ValueError('--mode wrong')

    bs = args.bs
    times_oomed = 0
    while times_oomed < args.ooms:
        # continuously double the batch size until we OOM
        try:
            print('Step bs=', bs)
            fwbw(model, bs)
            print('FW/BW succeeded. Doubling BS')
            bs *= 2
        except RuntimeError as rerr:
            if 'memory' not in str(rerr):
                # not the exception we wanted
                raise rerr
            # okay, we found the memory error! Now try to run a NOOP pass
            # for DDP nodes. Production example here:
            # https://github.com/pytorch/fairseq/blob/3658fa329b8cb987d951b2e38ec86c44b9e1fea5/fairseq/trainer.py#L361-L368
            times_oomed += 1
            print('OOM #{}! Running through a tiny batch to catch up worker'.format(times_oomed))
            fwbw(model, 2)
            print('Succeeded on the oom batch.')
            # start the doubling procedure again
            bs = args.bs


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument(
        '--mode', default='ddp', choices=('dp', 'ddp_multi', 'ddp_single', 'single'),
        help='DataParallel, DistributedDataParallel, or single gpu'
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        '--ooms', default=1, type=int,
        help='Number of times to OOM'
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        '--bs', default=START_BS, type=int,
        help='Initial batch size',
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()
    run_trial(args)
    print('Test passed.')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

> if oom:

Note that moving the OOM recovery logic outside of the `except` clause is not strictly necessary. The problem is that the exception (`rerr` here) also covers the traceback (`rerr.__traceback__`) which covers references to all the stack frames which covers references to all the local variables. But there is the function `traceback.clear_frames` which can remove those references. I.e. you could do this instead:

```python
import traceback

...

try:
    fwbw(model, bs)
    bs *= 2
except RuntimeError as rerr:
    if 'memory' not in str(rerr):
        # not the exception we wanted
        raise rerr
    # Got OOM.
    traceback.clear_frames(rerr.__traceback__)  # free locals
    # do recovery batch
```

Note, one thing to be careful about (and this is no matter whether you handle the OOM recovering inside or outside the `except` clause): Whenever you (or sth else, e.g. your debugger) accesses `tb_frame.f_locals` for any of the frames of the traceback, you might hit this CPython bug: https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/113939

In that case, it is tricky to free the references to any Torch tensors on the exception stack. Just calling `traceback.clear_frames(rerr.__traceback__)` is not enough. There is a tricky workaround to free the locals then: access `f_locals` again after the frame objects have been cleared, which potentially cleans up a previous copy of the locals (due to https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/113939). I.e. sth like this:
```python
tb = rerr.__traceback__
while tb:
    try:
        tb.tb_frame.clear()
    except RuntimeError:
        pass  # can happen if this still executing, e.g. the current frame
    else:
        # Using this code triggers that the ref actually goes out of scope, otherwise it does not!
        # https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/113939
        tb.tb_frame.f_locals  # noqa
    tb = tb.tb_next
```

## 🐛 Bug

PyTorch `1.1.0a0+c3e3c5c`. The GPU times reported are on a P100.

In this case matmul uses about 12 GB of memory when it shouldn't use more than ~3 MB. (i.e. it's using 4096x more memory than necessary)

#### A
```python
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096)
y = torch.randn(192, 4096, 1)
z = torch.matmul(x, y)
```

Note that this is equivalent to the following memory efficient operation:


#### B
```
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096)
y = torch.randn(192, 4096, 1)
z = torch.bmm(x.unsqueeze(0).expand(192, *x.shape), y)
```

It's also equivalent to the following which is memory efficient and faster, but may require a copy of y and the output may be batched-column-major without some extra work:

#### C
```
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096)
y = torch.randn(192, 4096, 1)
z = torch.matmul(y.permute(0, 2, 1), x.t()).permute(0, 2, 1)
```

On GPU, **A** takes ~125 ms and uses 12 GB of memory, **B** takes ~22 ms, and **C** takes ~1 ms.

Originally https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/unexpected-huge-memory-cost-of-matmul/41642/4

See also https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/13222 which may be related

----

I believe the problem is the unnecessary contiguous call here:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/15b318de840de61e2e789c013e34d23819715090/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebra.cpp#L460-L461

Instead of using `contiguous()` and `view()` it may be possible to use `reshape()`. That might achieve performance of **B**.

`The non-matrix (i.e. batch) dimensions are broadcasted (and thus must be broadcastable).`

So shouldn't the matrix dimensions be left untouched?

[skrah]: Probably I'm using `NumPy` terminology here (there is an explicit outer loop).  In this case the "broadcasting" just seems to happen internally before the operation, but the comment at the top of the function refers to the result dimensions. I have to take a closer look.

title: Pytorch performance bug 1963
body:
I think I encountered a memory leak situation potentially due to `expand_as`. I create a [gist](https://gist.github.com/zihangdai/5d4b6fa96ce1366f5bc7268fee0d4e9f) to reproduce my observations.

Basically, for three different (meaningless) models, once the `expand_as` function is used, the memory usage will keep increasing. 

To run the code, `python mem_leak_expand.py --run_expand --model_type [0,1,2]` where the `--run_expand` flag controls whether `expand_as` is used. Please run it long enough. 

I'm on Ubuntu 14.04 with python3.6. I tried two versions of pytorch, 0.1.12_2 and 0.1.12+da0fad8. 

**Side Note**: Even without using `expand_as`, the memory usauge can also increase for a while, but it will finally stablize at a level. What's more, when `Conv2d` (i.e. `--model_type [1,2]`) is used, it can take very long before the memory usage stablizes. I'm not sure whether this is a problem or not.
comments:
[zihangdai]: I think I'm sure there is a memory leak due to `expand_as`, and I found a weird way to do a temporary fix under pytorch version "0.1.12_2". 

The simplest example is as follows:

    tgt_var = Variable(torch.rand(32, 512))

        if args.fix:

        else:
            expanded = src_var.expand_as(tgt_var)

        if args.backward:
            ret.mean().backward()

        gc.collect()
        if i > 0 and i % 500 == 0:
            max_mem_used = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
            print("#{} {:.4f} MB".format(i, max_mem_used / 1024))

    main(args)
```

Basically, if we replace `expand_as` with `expand`, and pass in an unpacked list of numbers, (i.e., `src_var.expand(*list(tgt_var.size()))` instead of `src_var.expand(tgt_var.size())`), the memory leak is gone. Using `src_var.expand(tgt_var.size())` will also have the leak issue. Unfortunately, I don't know why this is working. 

Finally, since there are so many `expand_as` in pytorch code, to do a quick hacky fix, one can change the `expand_as` function in the file `torch/autograd/variable.py` as follows:
```python
    def expand_as(self, tensor):                                                                                                                            
        return Expand(list(tensor.size()))(self)
        # return Expand(tensor.size())(self)
```

---

[zihangdai]: After some more research, I think we have a much bigger problem here. My current conjecture is that: whenever we use `tensor.size()` (`torch.Size` object) as an argument to a function, there will be a memory leak. 

An example is the `pad_packed_sequence` function in `torch/nn/utils/rnn.py`, where [line 107](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/utils/rnn.py#L107) of the code is `output = var_data.data.new(len(batch_sizes), max_batch_size, *var_data.size()[1:]).zero_()` which uses `*var_data.size()`. 

Again, a minimal example for reproduction is as follows:

```python
from __future__ import print_function, division
import gc
import argparse
import resource

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Variable

import torch.nn.utils.rnn as rnn_utils

def main(args):
    max_len = 8
    hid_dim = 16
    batch_s = 4
    model = nn.GRU(hid_dim, hid_dim)
    for i in range(args.num_steps):
        
        embedding = Variable(torch.rand(max_len, batch_s, hid_dim))
        lengths = range(max_len, max_len-batch_s, -1)
        
        packed_emb = rnn_utils.pack_padded_sequence(embedding, lengths)
        packed_out, hidden_final = model(packed_emb)
        outputs, srclens = rnn_utils.pad_packed_sequence(packed_out)

        if args.backward:
            outputs.mean().backward()

        gc.collect()
        if i > 0 and i % 500 == 0:
            max_mem_used = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
            print("#{} {:.4f} MB".format(i, max_mem_used / 1024))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='PyTorch *tensor.size() memory leak')
    parser.add_argument('--num_steps', type=int, default=1000000)
    parser.add_argument('--backward', action='store_true', default=False)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    main(args)
```

As in the `expand_as` case, once I change the code to `output = var_data.data.new(len(batch_sizes), max_batch_size, *list(var_data.size())[1:]).zero_()`, memory leak is gone. 

So, in short, the problem is on the usage of `tensor.size()`.

We finally root the cause to theses change: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/utils/data/dataloader.py#L889-L891. It causes the exit of each epoch has additional 5 seconds.

title: Pytorch performance bug 24080
body:
We have noticed some differences in calculating the num_threads to spawn in different ATen Parallel backends, which, as far as we have observed, may lead to degraded performance of OpenMP backend under some circumstances.

In the OpenMP version:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e327df396564f937d17b5f28e2529229260c65bf/aten/src/ATen/ParallelOpenMP.h#L28
The logic seems to be: either do not parallel at all (if num < grain_size), or spawn as many as omp_get_max_threads() threads.

In other backends, e.g. Native:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e327df396564f937d17b5f28e2529229260c65bf/aten/src/ATen/ParallelNative.h#L41-L44
The logic is likely something as: min(get_num_threads(), num / grain_size).

We noticed this problem because after upgrading our PyTorch (>= 1.1.0 in our experince), the DataLoader, with pin_memory=True, is saturating our 36C/72T cpus even with some very small datasets (CIFAR10, resize=32, batch_size=40) and with num_threads=1, however, with no significant training speed boost. Further investigation shows that the copy operation to the pinned memory behaves very differently between two releases. After looking at the code we conjecture that this is due to the overhead that OMP tries to spawn an unecessarily large number of threads for small CPU Tensors.

We installed both PyTorch from conda so we are not absolutely certain about the build options. However we provide some code snippets that may possibly reveal the aformentioned problem:

1. Simple comparisons on copy operation:

``` python

import torch
print(torch.__version__)
from tqdm import tqdm

N = int(argv[1])

a, b = [torch.randn([N]) for _ in (0, 1)]

  b.copy_(a)
```

``` bash

```

> 1000000it [00:08, 123182.80it/s]
> 
> real    0m9.168s
> user    0m33.244s
> sys     0m0.194s

``` bash

```

> 1.0.1.post2
> 1000000it [00:53, 18525.88it/s]
> 
> real    0m55.207s
> user    0m54.584s
> sys     0m0.182s

```

> 1.0.1.post2
> 1000it [00:18, 54.57it/s]
> 
> real    0m19.421s
> user    0m19.192s
> sys     0m0.195s

It shows that the cpu usage of copying a 32768-sized Tensor drastically increase to approx. 3600% compared to approx. 100% for a 32767-sized Tensor. Although there was indeed some performance gain, it is only comparable to that when OMP_NUM_THREADS is limited to 4.
In 1.0.1, there is no such problem for a much larger Tensor (of size 10M), although the performance was worse than 1.1.0 given the same size.

2. Data Loading test
``` python

import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

class Dummy(Dataset):

  def __len__(self):
    return 1000000

    return torch.zeros([3, 32, 32])

loader = DataLoader(Dummy(), num_workers=int(argv[1]), pin_memory=int(argv[2]), batch_size=int(argv[3]))
loader = iter(loader)
next(loader)
print(torch.__version__)
for _, im in tqdm(enumerate(loader)):
  pass
```

> 

``` bash

```

> 1.1.0
> 99999it [01:09, 1439.45it/s]
>

> user    1m37.910s
> sys     0m39.113s


``` bash

```

> 1.1.0
> 90909it [00:58, 1551.88it/s]
> 
> real    1m3.575s
> user    1m26.514s
> sys     0m34.365s

We could observe that: 1) Dataloader with pin_memory=True and num_workers=1 leads to approx. 7200% cpu usage, and most time is in sys, and real speed is slower; 2) operations that avoid the multi-threaded copy (disable pin_memory, reduce batch_size or set 
 OMP_NUM_THREADS) could reduce the cpu usage, indicating that the problem is very possibly related to the copy operation.

However we have not yet submitted any PR for this, because we are not sure e.g. whether this is some side-effect of more important 'features', or whether the team is planning for a refactoring of the relevant code, etc. If it does need a fix, we are happy to provide one.

[linziyi96]: I'm sorry the description is kind of overwhelming... Trying to be clear:

1) The direct problem is that DataLoader with pin_memory=True in 1.1.0 is using all cpu cores at 100%. That interferes with the other programs on the same machine. But when the program is consuming small batches (CIFAR10, 40 * 3 * 32 * 32) at moderate speed (~20 batch / second). I assume loading such data does not need 72 cores running at full speed ...

So it would seem the performance regression is caused by a bug fix.

>In a more general consideration, will a gradual increase of num_threads based on input size (instead of either 1 or all) still benefit in some systems with many cpu cores? (as what's done in the Native backend)

I think this is the best solution, it's even in agreement with the comment on `GRAIN_SIZE`:
>no parallel algorithm (such as parallel_reduce) should split work into smaller than GRAIN_SIZE chunks.

title: Pytorch performance bug 24200
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Calling `torch.tensor` on a Python `list` of `np.float32` objects leaks memory.

## To Reproduce

```
import numpy as np
import torch

def mem():
	import os, psutil
	return psutil.Process(os.getpid()).memory_info().rss // 1024

a = np.zeros(10000, dtype = np.float32) # <-- 1. dtype is important
a = list(a) # <-- 2. has to be a python list

mem_base = mem()
for _ in range(10):
	torch.tensor(a) # <-- 3. must not pass `dtype=torch.float32` here
	print(mem() - mem_base)

# output on my machine:
# 1416
# 2884
# 3940
# 4996
# 6316
# 7372
# 8428
# 9484
# 10804
# 11860
```

## Expected behavior

The number being printed (memory usage) should be more or less constant.

## Environment

 - PyTorch Version: 1.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.2.0
 - OS (e.g., Linux): Linux
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): pip
 - Python version: 3.6.8

## Additional context

On pytorch==0.4.1, `torch.tensor(a)` throws:
```
RuntimeError: Could not infer dtype of numpy.float32
```

Also, this might be the underlying bug in [#17499](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/17499).

### How this shows up in real code

This shows up in real code if you have a 1d array in a dataset:

```
class Dataset:
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.X = x; self.y = y
    
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.X[i], self.y[i] # <-- self.y[i] is a np.float32
    
    def __len__(self):
        return self.X.shape[0]
```

`self.y[i]` is a `np.float32`, and in 1.2.0, a batch of these get wrapped in a `list` by `_MapDatasetFetcher`, and `default_collate` calls `torch.as_tensor` on it.

title: Pytorch performance bug 25010
body:
## 🐛 Bug
There seems to be an issue with CPU utilization when using a DataLoader with pin_memory=True and num_workers > 0. 

I revisited some old code that had `pin_memory=True` and two workers that weren't doing all that much. It pinned all of my CPU cores at or near 100%, with 40-50% of the usage in the kernel.  I've had performance issues with pinned memory in the past, but never to this level. Indeed, I cannot reproduce the issue going back to some older environments with 0.4 or 1.0.1. But on 3 machines w/ PyTorch 1.1 and 1.2 I can easily reproduce by running the MNIST main.py from the current examples master.

If I set either num_workers=0 or pin_memory=False the issue goes away and I'm left with the expected one core and change of usage for MNIST (or two cores and change for my original case). 

## To Reproduce

1. Run `main.py` from the MNIST example on master pytorch/examples repository.

## Expected behavior

For MNIST, with 1 worker I expect roughly 1 core's worth of CPU utilization plus some overhead. It consumes 50-100% of all cores on systems with 8-14 physical (16-28 logical) cores. A large % of the CPU usage is in the kernel, appears to be spinning/yielding, possibly due to contention. 

## Environment

I've reproduced on 3 machines.

 - PyTorch Version (e.g., 1.0): 1.1 and 1.2 (no issue on an older 1.0.1 and 0.4.1 environment on one of the machines)
 - OS (e.g., Linux): two Ubuntu 18.04 machines, one Ubuntu 16.04 machine

title: Pytorch performance bug 28370
body:
See repro below:

```python
import torch

def run(val):
    print("Running :", val)
    weights = torch.rand(100, 64, requires_grad=True)
    inp = torch.rand(val).mul(100).long()
    with torch.no_grad():
        torch.embedding_renorm_(weights, inp, 1.0, 2)
    print("This should be None: ", weights.grad_fn)

run(1000)
run(1001)
```
Outputs:
```
Running : 1000
This should be None:  None
Running : 1001
This should be None:  <CopySlices object at 0x7f02faa5e7a8>
```

Current supposition is that multi-threaded operations and thread local NoGradGuard could be problematic.

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @jerryzh168 @SsnL @albanD @gqchen @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel @mruberry
comments:
[albanD]: ## Identification of the current problem
So the problem is that `parallel_for` does not propagate thread local states into the thread pool it uses.
The problematic states here are the `GradMode::enabled` and wether or not to unwrap variables during dispatch.
Indeed, in the original function, we work with Tensors and GradMode is disabled. While in some of the worker threads, we now work with Variables and with GradMode enabled.

But after a quick look, others could be leading to unexpected behavior as well like
- `in_parallel_region_` used to check whether we are already in a parallel region, worker threads could actually re-spawn more threads in some cases?
- many jit stuff
- cuda current streams

## Main question

Is `parallel_for` supposed to be usable with Tensors. And so running operations on Tensors in each worker thread should do the same thing?
Or is `parallel_for` supposed to work only with pointers of raw data: Tensors should be unpacked before and only pointers should be passed to it?

## Proposed answer

After discussion, the main point is that making `parallel_for` work with Tensor operations is actually a big feature (as in a lot of work).
So for now we can fix this function to remove the use of Tensors and add a comment with `parallel_for` to let the user know that they should unpack all Tensors before doing operations.
We can open a new feature request for support of Tensors in `parallel_for`.

Any thoughts @ifedan @ngimel @VitalyFedyunin @ezyang  ?

---

[gchanan]: > After discussion, the main point is that making parallel_for work with Tensor operations is actually a big feature.

This statement is a bit ambiguous to me.  By big feature, do you mean "a lot of work" or "an important feature"?

---

[albanD]: @gchanan sorry, I meant "a lot of work". Updated above.
In particular, it would require for it to work and be sustainable to have a common way of using thread_local across the code base. Both to ensure that this actually works in all corner cases and that when new thread_local variables are added, this does not break.

---

[gchanan]: This analysis looks correct -- I'd file an issue about collecting the thread_locals across the code base to support that kind of thing.

I have a lazy loop that is used to evaluate the model. This version doesn't use any noticeable memory (memory_allocated < 1Gb):
```python
def apply_model(data_loader, model):

        yield log_probs
```

The context manager version:

@torch.no_grad()

    print('memory_allocated', torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1e9, 'memory_cached', torch.cuda.memory_cached() / 1e9)

        log_probs, output_lengths, loss = map(model(x, xlen, y = y, ylen = ylen).get, ['log_probs', 'output_lengths', 'loss'])
        yield log_probs
```

[peterbell10]: The decorator `torch.no_grad` effectively creates a new function:
```python

    with torch.no_grad():
        return apply_model(*args, **kwargs)

title: Pytorch performance bug 31690
body:
## 🐛 Bug

A `nn.ConvTranspose2d` can be up to two orders of magnitude slower when the `output_padding` option is set to a nonzero value then when it isn't.

## To Reproduce

```
class Test(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, output_padding):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.c1 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c3 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 3, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.c1(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c2(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c3(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        return x

def test(output_padding):
    network = Test(output_padding=output_padding).cuda()
    x = torch.rand((1028, 128, 6, 6)).cuda()


    for i in range(5):
        start = time.time()
        for i in range(10):
            network(x)
        print((time.time() - start) / 10)

test((0, 0))
test((1, 1))
```

On my V100 machine, I get timings of about 0.0004s per forward pass with `output_padding=(0, 0)` and about .05s with `output_padding=(1, 1)`.

## Expected behavior

Given that the `output_padding` option has minimal effect on the number of FLOPs required to compute the function, I would expect the computation time to be similar with and without the option.

A simple proof is this patch (demonstration only): https://github.com/CaoZhongZ/pytorch/pull/1 apply it and the leak goes away. Performance degradation will also be relieved.

[CaoZhongZ]: Confirmed the leakage was resulted by GOMP thread number thrashing, more threads more significant of the leakage. I changed the test script to isolate the problem solely to thread numbers. https://github.com/MichaelLutter/pytorch_debugging/pull/2 (with patch https://github.com/CaoZhongZ/pytorch/pull/1)

So I think that's the conclusion. Further investigation should put into why GOMP leak memory.

---

[imaginary-person]: > The parallel region created by the code throttled number of OpenMP threads to 2 (num_threads) in our testcase. We could observe exiting of 126 threads at the end of the block

Hello @CaoZhongZ, A `num_threads` clause isn't supposed to make the rest of the threads exit.
Were you able to figure out why they were exiting?

@milutter has deleted his PyTorch debug repo. Do you still happen to have the test scripts?
They'd be of great help!
Thank you!

---

[milutter]: Sorry, I wasnt aware that this was still of any use. When cleaning my repos, I did not remember the use case of the repo and deleted it. However, I found a local copy on my machine and uploaded it again at:
https://github.com/milutter/pytorch_debugging

---

[imaginary-person]: Thanks a lot for your help, @milutter! :)
I've copied those files. I'm not a PyTorch team member, but had requested those scripts for my own edification.
Have a nice weekend!

---

[imaginary-person]: @peterbell10, I've verified that even in the erstwhile `libgomp` version, the `num_threads` clause doesn't cause some threads to exit.
Moreover, unlike the current implementation, in which [the threads of the OpenMP thread pool are created when the first parallel operation is invoked](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/37461/files#r416935580), in PyTorch 1.4.0, more threads are added to the thread-pool when required, so only one more OpenMP thread was being created in the test-script, hence the total of 2 OpenMP threads in `at::parallel_for`. So, how can 126 threads exit if OpenMP only had 2?
 
Correlation doesn't necessarily imply causation, so while making the OpenMP thread-pool fixed-sized fixed the issue, I believe another factor would've been responsible for the 126 threads that @CaoZhongZ reported as exiting. @CaoZhongZ also mentioned MKL creating & destroying threads, [which has caused similar issues in the past as well,
but they are supposed to be fixed](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/13757#issuecomment-437472174).
So, it'd be great if we can figure out how to reproduce this issue, as I couldn't do so with the given information.

---

[imaginary-person]: In PyTorch 1.4.0, the threads of the OpenMP thread-pool were actually created when desired. For instance, only one additional OpenMP thread was created for the following snippet of code:
```
import torch
torch.eye(252)
```
On the other hand, the current implementation creates the threads of the OpenMP thread pool before any parallel operation is done, so it'd create threads equal to the number of physical cores (eg. 32 on a machine with 32 physical cores), but use only 2 for this snippet.

---

[imaginary-person]: I tried in vain to reproduce this issue with 3 PyTorch 1.4.0 builds on two processors with 20 & 32 physical cores respectively, both running on Ubuntu 18.04:

1. PyTorch 1.4.0 from Conda. It installed Intel MKL & Intel OpenMP with it.
2. PyTorch 1.4.0 from PIP. It uses libgomp.
3. PyTorch 1.4.0 built from the `release/1.4.0` branch. Intel MKL 2019.3-199 was used for the build.

The test scripts do matrix multiplication 100k times. One extra OpenMP thread is added to the thread pool, which, as expected, only exits at the end of the program, and not between each iteration of the matrix-multiplication. This can be verified with `gdb` by setting `breakpoints` for `pthread_create`, `pthread_exit`, & `exit`.

---

[imaginary-person]: @peterbell10 reported that this issue reproduced even without MKL on an AMD machine with the master branch's code and dynamic scaling (not assigning wasteful work to some OpenMP threads) enabled. 
However, I couldn't reproduce it with this issue's test-script, but with @peterbell10's code snippet:
```
import torch
import tqdm

a = torch.zeros((8, 256, 256))
for _ in tqdm.trange(10000):
    a[0].fill_(1)
    a.fill_(0)
```

I reproduced it on a 64-core AMD EPYC 7542 , Ubuntu 18.04, gcc 7.5.0/gcc 8.4.0/gcc 10.1 with dynamic scaling (not assigning wasteful work to some OpenMP threads) & the master branch's source-code. 
I could also reproduce the issue @peterbell10 alluded to on an Intel Xeon machine.

As for the issue reported by @peterbell10, threads are not exiting at the end of the `#pragma omp parallel` block but when `#pragma omp parallel` is reached in subsequent calls to `at::parallel_for`. This issue is not happening in the execution of simple `num_threads` example programs.**

**Scenario:**
1. `at::parallel_for` creates other threads in the OpenMP thread pool when a parallel region is entered.
2. These threads do NOT exit at the end of the OpenMP block.
3. `at::parallel_for `is invoked again.
4. While entering the parallel region for a subsequent op, the threads created in the previous invocation of `at::parallel_for` in step 1 exit, and new ones are created. 

I need more info before submitting a bug report.

---

[imaginary-person]: @CaoZhongZ, can you please confirm on what platform you had managed to reproduce this issue?
I see that @emfomenk & you work at Intel, so I'm confused about what platform you debugged this issue on.
I could only reproduce this issue on an AMD machine but not Intel Xeon machines.
Thank you!

[mingfeima]: @hl475 I do witness performance regression for certain configuration of inputs after switching a similar CPU. On particular, the following two are most serious:
* cat_M128_N1024_K2_dim1_cpu
* cat_M512_N512_K2_dim1_cpu

The performance regression should have come from in-efficient use of L1 cache. In the **PT OP Benchmark**, the input tensor list of [cat_test.py](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/benchmarks/operator_benchmark/pt/cat_test.py#L44) is actually the same tensor, e.g. [input_one, input_one].

In the old TH implementation, when iterating the length of the input tensor list, each inner line of `input_one` will be loaded only once and cached in L1 (size here is 1024 * 2 * 4 bytes).
However in #30806, the TensorIterator will copy the input tensors one after another, thus `input_one` will be loaded multiple times.

Anyway, I will provide a patch to make a fast path for such kind of scenario.

title: Pytorch performance bug 33647

title: Pytorch performance bug 34714
body:
## 🐛 Bug

When sampling from a torch.distributions.Categorical distribution initialized with a few distributions (e.g. 2 distributions each with 2**16 categories) the sample() functions allocates unnecessary huge amount of memory.

## To Reproduce
```
import torch 
p = torch.ones([2, 2**16], device='cuda:0')
dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(p)
dist.sample([2**16])
```


Output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../lib/python3.7/site-packages/IPython/core/interactiveshell.py", line 3326, in run_code
    exec(code_obj, self.user_global_ns, self.user_ns)
  File "<ipython-input-2-c4f33ee0a190>", line 4, in <module>
    dist.sample([2**16])
  File ".../lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/distributions/categorical.py", line 106, in sample
    probs_2d = probs.reshape(-1, self._num_events)
RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 32.00 GiB (GPU 0; 1.95 GiB total capacity; 1024.00 KiB already allocated; 1.15 GiB free; 2.00 MiB reserved in total by PyTorch)

## Expected behavior

Looking into the torch.distributions.Categorical source shows:
```
    def sample(self, sample_shape=torch.Size()):
        sample_shape = self._extended_shape(sample_shape)
        param_shape = sample_shape + torch.Size((self._num_events,))
        probs = self.probs.expand(param_shape)
        probs_2d = probs.reshape(-1, self._num_events)
        sample_2d = torch.multinomial(probs_2d, 1, True)
        return sample_2d.reshape(sample_shape)
```
The last three lines allocate the new memory and use it. probs_2d becomes a potentially huge tensor with repeated information. 
The following code snippet solves it and uses much less memory, but I'm not sure it covers all cases and whether the order of the dimensions is as expected. It's not thoroughly tested.
```
    def sample(self, sample_shape=torch.Size()):
        if not isinstance(sample_shape, torch.Size):
            sample_shape = torch.Size(sample_shape)
        samples = torch.multinomial(self.probs, sample_shape.numel(), True)
        return samples.reshape([-1] + list(sample_shape))
```







cc @vincentqb @fritzo @neerajprad @alicanb @vishwakftw @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel
comments:
[agolynski]: Thank you for the through diagnostic and code sample!

---

[neerajprad]: @jjabo - I think one issue is that the `probs` argument to `Categorical` can be batched (n-dimensional where n > 2, the last dim is taken as the event dim), whereas the argument to `multinomial` has to be 1 or 2D. I think the issue with the current code is the `expand` step which in this case expands probs to have shape more than `2**16 x 2**16`! I think we should be able to use your solution to work for the batched case too as follows:

```python
    def sample(self, sample_shape=torch.Size()):
        probs_2d = self.probs.reshape(-1, self._num_events)
        samples_2d = torch.multinomial(probs_2d, sample_shape.numel(), True).T
        return samples_2d.reshape(self._extended_shape(sample_shape))
```

Does that work on your test case?

---

[jjabo]: @neerajprad - The code you posted crashes for me with
 _AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'numel'_
since I give a list to sample_shape (is that wrong usage)? If I change your code to:
```python
    def sample(self, sample_shape=torch.Size()):
        if not isinstance(sample_shape, torch.Size):
             sample_shape = torch.Size(sample_shape)
        probs_2d = self.probs.reshape(-1, self._num_events)
        samples_2d = torch.multinomial(probs_2d, sample_shape.numel(), True).T

```
it works.
One peculiarity though is that the batch dimensions become the last dimensions of the output, e.g if I create categorical with probs.shape = [B,X] and call sample(sample_shape=[500]) the output has shape [500, B]. Is that as it should be? Shouldn't it be [B, 500]?

------+--------------+-------------+------------
shape = sample_shape + batch_shape + event_shape
```

title: Pytorch performance bug 34964
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Gradient update with `parameter.add_(val, grad)` of sparse matrices results in a memory leak that is not present in dense matrices with the same computation.

Freeing cache/calling the garbage collector does not remove the problem. The result of the computation is the same for both the sparse and the dense networks. The backward pass without an update of the matrix does not cause this problem.

## To Reproduce

Take a network that computes `||Wx||_F^2` with either a dense or a sparse `W` and minimize it. The part that produces the bug is
```
with torch.no_grad():
    net.weights.add_(-lr, net.weights.grad)
```
(Updating `net.weights.data` without in-place operations results in the same behaviour)

#### Steps to reproduce the behavior:
Imports and printing functions. The script prints the currently allocated tensors and the memory stats **after** zeroing the gradient.
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import gc

def print_stats(i):
    print('\nIteration %d' % i)
    print('Resources:')
    for obj in gc.get_objects():  # as in https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/how-to-debug-causes-of-gpu-memory-leaks/6741/2
        try:
            if torch.is_tensor(obj) or (hasattr(obj, 'data') and torch.is_tensor(obj.data)):
                print('\t', type(obj), obj.size())
        except:
            pass

    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Allocated', torch.cuda.memory_allocated(device) // 1024 ** 2))
    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Max allocated', torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated(device) // 1024 ** 2))
    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Cached', torch.cuda.memory_cached(device) // 1024 ** 2))
    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Max cached', torch.cuda.max_memory_cached(device) // 1024 ** 2))
```
The sparse and the dense networks are the same, but the first one uses a sparse `W` and `torch.sparse.mm(W,x)` instead of dense `W`/`torch.mm(W,x)` (`W` is `1 x n`):
```
def make_sparse_weights(input_length):
    values = torch.ones(input_length, dtype=torch.float)
    indices = torch.tensor([[0, i] for i in range(input_length)], dtype=torch.long).t()
    return torch.sparse.FloatTensor(indices, values, size=(1, input_length))


class SparseNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_length):
        super().__init__()
        self.weights = nn.Parameter(make_sparse_weights(input_length),
                                    requires_grad=True)

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.norm(torch.sparse.mm(self.weights, x)) ** 2


class DenseNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_length):
        super().__init__()
        self.weights = nn.Parameter(make_sparse_weights(input_length).to_dense(), 
                                    requires_grad=True)

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.norm(torch.mm(self.weights, x)) ** 2
```
The script does plain SGD with an option to free cache/collect garbage after zeroing the gradient:
```
def run_net(net, x, lr, device, n_iterations, 
            update_weight=True, empty_cache=False, collect_garbage=False):
    for i in range(n_iterations):
        # free the gradients and print resources

        if net.weights.grad is not None:
            net.weights.grad.detach_()
            net.weights.grad.zero_()

        if empty_cache:
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        if collect_garbage:
            gc.collect()

        if i % 1000 == 0:
            print_stats(i)

        # compute
        loss = net(x)
        loss.backward()

        # update
        if update_weight and net.weights.grad is not None:
            # the SGD implementation with p.data.add_() 
            # throws an error and suggests this solution:

            with torch.no_grad():
                net.weights.add_(-lr, net.weights.grad)

        if i % 1000 == 0:
            print('Loss: %f' % loss.item())
```

title: Pytorch performance bug 3498
body:
Here is an example of what seems to be a memory leak in pytorch, although it could be numpy?

```
import numpy as np
import gc
import resource
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Variable

model = nn.Linear(100, 2)

i = 0
while True:
    i += 1

    np_arr = np.ones(100).astype(np.float32)
    tensor = torch.from_numpy(np_arr[None]) # Issue seems to be use of [None] or [np.newaxis]
    variable = Variable(tensor)
    output = model(variable)

    if i % 1000 == 0:
        gc.collect()
        max_mem_used = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
        print("{:.2f} MB".format(max_mem_used / 1024))
```

The leak was only occurring when using the `[None]` or `[np.newaxis]` array unsqueezing methods in numpy. Also worth noting that the issue is resolved by removing the `.astype(np.float32)` from `np_arr` and casting the torch tensor to `float()` type.

An easy workaround is to reshape the array after turning it into a torch Tensor.

title: Pytorch performance bug 36120
body:
## 🐛 Bug

<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. -->
This PR https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/33427 tries to avoid clone for sparse tensors during accumulation of grads. However, `at::sparse_coo_tensor` performs value checks on input values which are very slow. It defeats the goal of avoiding clones to make it faster.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Running the following code in 1.4 and master
```python
from time import time
import torch

def main():
  batch_size = 2048
  num_features = 100000
  query_nnz = 100
  embed_size = 64

  ref_embedding = torch.nn.Embedding(num_features, embed_size, sparse=True).cuda()

  indices = torch.randint(0, high=num_features, size=(batch_size, query_nnz), device="cuda")
  grad = torch.rand(batch_size, query_nnz, embed_size, device="cuda")


  torch.cuda.synchronize()
  start = time()
  for _ in range(100):
    ref_embedding.weight.grad = None
    ref_lookup = ref_embedding(indices)
    ref_lookup.backward(grad)
  torch.cuda.synchronize()
  stop = time()
  print(F"Elapsed time {(stop - start) * 1000.:.1f} ms.")


if __name__ == '__main__':
  main()

```

<!-- If you have a code sample, error messages, stack traces, please provide it here as well -->

## Expected behavior

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen. -->
Tested on V100

Pytorch 1.4:  `Elapsed time 41.6 ms.`
Pytorch master: `Elapsed time 692.5 ms.`

body:
## 🐛 Bug
We saw the performance regression of convolution 3d(fp32) when benchmarking against C2. The problems mainly arise from:
1) We don't have a batched group convolution, and each group is computed separately.
```
for (int g = 0; g < params.groups; ++g) {
        auto input_g = subtensor(input, 1, params.groups, g);
        auto weight_g = subtensor(weight, 0, params.groups, g);

title: Pytorch performance bug 36452
body:
## 🚀 Feature
<!-- A clear and concise description of the feature proposal -->
An asynchronized implementation w.r.t to the host thread

## Motivation

<!-- Please outline the motivation for the proposal. Is your feature request related to a problem? e.g., I'm always frustrated when [...]. If this is related to another GitHub issue, please link here too -->

Current implementation of ``SyncBatchNorm`` is not only synchronized with other workers but also block the host thread, so the host cannot continue issue computing task to the GPU like it does with ``Module`` without ``SyncBatchNorm``. So the GPU cannot be saturated during training. 

After I do some research on the current implementation, I find there are 2 draw backs:
1. ``AllGather`` must be Synchronized with host thread to guarantee the all data is gathered. This is the main reason that host thread must be blocked in current implementation. Code is at [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/_functions.py#L33-L35)

2. The last argument of  ``batch_norm_gather_stats_with_counts``, a.k.a. ``counts`` must be a ``IntArrayRef``, but later is converted back into ``CUDATensor`` in [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Normalization.cu#L136-L137), which cause unnecessary ``MemcpyDtoH`` and ``MemcpyHtoD`` and also block the host thread. 

Here are timelines of NVVP of DPP training with and without ``SyncBatchNorm``.
![with_sync_bn](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2868493/79064328-91db3b00-7cda-11ea-952d-4940ed80dab7.png)
![without_sync_bn](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2868493/79064331-956ec200-7cda-11ea-9076-78ea3e47b829.png)
With ``SyncBatchNorm``, forward pass is abount 700ms
Without ``SyncBatchNorm``, forward pass is about 100ms

## Pitch

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you want to happen. -->
1. NCCL colloective functions may be submit to task sequence of a stream just like other CUDA operation, so host thread does not have to be blocked in SyncBatchNorm and other synchronization operation like gradient reduction.
2.  The last argument of  ``batch_norm_gather_stats_with_counts``, a.k.a. ``counts`` should accept ``CUDATensor`` rather than ``IntArrayRef`` or list of ``int`` at Python layer.

## Alternatives

<!-- A clear and concise description of any alternative solutions or features you've considered, if any. -->

## Additional context

<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->


cc @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel
comments:
[winggan]: After some further research, I found that 

> ``AllGather`` must be Synchronized with host thread to guarantee the all data is gathered. This is the main reason that host thread must be blocked in current implementation. Code is at [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/_functions.py#L33-L35)

is not true according to [this](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.hpp#L48-L50
). That is ``wait()`` for NCCLProcessGroup actually enqueue an operation to current stream that wait for operations in NCCL communication stream, and will not block host thread.

Hence the **ONLY REASON** that host thread is blocked is the unnecessary ``MemcpyDtoH`` and ``MemcpyHtoD`` caused by argument ``counts`` being of type ``IntArrayRef``, since they cannot be async ops under PyTorch.

    torch.cuda.synchronize()

## 🚀 Feature
Add a faster implementation of multinomial sampling.

## Motivation
As for now, sampling without replacements is very slow because the code runs in `O(n*m)` and is sequential: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9a1fc2b31ded472c63b227ad24859bc14131f42/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/MultinomialKernel.cpp#L105-L127.

There exists a faster way to sample from multinomial distribution without replacements: https://stackoverflow.com/a/20548895/1894478

python code is pretty simple:
```python
def WeightedSelectionWithoutReplacement(weights, m):
    elt = [(math.log(random.random()) / weights[i], i) for i in range(len(weights))]
    return [x[1] for x in heapq.nlargest(m, elt)]
```
which runs in `O(n+mlogm)` with possible parallelization to `O(n)` part.

title: Pytorch performance bug 39694
body:
## 🐛 Bug

```
>>> a = torch.tensor(100000, device="cuda")
>>> b = a.to("cpu", non_blocking=True)
>>> b.is_pinned()
False
```

The cpu dst memory is created as pageable, so the memcpy is host blocking (["For transfers from device memory to pageable host memory, the function will return only once the copy has completed."](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/api-sync-behavior.html#api-sync-behavior)).  We have one user with evidence that the pageable memcpy also blocks side streams (ie DALI dataloader streams).

Fix might be as simple as setting [options.pinned_memory](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c767d65cafc2615bcee9ec1bbc8d5dadc07ea0e8/c10/core/TensorOptions.h#L216) for the new dst tensor around [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/1f7557d173c8e9066ed9542ada8f4a09314a7e17/aten/src/ATen/native/TensorConversions.cpp#L24) in to_impl.  I'd PR it myself but if it turns out to be a rabbit hole (for example, since pinned cpu memory is a valuable resource, do we want the returned tensor to live in pinned cpu memory by default, or do we want `to` to include a further host-side memcopy or unpinning such that the returned tensor lives in pageable memory?) I can't afford to go down another rabbit hole right this second.  Filing now so we don't forget.

body:
## 🐛 Bug

After some quantization operations are called on cuda tensors (in particular, _make_per_tensor_quantized_tensor, maybe some others) all subsequent cpu allocations are using pinned memory
## To Reproduce
```
import torch
x = torch.randn(3)
print(x.is_pinned()) # False, as expected
q_int = torch.randint(0, 100, [1, 2, 3], device="cuda", dtype=torch.int)
q = torch._make_per_tensor_quantized_tensor(q_int, scale=0., zero_point=0)
x = torch.randn(3)
print(x.is_pinned()) #True, all host allocations after this point are in pinned memory
```
Quantization operations should not affect subsequent cpu allocations
This is important because with pinned allocations all the cpu operations will be slowed down significantly. E.g. `test_histogram_observer` runs for 40s in isolation, but for 400s if there were previous cuda quantization operations, and all the allocations as a result are forced to be pinned allocations.

title: Pytorch performance bug 41359
body:
We now fully support undefined Tensors in the backward pass to represent a Tensor full of zeroes.
We should leverage this and stop creating full size Tensors for custom Function (both on python and cpp side)

cc @ezyang @SsnL @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @yf225 @glaringlee @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel
comments:
[albanD]: More details of the two part that are covered by this issue.

1. Stop materializing outputs
For this part, we just want to make sure that `None` or `undefined` Tensors returned by the custom backward are passed as `undefined` to the rest of the computations.
The only BC breaking change this leads to is when this output is directly linked to either an `AccumulateGrad` (and so the .grad field of a leaf Tensor) or an input Tensor from `autograd.grad()`. In this case, the user will get None/undefined for Tensors that used to get a Tensor full of 0s.
This is properly handled by our optimizers and will cause clear errors for users that expect a Tensor here.
We already use None, an error or a Tensor full of 0s to represent a Tensor full of 0s and which one the user get depends on the internal implementation.

2. Stop materializing the inputs (can be done in a second PR)
This one would mean that we stop creating Tensor full of 0s and give undefined Tensor in cpp and None in python.
This one is more problematic from a BC point of view because it means that all the user's custom Function need to handle such special inputs.
Given that this is only for performance in very specific case, we can add this as an opt-in feature. So the behavior wouldn't change for current users but users that define a static attribute `dont_materialize_grads = True` will get the new behavior and get None/undefined gradients that they need to properly handle.

---

[ssnl]: > This is properly handled by our optimizers and will cause clear errors for users that expect a Tensor here.
We already use None, an error or a Tensor full of 0s to represent a Tensor full of 0s and which one the user get depends on the internal implementation.

I just want to say that this is **not** properly handled by the optimizers. For the ones doing weight decay and/or momentum, having `None` gradient vs having `zero` gradient do different things. It is use to decide when a variable starts to accept momentum / weight decay. I would agree with the argument that this is a somewhat weird behavior though.

---

[albanD]: > I just want to say that this is not properly handled by the optimizers.

Good point. It is handled but not the exact same way.

My reasoning is:
- We don't guarantee this behavior (you can get None, an error or a Tensor full of 0s already). So the behavior for inputs independent of the output is already in a bad state.
- This will affect a very small number of users
- A user returning None from their backward will get None for their .grad field which feels consistent
- The performance improvement can be significant depending on the tasks (following Node will also skip computations)
- Drawback: Some user custom Functions that are independent of the input (from the grad point of view, not forward point of view) will now return None gradient instead of a Tensor full of 0s.
  - This can confuse the user for that used to get a Tensor full of 0s. But I would argue that None is more consistent if their custom function returned None.
  - This will change the optimizer behavior.

Do you agree that this BC-breaking change is worth it?

---

[ssnl]: @albanD It would break some reproducibility silently though, which is my main concern. I think we should more properly define what to do with momentum/decay when grad is `None` and zeros. Also another thing to think about is whether we want to change `.zero_grad()` to set `None` instead.

---

[albanD]: > @albanD It would break some reproducibility silently though, which is my main concern. 

Yes we marked it as BC-breaking.
Given that it only affects people that will return `None` for a Tensor that requires grad in a custom function, I think this is ok. Mainly because very few people actually do that, or are even aware that they are allowed to return `None` for inputs that require gradients.
If you feel very strongly about this, we can make this materialization of the output conditional on the same flag as https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/41490 ? And that way it is only an opt-in feature that won't change the default behavior. You think that would be better?

>  Also another thing to think about is whether we want to change .zero_grad() to set None instead.

This is discussed there: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/41696
I'm not sure we really want to change the default. But giving the user both options very clearly sounds good.
Please do send any feedback you have there!

## 🐛 Bug

For two simple einsum cases, Case 2 is running ~30% slower than Case 1, despite needing to perform 101x fewer ops.

## To Reproduce

**Case 1**
```
a = torch.randn(10000, 100, 101).cuda()
b = torch.randn(10000, 101, 3).cuda()

%%time

    torch.einsum("bij, bjf->bif", a, b)

```

## 🐛 Bug

I am experimenting with dynamic quantization as described here:
https://pytorch.org/blog/introduction-to-quantization-on-pytorch/

I got a pretty good speedup when running with a single thread. (This is a GRPC server application that serves pytorch models). However, I do not see any improvement when using multiple threads and processing multiple concurrent requests. This does not happen when dynamic quantization is not being used: I see pretty good scaling up to about 10 threads. The CPU utilization when running with 10 threads but without quantization is well over 700%. However, when dynamic quantization is enabled, CPU load peaks around 150%, meaning that most of the cores sit idle.

This leads me to believe that python's GIL is the culprit. I noticed that in many parts of the code, pytorch does the following:

pybind11::gil_scoped_release no_gil;

But this does not happen in qlinear_dynamic.cpp which runs on dynamic quantization. This again implies that when dynamic quantization is used, GIL does not get released. This would certainly explain why we see improved performance with one thread but not with multiple threads.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 environment variable.

2. Load any model and apply dynamic quantization:

model = torch.quantization.quantize_dynamic(model, {torch.nn.Linear}, dtype=torch.qint8)

3. Use threadpool to make multiple concurrent calls to to the model.

## 🐛 Bug
We observed a big increase in inference latency after adding `torch.inverse()` in the code path. After investigation and comparison with moving the op to CPU we found that there is a huge difference in performance of that op on GPU vs CPU.
The matrix size in our case is 4x4 which small for the GPU but `torch.inverse()` should be using `magma` library which has heuristics to move the op to CPU. We didn't see any magma invocations as well.

Based on @ptrblck suggestion we tried `inverse` on batched matrix to see if that made any difference but that also didn't result in any improvement.

**Performance Difference:**
```
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 8.78560 ms
CPU Time: 0.07149 ms
cpu/gpu: 122.90x
```
We increased the matrix dimensions to 1024x1024 but even then GPU is slower than CPU:
```
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 17.25289 ms
CPU Time: 9.54982 ms
cpu/gpu: 1.81x
```
## To Reproduce
Here is the snippet of code which can be run to reproduce the performance difference:
```
import torch
import time

a = torch.randn(4,4).cuda()
torch.cuda.synchronize()

num_iter = 100
def test1():
    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        x = torch.inverse(a)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    gpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  gpu_time

    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        b = a.to('cpu')
        d = torch.inverse(b)
        y = d.to('cuda')
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    cpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  cpu_time

gpu_time = test1()
print("GPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format(gpu_time*1000))

cpu_time = test2()
print("CPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format( cpu_time*1000))

print("cpu/gpu: {:.2f}x ".format(gpu_time/cpu_time))

title: Pytorch performance bug 42371
body:
## 🐛 Bug

The function `torch.nn.functional` but also the different `torch.nn.functional.convXd` keep allocated the input also when the weight does not require the gradient.

## To Reproduce

The following code shows the issue by comparing `torch.nn.functional` against a custom implementation of it.

```
import torch

from torch.nn.functional import linear


# Creating the customized function
class MyLinear(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, i, w):

        if ctx.needs_input_grad[1]:
            ctx.save_for_backward(w, i)
        else:
            ctx.save_for_backward(w)
        return i.mm(w.t())

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        saved = ctx.saved_tensors
        return grad_output.mm(saved[0]), grad_output.t().mm(saved[1]) if ctx.needs_input_grad[1] else None

# Input requiring gradient
x = torch.rand(1000, 10).cuda().requires_grad_()

# Weights NOT requiring gradient
weight = torch.rand(20, 10).cuda()


# This function performs some operations using the function f and keeps track of the
# allocated gpu memory within the function.
def test(f, x, weight):
    s = torch.cuda.memory_allocated()
    x = x + 2
    x = f(x, weight)
    print(f"Allocated memory: {torch.cuda.memory_allocated() - s}")
    return x


# I report the amount of allocated memory by torch.nn.functional
print("Test Pytorch linear")
y1 = test(linear, x, weight)

# I report the amount of allocated memory by the customized implementation
print("\nTest MyLinear")
y2 = test(MyLinear.apply, x, weight)

# Check that the obtained outputs agree
print(f"\nSame output? {y1.allclose(y2)}")

y1.norm().backward()
z1 = x.grad.clone()

x.grad.zero_()
y2.norm().backward()
z2 = x.grad.clone()

# Check that the gradient wrt input agrees.
print(f"Same gradient? {z1.allclose(z2)}")
```

The output I get:
```
Test Pytorch linear
Allocated memory: 120832

Test MyLinear
Allocated memory: 80384

Same output? True
Same gradient? True
```


## Expected behavior

`torch.nn.autograd.linear` should return the same amount of memory allocated by the custom implementation.
Specifically, when the weight does not require the gradient, the input should not be stored for later use.

NOTE: this applies not just to `linear` but also to the convolution operator of Pytorch.

## Environment

```
Collecting environment information...
PyTorch version: 1.6.0
Is debug build: No

title: Pytorch performance bug 42890
body:
Currently, when a call to the autograd engine is done, the original task is always placed on the CPU worker queue.
While this works great, it can lead to surprising behavior, in particular when re-entrant autograd happen from a GPU thread.

Indeed, even though the whole code runs on a GPU and should run serially on the GPU thread, the original task happening on the CPU can lead to non-determinism and bad ordering of the execution (which can lead to very bad memory usage when using checkpointing and independent branches).

From the top of my head, I think we should:
- Remove [this code](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/engine.cpp#L867) when there is a single input: we can just use that input's grad_fn as the graph root. That will be better perf-wise, especially for very small graphs.
- Change [this code](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/engine.cpp#L892-L893) to push on the right queue based on the inputs (mimicking the logic [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/input_buffer.cpp#L121-L137)).

Even though I wouldn't expect anyone to rely on this, this would be BC-breaking. But I think the determinism and gain in memory in these cases will be worth it.

cc @ezyang @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @pearu @nikitaved @gchanan @SsnL
comments:
[wanchaol]: Seems to me that the main change here is to determine the correct device ready queue for GraphRoot by examing the inputs device? This sounds good to me as I didn't see any potential issues for this approach. 

For distributed engine, we are still doing similar thing like the current local autograd engine, but it's a bit different, we maintain a `ready_queue` per GraphRoot, and always push to this newly allocated ready queue (see code [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54c05fa34e1fbbb5096746a8ae92e27a08116de4/torch/csrc/distributed/autograd/engine/dist_engine.cpp#L291)). since it's manually polled off tasks from this newly allocated queue, the approach you proposed might not just work for the dist engine. @pritamdamania to confirm here.

---

[albanD]: > we maintain a ready_queue per GraphRoot

What about the re-entrant case?
A particular example that can be problematic is something like 
```python
inp = torch.rand(10, requires_grad=True, device="cuda")
out1 = checkpoint(f1, inp)
out2 = checkpoint(f2, inp)
loss = crit(out1, out2)
loss.backward()
```
Here, when the first checkpoint backward is hit, the re-entrant enqueues the GraphRoot on the CPU queue. And so the GPU worker starts doing the second checkpoint (recomputing another forward, etc).
So there will be no memory benefit by using checkpoint in this case because the engine runs both of them in an interleaved manner even even though they only contain GPU tasks that should run sequentially on a single thread.

What would happen if we do this in the distributed engine?

---

[wanchaol]: > What about the re-entrant case?
> A particular example that can be problematic is something like
> 
> ```python
> inp = torch.rand(10, requires_grad=True, device="cuda")
> out1 = checkpoint(f1, inp)
> out2 = checkpoint(f2, inp)
> loss = crit(out1, out2)
> loss.backward()
> ```
> 
> Here, when the first checkpoint backward is hit, the re-entrant enqueues the GraphRoot on the CPU queue. And so the GPU worker starts doing the second checkpoint (recomputing another forward, etc).
> So there will be no memory benefit by using checkpoint in this case because the engine runs both of them in an interleaved manner even even though they only contain GPU tasks that should run sequentially on a single thread.
> 
> What would happen if we do this in the distributed engine?

I think when we added the functionality of maintaining separate ready_queues for each graph root, we had the assumption that we don't support re-entrant bnackward case in dist_engine. And there's no distinction for all ready_queues in the dist_engine as we all do this `execute until empty` style on a separate CPU thread (no dedicated GPU thread). 

For the case that you mentioned above, I agree with you that it's kinda losing the benefits of checkpointing. I don't really know how would checkpointing works together with the dist engine in today's design. @pritamdamania can you chime in here?

---

[pritamdamania87]: reentrant-backward/checkpointing are not officially supported in the distributed engine and we explicitly didn't target support for this to keep the original implementation simple.

Although to resolve this issue for the distributed engine, why can't we first check the root to see if it needs to be enqueued on the GPU queue and push it to the appropriate GPU queue instead of enqueueing it on the CPU queue. If we have a CPU task, we create a new queue and just execute until empty.

---

[albanD]: After more exploration, the change in the threading system, when we perform re-entrant from a GPU worker thread, it is (wrongfully?) picking up the GPU worker thread queue as its new CPU queue and so the new task is actually enqueued on the right queue.
So the non-determinism mentioned above does not actually exist in master anymore and this won't be BC-breaking.
