title: Pytorch performance bug 43036
body:
A silly performance test linearly depends(1000 times slower on 1000x larger tenor) on tensor size on macOS(with 6 cores i9) but  can be 4-10 time faster on Linux or Windows:
```
In [2]: t = torch.ones(1000, device='cpu')

In [3]: timeit t.pow(123)
7.45 µs ± 343 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100000 loops each)

In [4]: t = torch.ones(1000000, device='cpu')

In [5]: timeit t.pow(123)
5.83 ms ± 246 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```

`torch.__config__.parallel_info()` says for all OSes that PyTorch was compiled with OpenMP but it's not actually available on macOS:

```
at::get_num_threads() : 1
at::get_num_interop_threads() : 6
OpenMP not found
...
ATen parallel backend: OpenMP
```

Version.cpp:
```
std::string get_openmp_version() {
#ifdef _OPENMP
...
#else
  ss << "OpenMP not found";
#endif
}
```

ParallelOpenMP.h:
```
inline void parallel_for(..., const F& f) {
...
#ifdef _OPENMP
...
#else
  f(begin, end);
#endif
}
```
which looks like serial invocation.

This affects at least PyTorch 1.3.0-1.6.0 both pip and conda

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @malfet @VitalyFedyunin
comments:
[malfet]: Grabbing this one for myself.

---

[malfet]: I think this is controlled here:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/059aa34b124916dfd761f3cbdb5fa97d7a01fc93/caffe2/CMakeLists.txt#L13-L17

---

[ezyang]: As follow up, we should have binary testing that ensures we are actually getting multithreaded speed up.

---

[rfeinman]: @malfet @pbelevich I wonder if switching to native threading was the best solution for this. Here is my concern.

#### Problem

I've been working with the pre-built Mac OS binaries from the conda pytorch channel (both stable and nightly). Since the binaries use native threading, I am unable to call `torch.set_num_threads` more than once. When I do, I get the following message:

```
Warning: Cannot set number of intraop threads after parallel work has started or after set_num_threads call when using native parallel backend (function set_num_threads)
```

This is a bummer, since I can't tune the number of threads for an op as per the [PyTorch threading tutorial](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cpu_threading_torchscript_inference.html#tuning-the-number-of-threads). I also can't use the "num_threads" feature in the new `torch.utils.benchmark.Timer` tool to test runtime performance at different thread counts. An unintended consequence for Mac users is that, once you have called a Timer with the default num_threads=1, parallelism will now be disabled for the remainder of your notebook/script (especially concerning in notebooks, since the above warning message is printed to terminal and thus the user doesn't know this happened).

Another strange finding with the Mac OS binaries is that, looking at `torch.__config__.parallel_info()`, pytorch seems to think my mkl distribution is configured with `mkl_get_max_threads() : 1`, even though it reports `at::get_num_threads() : 6`. When I check the same mkl distribution in C++ (e.g. by linking the library and include directories from my conda environment), I see that `mkl_get_max_threads() == 6`. It's unclear what the performance implications are, but if MKL-based BLAS and LAPACK ops are unable to benefit from parallelism, this would certainly be a concern. In an equivalent linux binary, I see that mkl_get_max_threads() matches at::get_num_threads(), the expected behavior.

#### Suggestion

Rather than use native threading, there is an easy fix to make OpenMP work properly as per Linux and Windows binaries. According to [this discussion](https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneDNN/issues/591) on oneDNN, the problem seems to be that [FindOpenMP.cmake](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/cmake/Modules/FindOpenMP.cmake) does not work properly with Apple Clang. They found two quick fixes - [number 1](https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneDNN/issues/591#issuecomment-552293435) and [number 2](https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneDNN/issues/591#issuecomment-553742873) - which can be used to solve the issue with Homebrew Clang and native Apple Clang, respectively. Perhaps we can add these fixes to whatever Clang compiler is used to build the conda Mac OS binaries. 

P.S. - I was planning to submit a new issue about fixing Mac OS binaries, but I found the ticket here which seemed to address the same topic, so I decided to comment instead.

## 🐛 Bug

I noticed a high performance difference when repeating a variable that requires grad. If I repeat the variable with torch.repeat, the backward pass will take 10x more time than when using torch.repeat_interleave. Below you find a minimal example for reproduction, however here i found only a ~2x difference.

iter time:  0.0019862818717956542

 - OS (e.g., Linux): Ubuntu 18.04
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): pip
 - Build command you used (if compiling from source): -
 - Python version: 3.6

 - GPU models and configuration: Problem appears on both GTX 1660 (CUDA 10.1) and Tesla V100 (CUDA 10.0)
 - Any other relevant information:



cc @ezyang @SsnL @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel
comments:
[zou3519]: I can reproduce this, but I'm not sure if it is worth fixing. The repeat pattern being used here is repeating a Tensor along some dimension of size 1. The best thing to actually do here is to expand the tensors along a dimension to avoid a copy; replacing the `repeat` in the benchmark code with a `expand` produces the best performance on my machine:

```
z = torch.rand((1, 32)).requires_grad_()

repeated = z.repeat(1024, 1)
repeated = z.repeat_interleave(1024, dim=0)
repeated = z.expand(1024, 32)
```
@tobiasfshr: are you repeating a tensor along some dimension that does not have size 1? `repeat` and `repeat_interleave` have different semnatics in that case.

---

[ngimel]: Regardless of a particular case, backward of `repeat` is inefficient due to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e7564b076c13325fba1704d9d07844a26041f10f/torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.cpp#L645. `sum_tensorlist` is inefficiently implemented as a sequential sum. `grad` is guaranteed to be evenly split into necessary-size pieces, so instead of chunk + sum_tensorlist `grad` tensor can be reshaped and `sum` can be called on it, that should give similar performance to`expand`.

---

[tobiasfshr]: @zou3519 Thanks for the suggestion! I'm actually repeating the tensor in my code along a dimension with size > 1. Specifically, I have a tensor x with size B*N, C and the tensor y that is to be repeated, which has size B, C. To concatenate them, i repeat the tensor N / B times. However, you can solve this also in this way by expanding y:
`y.unsqueeze(1).expand(B, N, C).contiguous().view(-1, C)`

title: Pytorch performance bug 43837
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Currently multivariate normal broadcasts `loc` and `covariance_matrix` tensors together, effectively creating `loc_` tensor of shape `(*batch_dims, n, n)` and slicing from it after instead of creating tensor of shape `(*batch_dims, n)`. Although there's not much performance difference during forward pass, it creates massive `fill_` operation during backward pass which just zeroes gradient in `loc_` gradient tensor as you can notice in profiler trace. Moreover, it probably sums gradients over the whole `loc_` grad tensor after, but this is not that pronounced in profiler trace. In the end, both fill and sum ops are useless.

## To Reproduce
In this script I tried to provide possible fix, although I do not like double `broadcast_tensor` in each branch. Maybe there's a way to do it in more efficient and elegant way. I was looking for `broadcast_to` method which favours AD flow, but found only #8076.
```
import torch
import torch.distributions as td
from torch.autograd import profiler, grad

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
torch.set_num_threads(1)


class StubMultivariateNormal(td.MultivariateNormal):
    def __init__(self, loc, covariance_matrix=None, precision_matrix=None, scale_tril=None, validate_args=None):
        super().__init__(loc, covariance_matrix, precision_matrix, scale_tril, validate_args)
        # retry procedure with broadcasting
        loc_ = loc.unsqueeze(-1)  # temporarily add dim on right
        if scale_tril is not None:
            if scale_tril.dim() < 2:
                raise ValueError("scale_tril matrix must be at least two-dimensional, "
                                 "with optional leading batch dimensions")
            self.scale_tril, _ = torch.broadcast_tensors(scale_tril, loc_)
            self.loc, _ = torch.broadcast_tensors(loc, scale_tril[..., 0])

title: Pytorch performance bug 44206
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Upsample with a trilinear interpolation works at least 10x slower using Mixed Precision than with FP32.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Run python debug.py --input_shape 8 4 4 4 --batch_size 4 --iterations 100
2. Run python debug.py --input_shape 8 4 4 4 --batch_size 4 --iterations 100 --amp
3. Compare results

## Expected behavior

Upsample with a trilinear interpolation works at least as fast using Mixed Precision as FP32

## Environment

I tried it in nvidia containers back to 20.01 so it seems it's pytorch version agnostic.

## Additional context
It seems that the main culprit is **backprop**. Fprop is actually faster in Mixed Precision.
kernel breakdown:
FP32:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43240942/92271388-ff853f00-eee7-11ea-8dbd-1caa57d182a2.png)

FP16:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43240942/92271411-09a73d80-eee8-11ea-92c3-aece946ce6be.png)


code:

```python
import argparse
from time import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.cuda.amp import GradScaler
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv3d(in_channels=8, out_channels=1024, kernel_size=(3, 3, 3), bias=False, padding=(1, 1, 1))
        self.upsample = nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2, mode="trilinear", align_corners=True)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv(x)
        x = self.upsample(x)
        return x


def main():
    flags = parse_arguments()
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True
    nvtx_enabled = False
    if flags.profile:
        import torch.cuda.profiler as profiler
        import pyprof
        pyprof.init(enable_function_stack=True)
        nvtx_enabled = True
        print("Profiling is enabled")

    model = Model()
    device = torch.device("cuda:0")
    model.to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), 1e-8)
    scaler = GradScaler()

    data = torch.rand(size=(flags.batch_size, *flags.input_shape)).to(device)
    with torch.autograd.profiler.emit_nvtx(enabled=nvtx_enabled):
        model.train()
        iteration = 0
        start_marker = time()
        for i in range(flags.iterations):
            iteration += 1
            if flags.profile and iteration == 10:
                profiler.start()
            optimizer.zero_grad()

            with autocast(enabled=flags.amp):
                outputs = model(data)
                loss = torch.sum(outputs)

            if flags.amp:
                scaler.scale(loss).backward()
                scaler.step(optimizer)
                scaler.update()
            else:
                loss.backward()
                optimizer.step()
        if flags.profile:
            profiler.stop()
        elapsed = time() - start_marker
        print("Finished in", round(elapsed, 2),
              "s. One iteration took on average", round(elapsed/flags.iterations), "s.")


def parse_arguments():
    PARSER = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="UNet-3D")
    PARSER.add_argument('--amp', dest='amp', action='store_true', default=False)
    PARSER.add_argument('--batch_size', dest='batch_size', type=int, default=1)
    PARSER.add_argument('--input_shape', nargs='+', type=int, default=[32, 64, 64, 64])
    PARSER.add_argument('--profile', dest='profile', action='store_true', default=False)
    PARSER.add_argument('--iterations', dest='iterations', type=int, default=100)
    return PARSER.parse_args()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

body:
## 🐛 Bug

When using the new [fp16_compress_hook](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/algorithms/ddp_comm_hooks/default_hooks.py) in torch 1.7 nightly the peak memory usage increases by an amount equal to the (in memory) size of the gradient tensors. In the example below the size of the 32bit grads are 8MB so the expected peak allocated memory is ~24MB (parameter tensors + gradient tensors + DDP buffers), and I have confirmed this is the case in the standard setting.

However when using the hook this increased to 32MB, presumably caused by the `bucket.get_tensors()[0].to(torch.float16)` copy, I would have expected this memory to be released after the synchronization was complete, but that does not seem to be the case. Is there a way to avoid this extra copy as it becomes an issue when dealing with very large models. 

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

```python
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
import torch.multiprocessing as mp


def main(rank, world_size):

    os.environ['MASTER_ADDR'] = 'localhost'
    os.environ['MASTER_PORT'] = '12355'
    # initialize the process group
    dist.init_process_group("nccl", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)

    model = torch.nn.Linear(512, 4096).to(rank)

    ddp_model = DDP(model, device_ids=[rank])
    ddp_model._register_comm_hook(state=None, hook=fp16_compress_hook) 
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(ddp_model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)

    for _ in range(5):
        y = ddp_model (torch.randn(64, 512, device=rank)).mean()
        y.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        
    print(rank, torch.cuda.memory_allocated(device=rank) / (1024 ** 2))
    dist.destroy_process_group()

# as per https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/algorithms/ddp_comm_hooks/default_hooks.py
def fp16_compress_hook(process_group: object, bucket: dist._GradBucket):
    """
        This DDP communication hook implements a simple gradient compression
        approach that converts ``GradBucket`` tensors whose type is assumed to be
        ``torch.float32`` to half-precision floating point format (``torch.float16``).
        It allreduces those ``float16`` gradient tensors. Once compressed gradient
        tensors are allreduced, its then callback called ``decompress`` converts the
        aggregated result back to ``float32`` and takes the mean.
        Example::
            >>> ddp_model._register_comm_hook(process_group, fp16_compress_hook)
    """
    group_to_use = process_group if process_group is not None else dist.group.WORLD
    world_size = (
        process_group.size() if process_group is not None else dist.get_world_size()
    )

    compressed_tensor = bucket.get_tensors()[0].to(torch.float16)

    fut = dist.all_reduce(
        compressed_tensor, group=group_to_use, async_op=True
    ).get_future()

    def decompress(fut):
        return [fut.value()[0].to(torch.float32).div_(world_size)]

    return fut.then(decompress)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mp.spawn(main, args=(2,), nprocs=2, join=True)
```

1 24.04736328125
```

With fp16 hook

0 32.06298828125
```

The peak memory usage to be the same with and without the hook

title: Pytorch performance bug 47313
body:
`addr` implementation here 
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebra.cpp#L147-L159
does explicit multiplications by `alpha` and `beta`  even though by default `alpha` and `beta` are 1, so no multiplication is necessary. This degrades performance and memory usage. 
In addition, line 55 does invalid cast, so invocation with complex beta results in an error:
```
a=torch.randn(3, dtype=torch.complex64)                                                                                                                                                                
b=torch.randn(3, dtype=torch.complex64)                                                                                                                                                                
c=torch.randn(3,3, dtype=torch.complex64)   
c.addr(a,b, beta=0+0.1j)
```
```
RuntimeError: value cannot be converted to type double without overflow: (0,0.1)
```  
related: #44364
cc @vishwakftw @jianyuh @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry @heitorschueroff
cc @ivannz
comments:
[RockingJavaBean]: @mruberry I would like to help fix the performance and memory issues, as well as the bug when inputs are complex numbers.

Please kindly confirm which option we should adopt.
- implement `torch.addr` as a composite op and prevent unnecessary multiplications when `alpha` or `beta` is the default value
- implement `torch.addr` based on BLAS libraries.

CC @ngimel @IvanKobzarev

---

[ivannz]: In my opinion, the implementation of `torch.addr(input, vec1, vec2, beta=1, alpha=1, out=None)` as [a composite op](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebra.cpp#L154) *by design* incurs an impractical allocation of the product `vec1 * vec2^T`.

As a *standalone* outer product, produced by `torch.outer`, this is fine, because the caller presumably *knows and agrees* that the output is a rank-one matrix. However as an *inplace* operation, all of which are aimed at conserving memory, it is tacitly assumed that the implementation does not require extra storage beyond that of the arguments (since it is reasonable to expect it to be implemented as `out[i,j] = out[i,j] * beta + vec1[i] * vec2[j] * alpha` in an `i-j` loop).

Hence, I think, `torch.outer(vec1, vec2, out=None)` could be implemented as `torch.addr(input, vec1, vec2, beta=0, alpha=1, out=None)`, wherein `input` is completely ignored if `beta` is exactly *zero*. This way, I believe, both the maintainability and versatility objectives would be feasible: `torch.outer` would always be a *wrapper* around `torch.addr`, while `torch.addr`, being the core procedure, would be responsible for dispatching to the correct `dtype` and `device` pathway.

---

[ngimel]: I agree that current addr implementation allocates unnecessary intermediate buffer, however, I'm not convinced that bringing back blas/cublas bindings for it is good idea. 
1) they don't support bfloat16 and half datatypes. 
2) they are cumbersome to use for complex
3) they are cumbersome to use with ROCm
4) as shown in the benchmarks in original port, `outer` is significantly faster implemented as a pointwise multiply, and addr suffers from needlessly inefficient implementation due to extra scalar multiplies, as mentioned in this issue. 

`addr` can be efficiently implemented not relying on cublas, by using TensorIterator-based kernels (`cpu_kernel_vec` and `gpu_kernel`) To do it, one needs to create TensorIterator with correct inputs and declare cpu/gpu stubs specifying the correct pointwise operation for the kernels, you can look at how many pointwise operations are implemented to get the idea.

---

[RockingJavaBean]: @ngimel Thanks for the kind and detailed suggestions, I will start to implement `torch.addr` using `TensorIterator-based kernels`.

## 🐛 Bug

observation: pytorch native amp consumes 10x memory as compared to fp16/apex or no `--fp16` usage.

The issue has been originally discovered and tracked at https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/8403 and on slack, but now we know for sure that this is a pytorch issue, so let's concentrate the discussion here.

## To Reproduce

What's following is the minimal script that was reduced from a rather complex logic of `finetune.py` in `transformers`. It originates in a complex stack of `pytorch-lightning` feeding `transformers` generate/beam_search logic finally feeding to real pytorch logic in `BartForConditionalGeneration`. If you want to see the full blow up and how to set it up, it's described [here](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/8403).

I found at least part of the culprit or trigger of the leak - it's `@torch.no_grad()` used for `generate` https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/eb3bd73ce35bfef56eeb722d697f2d39a06a8f8d/src/transformers/generation_utils.py#L281-L282

Here is a short script that reproduces the leakage. It removes all the generate/search logic and feeds the same random `input_ids` to `BartForConditionalGeneration` pre-trained model.

Please first run:
```
pip install ipyexperiments 
```
to get the memory tracing, but feel free to disable it if for some reason it's not working for you and use some alternative like `nvidia-smi` dumping. (but it should work)

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

import os
import sys
import torch
os.environ["USE_TF"] = "0"
sys.path.insert(1, "src")

# !pip install ipyexperiments 
from ipyexperiments.utils.mem import gpu_mem_get_used_mbs, gpu_mem_get_used_no_cache_mbs

from transformers import BartForConditionalGeneration

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

model = BartForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained('sshleifer/student_cnn_12_6').to(device)
model.eval()

vocab_size = 50264 # model.config.vocab_size

[ezyang]: I read through the downstream discussion. I agree that there are (multiple) legitimate bugs; but furthermore, I think we were wrong to close earlier reports that AMP leaks memory when you use AMP outside of your training loop. This should work. @mcarilli, I'll try to explain why below.

On its face, it would make sense that a cache that only gets cleared when you exit AMP would leak memory over time. But AMP only caches casts on parameters: you should be using the same parameters in each loop of the training loop (and updating them in place). What is there to leak? In fact, there should be no leak, and instead we have a correctness bug where we will improperly use casts even when the original parameters have been updated. We ought to fix that.

But let's suppose that, somehow, you're generating fresh new parameters every iteration of the loop. Those parameters are ostensibly going dead when you go around the loop, and so if we implemented a weak map correctly, they should still get pruned anyway. Well I looked over the code and there are still some problems:

* We don't seem to ever traverse the map to get rid of dead entries, where the key is dead. This is a big deal because even though the source parameter's data gets deallocated when it becomes dead, the *cached cast output* doesn't get deallocated unless you remove it from the map. So the weak pointer is only solving half the problem: we prevented the source parameter from getting leaked, but we're still leaking the cached output.
* I stared at the code some more and I got worried about another possible memory leak: the cached output cast has a `grad_fn` that will refer to the parameter via a grad accumulator. I now don't remember if this is a weak reference or a strong ref; if it's strong, that's a reference cycle and would also prevent the weak pointer key from ever getting collected either.

We probably didn't notice any of this because it's mostly OK to just leak everything until the end of one step in the training loop... except in situations like this.

PS. I'm kind of sad we don't live in a GC'ed language, as a lot of this weak pointer/map business gets a lot simpler if you can assume there's some GC process that will clean up after you.

btw, cc @swolchok, this is an example of weak pointers actually being important for tensors

---

[agolynski]: @mcarilli

---

[mcarilli]: I was still confused because https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/autocast_mode.cpp#L71 should ensure the only things that get cached are leaves (model params) that require grad.  These don't move between iterations of the loop under `no_grad`.  @ptrblck investigated yesterday in depth yesterday and we realized there are 3 ingredients that cause the cache blowup we didn't discuss so far:
1. All tensors created in a `no_grad` context are considered leaves, because they don't have autograd history.
2. Linear layers don't send their weights directly to the matmul call, rather, they send [`weight.t()`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9b526546202cf53c90ed3a438c16260386475680/torch/nn/functional.py#L1665-L1667), which is a new Tensor (with a new TensorImpl) each time.  (further unfortunate consequence:  this means without `no_grad`, the cache was doing nothing for linear layers, because it never saw incoming `weight.t()`s as leaves.)
3. View ops (like `t()`) in `no_grad` context _do_ propagate requires_gradness from their source tensor.

With 1, 2, and 3 together, when `forward` with many linear layers is called in a loop under `no_grad`, in every matmul in every iteration `cached_cast` sees incoming weights as leaves that require grad and have a new TensorImpl, so it creates a new cache entry with a new fp16 copy every time.

The plot thickens, though.  3. is an _inconsistent behavior_ between view ops and out-of-place ops in `no_grad` contexts.  View ops propagate requires_gradness of the source, ordinary out-of-place ops don't:
```python
with torch.no_grad():
    print(a.requires_grad) # True
    b = a.clone()
    print(b.requires_grad) # False
    b = a.t()
    print(b.requires_grad) # True
    b = a.view(-1)
    print(b.requires_grad) # True
```
This may be due to some short-circuiting in view ops, I haven't looked in detail.
@albanD , is the above behavior expected, or a bug?  Seems like a bug to me: since view ops do create distinct tensors, they should have the same source-tensor-attribute-propagation policy as out-of-place ops.  But maybe the different policy is a deliberate choice for some reason I don't get.

One option:  If we changed view ops to _not_ propagate requires_gradness under `no_grad` (consistent with the behavior of out-of-place ops) it would fix the cache blowup, because the incoming `weight.t()`s would have `requires_grad=False`, therefore `cached_cast` would not try to cache their casts.  It wouldn't be ideal because it would defeat the purpose of caching, but it would be no worse than running without `no_grad` (see "2....further unfortunate consequence")

---

[t-vi]: The special handling of views in `no_grad` is required, this is part of `DifferentiableViewMeta` in `torch/csrc/autograd/variable.h`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/98fddc1f061fb5b0dcac9f49b3b096bcdc124a12/torch/csrc/autograd/variable.h#L322-L337

I think checking `t._base()` to detect non-leaves to handle that case could eliminate 1.

---

[albanD]: Yes views need to inherit the requires grad from their base otherwise code like the following would not work
```python
base = torch.rand(1, 5)
slice1 = base[0]
slice2 = base[0]

# This makes slice1 and base properly require gradients
slice1.copy_(torch.rand(5, requires_grad=True))
# Other views need to also be properly updated by reading the base's status
loss = slice2.sum()
loss.backward()
```


Do I understand properly that the issue is that this view op makes it so that the input to the linear (and thus your cache) is different at each iteration and so a new entry is created every time (and never cleaned up even when the Tensor goes out of scope)?

---

[mcarilli]: @albanD thanks for the thorough analysis!  i need some time to digest it all :P but it sounds like we can fix the main issue without waiting for my brain to catch up.

> I think checking t._base() to detect non-leaves to handle that case could eliminate 1.

Are you proposing we check `t._base()` somehow in the line where we check for cache eligibility (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/autocast_mode.cpp#L71)?

---

[albanD]: I guess you could check `!t.is_view()` there indeed. If you say that you never want to cache the result for a view of a larger Tensor?
But then what happens if someone actually have weights that are views of a bigger Tensor for some reason? The caching will just miss them completely.
So I don't think you can have something that will work for everything here by just looking at the Tensor. But maybe never caching views will be a good enough heuristic.

---

[ezyang]: Thanks, this is a good analysis. A quick thoughts: view cache blow up due to .t() can be solved with a simple heuristic: if we have a view of a parameter, cast the *source* of the view and cache that. Then, when checking the cache, if we are given a view, check if we have a cache of the view base, and if so, redo the view on top of that.

---

[albanD]: Users might have the bad idea to assign as a parameter a small slice of a much bigger Tensor. Such approach would process a very big Tensor that should not be be processed.
But this would be rare as well.

---

[ezyang]: If this is a concern, you can update the heuristic to only see through view operations that preserve numel.

Also, it is only a problem to cast the bigger tensor *if you don't actually use the rest of the parameters in the bigger tensor in that run*. If you do use them, then you probably are going to autocast them too, in which case you're just paying for it up front.

---

[mcarilli]: > update the heuristic to only see through view operations that preserve numel.

I like this idea, but I don't think it should block https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/48696, which is a simple fix that's strictly better than current code.

---

[stas00]: May I also ask in this context why caching is skipped if: `!arg.requires_grad()` - e.g. multple transformers models have static positional embedding (not part of the grad tree) which don't ever change so I'd think those should be cached.

And moreover, since they don't ever change these would be a candidate for a constant cache and not re-calculated on each enter/exit from autocast context (if memory allows for that luxury).

Unless there is a way to force tensors to have both float and half values on the user side if the user knows that it'd be beneficial to have those converted values cached once.

I don't know whether there has been a discussion about a session-level cache.

---

[mcarilli]: > May I also ask in this context why caching is skipped if: !arg.requires_grad()

@stas00  `is_leaf()`, as far as I know, checks if the tensor has any autograd history (@albanD knows more).  If we're not under no_grad, you're probably right:  `arg.is_leaf()` suffices to tell us if an incoming param is a static model param in most cases.

But if we are under no_grad, all newly created tensors pass the `arg.is_leaf()` check, because they don't have autograd history.  If we get rid of the `arg.requires_grad()` check, all fp32->fp16 casts for such internal temporaries will be cached, more such temporaries will be cached every iteration of the `forward` loop, and we have another cache blowup.  In this way, under no_grad the `arg.requires_grad()` check is the best way of ensuring we only cache casts for the true static model params, because most** of the temporaries will have `arg.requires_grad() == false` and be ineligible for caching.  It's not a perfect heuristic but I'm not sure how we can make it perfect.  The only information `cached_cast` has is `is_leaf()`, `requires_grad()`, and `is_view()`, and with those it needs to make its best guess whether to cache or not (while hopefully avoiding blowups in calling code).

** the exception is view temporaries like `weight.t()`, which _do_ inherit requires_grad-ness from their parents, so they passed both the is_leaf() and requires_grad() checks to cause the original blowup.

---

[stas00]: Thank you for the detailed explanation, @mcarilli. 

Following this discussion it sounds like the main problem here is that there is an expectation that `autocast` is supposed to magically optimize everything - and everything is different, so as you all have been saying this is an impossible task, and battles have to be picked.

Would the developers consider adding some manual options in addition to the magical `autocast`. For example, could a tensor have a flag that will make it cachable unconditionally?

For example for static positional embeddings we already call `detach` and turn grads off, so we could just as well turn on a hypothetical "cache-these-weights-if-under-fp16" flag. And then another flag for the caching scope `{autocast|session}` - so the tensor will still get cached under `autocast` even if normal conditions for caching won't apply.  And in the case of the `session` scope `autocast` will not release these at the end of its scope.

This is a half-baked idea since I haven't measured the actual impact and the importance of such need. But perhaps some of you who have a lot more practical experience can think of situations where being able to manually control such caching would lead to a faster program at a reasonable memory cost and no memory leaking. I could be wrong and perhaps such need is very minor and is not worthy the added complexity.

So this is not a request but just an idea that I'm asking whether it is reasonable/useful/worthy consideration.

Thank you.

[albanD]: Reopening as the PR was just a quick fix and more might need to be done

[stas00]: Now that the nightly binary build was updated with this fix I verified that both the short reproduction script in the first comment and the original application where I discovered this leak no longer have the leak, and I get about 30% speed increase with native `--fp16` - yay!  The memory usage is about the same w/ and w/o --fp16.

Thank you so much!

title: Pytorch performance bug 51206
body:
Using nn.functional.interpolate is very slow when using mixed precision training. This seems to have already been an issue in the past (#12409) and should be fixed, but I am still seeing a performance regression of up to 5x (yes, that is 5x the runtime of fp32) depending on the network an GPU.

To demonstrate the issue I have created a small script that reproduces it. I am mostly interested in 3D images which is why that example uses 3D convs, but the same issue appears also with 2D inputs (see below, I will add a separate section for that).

What my script does is the following:
It builds a very simple convolutional encoder network (VGG style) that downsamples the input 1x64x64x64 to 512x4x4x4. It then blows up the small representation back to 512x64x64x64 using interpolate. The loss is then simple the MSE between input and upsampled output. 
This workflow does not represent a useful application, it is just there to put some load on the GPU and isolate the issue.

I run 100 iterations with this setup in three settings
1) regular fp32
2) regular AMP
3) AMP but with a hack: the encoding (512x4x4x4 tensor) is cast to float, then upsampled and then cast to half.

**Expected behavior:**
2. should be much faster than 1. due to tensor core acceleration of the convolutions, 3. should be slower than 2. due to additional overhead (casting)

**Actual behavior:**
2. is slower than 1.. 3. is faster than 2.

**Environment:**
I am using pytorch 1.7.0 compiled with cuDNN 8.0.5.39. OS is Ubuntu 18.04 (RTX 3090) and centOS (RTX 2080ti, V100).

I am also showing results for 1.7.1 with cuDNN 7.6.5 (installed with pip today) to demonstrate that is not related to my build.

**Details and standalone script**

```python
from time import time

from torch import nn
import torch
from torch.cuda.amp import GradScaler, autocast
from torch.nn import functional
from torch.optim import SGD


class Network(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cast_for_upsample=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.cast_for_upsample = cast_for_upsample

        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv3d(1, 32, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),
            nn.LeakyReLU(1e-2, True),
            nn.Conv3d(32, 32, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, False),

We find it important to keep the groundtruths intact and instead upsample the final logits, since downsampling the groundtruths removes the fine annotations resulting in no back-propagation of details. I wanted to try that myself. When I did that (note that this is on pytorch 1.7 with cudnn 8.0.5 and amp enabled) I noticed that my epoch time went up from 95s to over 300s. After some searching I found the trick of casting feature maps to float prior to applying interpolation and that cut down my epoch time to ~140s. So yeah - for me it's a real use case and a real problem but I don't know how many people could be (unknowingly) affected. Just to give some more details: In the network I was using the following tensor sizes were upscaled to the original image resolution: (2, 3, 8, 8, 8), (2, 3, 16, 16, 16), (2, 3, 32, 32, 32), (2, 3, 64,64,64) The original resolution was (2, 3, 128, 128, 128). The code I was using is nnU-Net, a segmentation method for biomedical images that I developed. It has a fairly large userbase (https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet, 1.3k stars) and if upscaling the logits provides a benefit to segmentation accuracy I would like to make this feature available. This will however require the performance of interpolate to be good enough. Even a regression of 95->140s per epoch (with the hack) is too much given that training times are rather long already. Finally, I would like to recap the two problems that were uncovered as part of this issue. They are not necessarily related: 1. In 1.7, the upsampling is 2x (or more) slower with amp enabled than it is with fp32. This should not be the case. I would expect it to be equally fast with amp enabled (as far as I know this operation does not benefit from tensor cores). Note that this issue is, like you confirmed, related to the backwards pass. 2. In master, upsampling is much slower than in 1.7. Such a performance regression is certainly not intended. Also, again, fp16 is a bit slower than fp32 which is not what I would expect. Best, Fabian --- [ngimel]: @xwang233 please benchmark #48675 on a wider range of input sizes, and at the very least switch to the old implementation for cases that regress. --- [xwang233]: Thanks @FabianIsensee for discovering the issue. @ngimel , I'll check the benchmark for the interpolation backward. --- [FabianIsensee]: Hi there, are there any updates on this?

## 🐛 Bug

using `torch.autograd.grad()` with `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)` will cause memory leak

## To Reproduce

Run the code snippet below.
It will have about 2MiB GPU memory consumption increasing each iteration.

If comment out the `set_detect_anomaly` line, then there is no memory leak, with constant memory consumption.

```python
import torch
torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) # if comment out this, no leak
for rep in range(1000):
    batch = torch.ones(10, 30000).cuda().requires_grad_()
    y=batch.norm()
    grad = torch.autograd.grad(
        outputs=y, inputs=batch,
        create_graph=True, retain_graph=True, only_inputs=True)[0]
    print("memory allocated:", float(torch.cuda.memory_allocated()/1024**2), "MiB")
    pass
```

## Expected behavior

No memory leak with or without `set_detect_anomaly(True)`

## Environment

 - PyTorch Version: 1.7.1
 - OS: Linux
 - How you installed PyTorch: conda, source: `-c pytorch`
 - Python version: 3.8.5
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: cuda11.0

## Additional context

BTW, if replace `y=batch.norm()` with `y=batch.mean()`, then there is no memory leak with or without `set_detect_anomaly`, which makes me very confused.

title: Pytorch performance bug 5169
body:
- OS: Ubuntu 16.04
- PyTorch version: master
- How you installed PyTorch (conda, pip, source):source
- Python version:3.6
- CUDA/cuDNN version:9.0
- GPU models and configuration:
- GCC version (if compiling from source):

Using .view that actually changes dimensions in a model introduces 4(!) extra memcopies of the size of gradOutput in backward pass.  Minimum reproducer below, in the first loop where input is 3d and view is flattening it to 2D, there are 4 memcopies after softmax backward, in the second loop where view is a noop there is none. Running with emitted nvtx shows that the first memcopy comes from AsStridedBackward, 3 extra ones come from autogradCopySlices, it is possibly related to  #3970. This is a regression from 0.3 that did not have those memcopies regardless of the view. It is also likely that this issue affects memory usage, as we are not able to fit the models on master that used to fit on 0.3.  cc @colesbury 
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = torch.nn.Linear(256,256)
       
    def  forward(self, input, target):
        input = self.fc(input)
        input = input.view(-1, input.size(-1))
        loss = F.cross_entropy(input, target, size_average=False)
        return loss


input =torch.randn(20,400,256).cuda()
target = torch.ones(8000).cuda().long()
model = Model().cuda()    
for i in range(5):
    loss = model(torch.autograd.Variable(input, requires_grad = True), torch.autograd.Variable(target))
    loss.backward()

input =torch.randn(8000,256).cuda()
for i in range(5):
    loss = model(torch.autograd.Variable(input, requires_grad = True), torch.autograd.Variable(target))
    loss.backward()
```
comments:
[ngimel]: Bisection points to #3384 as the offending commit. cc @colesbury

---

[colesbury]: The issue is due to a combination of a 3d x 2d `matmul` (from the nn.Linear) with the behavior for 3384. 3384 added specific behavior for in-place operations on views.  The 3d x 2d case of matmul ends with a viewing operation:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/bf603299b6a61d05744dbee8a4ee642bbac2979f/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebra.cpp#L197

After the matmul, `linear` performs an in-place addition:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/5bcacb21d512c359a2a4e7f19d020b68b3103284/torch/nn/functional.py#L903-L906

The in-place operation on the view triggers the `CopySlices` backward.

There are two ways we can fix this:

1) Try to avoid copying in `CopySlices` and `AsStridedBackward` in favor of viewing operations when possible. This is a bit tricky, but doable at least for some common cases.
2) Specify an explicit derivative for matmul instead of differentiating the individual operations. This would avoid treating the output as a view of another Tensor.

(We can also do both)

---

[csarofeen]: Redefining nn/functional.py linear as (as you recommend in 2):
```.py
def linear(input, weight, bias=None):
   """                                                                                                                                                                                                    
   Applies a linear transformation to the incoming data: :math:`y = xA^T + b`.                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                           
   Shape:                                                                                                                                                                                                  
       - Input: :math:`(N, *, in\_features)` where `*` means any number of                                                                                                                                
         additional dimensions                                                                                                                                                                            
       - Weight: :math:`(out\_features, in\_features)`                                                                                                                                                    
       - Bias: :math:`(out\_features)`                                                                                                                                                                    
       - Output: :math:`(N, *, out\_features)`                                                                                                                                                            
   """

   input = input.contiguous()
   sizes = input.size()[:-1]
   input = input.view(-1, input.size(-1))
   if input.dim() == 2 and bias is not None:
       # fused op is marginally faster                                                                                                                                                                    
       output = torch.addmm(bias, input, weight.t())
       return output.view(*sizes, -1)

   output = input.matmul(weight.t())
   if bias is not None:
       output += bias
   return output
```
Was enough to avoid the mem copies in fairseq. Should we just route though to addmm for now until someone tackles 1?

---

[colesbury]: @csarofeen that might work. I think fairseq uses 3d input, so you may need some viewing before and after the addmm call.  That should be fine as long as the bias addition is part of the `addmm` call and not a subsequent in-place addition.

---

[ngimel]: That's exactly what we are doing (viewing before and after) and we've verified that it works for fairseq (no ooms, performance back at 0.3 levels). We'll submit a PR then.

---

[soumith]: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/5279 is merged now.

title: Pytorch performance bug 52264
body:
I am seeing some big performance regressions from two benchmarks in [TorchBench](https://github.com/pytorch/benchmark/) when I enable `torch._C._jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(True)`.  LearningToPaint has the performance regression both with and without freezing, while pytorch_mobilenet_v3 only has the regression when I enable freezing as well (in this case a 922x regression).

Code to reproduce:
```
import torch, re, multiprocessing
from timeit import timeit
from torchbenchmark.models import LearningToPaint, pytorch_mobilenet_v3


def measure(fuse, benchmark_module, warmup=1, number=100):
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    torch._C._jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(fuse)
    name = re.sub(r"^.*[.]", "", benchmark_module.__name__)
    benchmark = benchmark_module.Model(device="cpu", jit=True)
    model, example_inputs = benchmark.get_module()
    assert isinstance(model, torch.jit.ScriptModule)

    model = model.eval()
    timeit(lambda: model(*example_inputs), number=warmup)
    print(f"    script({name:20})         = {timeit(lambda: model(*example_inputs), number=number):.3f} sec")

    model = torch.jit.freeze(model)
    timeit(lambda: model(*example_inputs), number=warmup)
    print(f"    freeze(script({name:20})) = {timeit(lambda: model(*example_inputs), number=number):.3f} sec")


for fuse in (False, True):
    print(f"_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu({fuse}):")
    for benchmark_module in (LearningToPaint, pytorch_mobilenet_v3):
        # Doing a subproc to ensure we aren't running cached code
        p = multiprocessing.Process(target=measure, args=(fuse, benchmark_module))
        p.start()
        p.join()
```

Output:
```
_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(False):
    script(LearningToPaint     )         = 5.862 sec
    freeze(script(LearningToPaint     )) = 5.131 sec
    script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)         = 1.089 sec
    freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) = 0.460 sec
_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(True):
    script(LearningToPaint     )         = 275.655 sec
    freeze(script(LearningToPaint     )) = 274.557 sec
    script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)         = 1.108 sec
    freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) = 424.520 sec
```

I am running on PyTorch==96fd5d87f7c739fd62b57b6cb08fd41a60d0bf40 on Ubuntu 20.10/gcc-9.3.


cc @gmagogsfm
comments:
[jansel]: cc @bertmaher  @Krovatkin @zheng-xq @navahgar @eellison

---

[ZolotukhinM]: @jansel, is your pytorch built with LLVM? A common pitfall is that when LLVM is not available, the fused code gets interpreted.  One way to check it is to enable `PYTORCH_JIT_LOG_LEVEL=">>llvm_codegen"` - if the output is empty, then probably you'd need to rebuild pytorch with `USE_LLVM` (a side note: we probably should start including it to the builds by default).

---

[navahgar]: This perf regr is only because of PyTorch built without LLVM, as @ZolotukhinM mentioned. I just confirmed this:

**Without LLVM**

```
_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(False):
    script(LearningToPaint     )         = 8.731 sec
    freeze(script(LearningToPaint     )) = 8.006 sec
    script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)         = 1.607 sec
    freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) = 0.784 sec
_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(True):
    script(LearningToPaint     )         = 513.627 sec
    freeze(script(LearningToPaint     )) = 512.031 sec
    script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)         = 1.548 sec
    freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) = 782.914 sec
```

**With LLVM**

```
_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(False):
    script(LearningToPaint     )         = 9.847 sec
    freeze(script(LearningToPaint     )) = 8.631 sec
    script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)         = 1.997 sec
    freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) = 1.326 sec
_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(True):
    script(LearningToPaint     )         = 9.890 sec
    freeze(script(LearningToPaint     )) = 9.014 sec
    script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)         = 1.986 sec
    freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) = 2.400 sec
```

Note that there is no way to get PyTorch with LLVM from prebuilt nightlies AFAIK. You will have to build PyTorch from source with USE_LLVM flag set in order to get the LLVM backend.

---

[jansel]: Ah, that explains it.  Should we make this an error?  Or emit a warning?  I doubt anyone would want the 50x slower behavior.

Also, it looks like even with LLVM freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) is slower.

---

[wconstab]: It seems like it'd be easier on devs and users to keep things straight if we were clearer in requiring llvm or error;  are there good arguments in favor of supporting JIT without llvm?

---

[navahgar]: I agree that it is better to keep things clearer w.r.t. requiring llvm. But sometimes users fail to realize that they are building without LLVM, even though thats not their intention and they have LLVM setup already. I know this because I have done this many times already. At the least, we should make sure that users understand that they are building without LLVM and their performance on CPU will be >50x slower. 

> Also, it looks like even with LLVM freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3)) is slower.

I updated my repo and checked again. That still seems to be ~2x slower. Anyone familiar with `freeze` have cycles to look into this?

---

[Krovatkin]: I can look into the `freeze` slowdown

---

[Krovatkin]: I was thinking that 

The most natural behaviour for most users would be that 
a) we don't have to fuse on CPU if we built without LLVM

For developers and early adopters that do want to test with LLVM
b) we could add a STRICT_LLVM flag to make sure we error out in case PyTorch was built without LLVM

---

[navahgar]: Thanks @Krovatkin.

> a) we don't have to fuse on CPU if we built without LLVM

This would work for now. In future, assuming we have better performance when fused on CPU, users may not know to enable the appropriate flag to use that.

How about making the default build use LLVM and asking the users to specify a `NO_LLVM` flag if they do not want to use LLVM? Basically, the reverse of what is happening now. If the users didn't have LLVM, then the default build will fail (without the `NO_LLVM` flag). If they specify the `NO_LLVM` flag we can decide to not fuse on CPU.

---

[jansel]: For the current behavior, I'd suggest `_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(True)` throws an error if you don't have LLVM.  Once fusing becomes the default maybe we need to switch to the `NO_LLVM` flag.

---

[ZolotukhinM]: Yeah, it's done this way simply because there hasn't been many users of CPU fusion and for our own experimentation it worked fine. Now that we're getting users we should change the behavior to more sane. I think trying to turn on fusion on CPU when no LLVM is available should either throw an error or do nothing unless we have another explicit option telling us to use IR eval instead of LLVM (that option would probably interest no one except us, NNC developers).

---

[navahgar]: Throwing an error on `_jit_override_can_fuse_on_cpu(True)` is probably not the right approach for the following reasons:
1. It looks like all tests are run in CI without LLVM. So, all of them fail when we throw an error on this.
2. Disabling all these tests when LLVM is not set does not seem correct, since they will never run on CI in that case.
3. Even if we decide to disable all of them, there are 850+ tests (that failed for me) to disable. 

My suggestion is to go with the `NO_LLVM` flag as I described above. That will be off by default but can be set for CI builds to get around the problem with tests.

---

[jansel]: Can we enable LLVM in CI?  I'd imagine those tests would be better if they actually checked the correctness of our generated LLVM.  What are they testing if LLVM is disabled?

---

[ZolotukhinM]: Overall that sounds good to me, but how would we find LLVM without `USE_LLVM`? That option currently serves two purposes: 1) tells the build that LLVM is available, 2) points to the LLVM folder. If we switch to `NO_LLVM`, how would we do (2)?

---

[ZolotukhinM]: > Can we enable LLVM in CI

I believe we have one or several builds with LLVM enabled in CI. Majority of the builds are done without LLVM though.

---

[navahgar]: I had a chat with @bertmaher and his suggestion might work. We have a flag `te_must_use_llvm_on_cpu` which is off by default and is used in TE to enforce LLVM backend. The plan is to turn this flag on by default, which would ensure that we error out when CPU fusion is enabled without LLVM. And we can turn this flag off for all tests. Trying this now.

> What are they testing if LLVM is disabled?

It is still useful to test without LLVM, since we can then test other parts of our code base without LLVM codegen. However, I agree that these tests should be run with LLVM enabled as well. 

> If we switch to NO_LLVM, how would we do (2)?

NO_LLVM will be in addition to USE_LLVM. The purpose of USE_LLVM will be to just point to the LLVM build. 

Anyways, I realize that changing the default build options is a much bigger impact change. If we decide to go that route, that probably has to be done with proper messaging.

---

[bertmaher]: > > Can we enable LLVM in CI
> 
> I believe we have one or several builds with LLVM enabled in CI. Majority of the builds are done without LLVM though.

Yeah this is correct, it's on for some but not all builds.  I think in the current state where the llvm fuser is off-by-default it makes sense to have some covered each way (mainly to catch build errors that could creep in -- I don't think we should care about testing the TE interpreter from Python; the interpreter mainly exists to support IR simplification).

---

[navahgar]: Created a new issue to track the perf decrease with `freeze(script(pytorch_mobilenet_v3))`: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/52465

## 🐛 Bug

## To Reproduce

import time

import torch

world_size = 4
master_rank = 0


def init_distributed(
    rank: int,
    world_size: int = world_size,
    backend: str = "nccl",
    hostname: str = "127.0.0.1",
    port: int = 29500,
    timeout: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=30),
) -> torch.distributed.TCPStore:
    is_master = rank == master_rank
    store = torch.distributed.TCPStore(hostname, port, world_size, is_master, timeout)
    torch.distributed.init_process_group(
        backend, store=store, timeout=timeout, world_size=world_size, rank=rank

body:
I've come accross a weird memory leak when using matmul() and permute() on GPU tensors:

```python
l, m, n = 1, 9, 1
w = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.Tensor(1024, 2, l, m).cuda())

- How you installed PyTorch (conda, pip, source): source
- Python version: 3.6.4

Here is the same code with imports and GPU memory monitoring

```python
import subprocess
import torch
from torch.autograd import Variable

# This is from https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/access-gpu-memory-usage-in-pytorch/3192/4
def get_gpu_memory_map():
    """Get the current gpu usage.

    Returns
    -------
    usage: dict
        Keys are device ids as integers.
        Values are memory usage as integers in MB.
    """
    result = subprocess.check_output(

```python
from argparse import ArgumentParser

import torch
import torch.backends.cudnn as cudnn
import torch.cuda as cuda

from torch.nn import Sequential, Conv2d, ReLU, Linear, Module, AvgPool2d, BatchNorm2d
from torch.nn.functional import binary_cross_entropy_with_logits, avg_pool2d
from torch.nn.utils import spectral_norm
from torch.optim import Adam

__author__ = 'Morgan Funtowicz'


class Flatten(Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        return x


class _ResidualDownSamplingBlock(Module):

    def __init__(self, n_in, n_out, ksize, stride=1, padding=1):
        super().__init__()
        self._f = Sequential(
            ReLU(),
            spectral_norm(Conv2d(n_in, n_out, ksize, stride, padding)),
            ReLU(True),
            spectral_norm(Conv2d(n_out, n_out, ksize, stride, padding)),
            AvgPool2d(2, 2)
        )
        self._sc = spectral_norm(Conv2d(n_in, n_out, 1, padding=0))

    def forward(self, x):
        return avg_pool2d(self._sc(x), 2, 2) + self._f(x)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Ensure Tensor are allocated as FloatTensor
    cudnn.benchmark = True
    torch.set_default_tensor_type('torch.FloatTensor')
    torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float32)

    # Parse provided arguments
    args_parser = ArgumentParser()
    args_parser.add_argument('-d', type=int, default=-1, dest='device', help='Device to use for training (-1 = CPU)')
    args_parser.add_argument('-b', type=int, default=-16, dest='batch', help='Size of the minibatch')

    args = args_parser.parse_args()
    args.gpu = args.device >= 0 and cuda.is_available()
    device = torch.device("cuda:%d" % args.device if args.gpu else "cpu")

    # Define the model & Optimizer
    model = Sequential(
        _ResidualDownSamplingBlock(3, 64, ksize=3),
        _ResidualDownSamplingBlock(64, 64, ksize=3),
        _ResidualDownSamplingBlock(64, 128, ksize=3),
        _ResidualDownSamplingBlock(128, 128, ksize=3),
        _ResidualDownSamplingBlock(128, 128, ksize=3),
        _ResidualDownSamplingBlock(128, 64, ksize=3),
        BatchNorm2d(64), ReLU(True), Flatten(),
        spectral_norm(Linear(256, 1))
    ).to(device)

    opt = Adam(model.parameters())

    # Train
    for epoch in range(20000):
        print('Starting epoch %d' % epoch)

        x, y = torch.randn((args.batch, 3, 128, 128), device=device), torch.rand((args.batch, 1), device=device)
        y_hat = model(x)

        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(y_hat, y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
```

title: Pytorch performance bug 9168

## Issue description

When naively serializing a pytorch tensor (or model) with pickle the process takes longer than it probably should when comparing it to Numpy serialization of the same data.  It appears that at some point we're converting things into a list rather than returning the buffers directly.

## Code example

```python
In [1]: import numpy, torch, pickle

In [2]: x = numpy.random.random((10000, 10000))

In [3]: t = torch.tensor(x)

In [4]: %time len(pickle.dumps(x)) / 1e6                    # around 1GB/s
CPU times: user 298 ms, sys: 415 ms, total: 713 ms
Wall time: 711 ms
Out[4]: 800.000162

In [5]: %time len(pickle.dumps(t)) / 1e6                    # around 50MB/s
CPU times: user 14.6 s, sys: 1.03 s, total: 15.7 s
Wall time: 15.7 s
Out[5]: 900.200098
```
The majority of this time is spent in converting the `t.storage()` object into a list

```python
In [11]: %time _ = t.storage().tolist()
CPU times: user 12.3 s, sys: 891 ms, total: 13.2 s
Wall time: 13.2 s
```

Instead, we might consider passing around a numpy array, `buffer`, or `memoryview`, each of which will serialize much more quickly than converting to many Python objects

```python
In [1]: import torch

In [2]: torch.__version__
Out[2]: '0.4.0'
```

title: Pytorch performance bug 9646
body:
There is a cost to creating, retaining, and destroying CUDA streams in PyTorch master. In particular:

- Tracking CUDA streams requires atomic refcounting
- Destroying a CUDA stream can (rarely) cause implicit device synchronization

The refcounting issue has been raised as a concern for expanding stream tracing to allow streaming backwards, for example, and it's clearly best to avoid implicit device synchronization as it causes an often unexpected performance degradation.

For static frameworks the recommended best practice is to create all the needed streams upfront and destroy them after the work is done. This pattern is not immediately applicable to PyTorch, but a per device stream pool would achieve a similar effect. In particular, it would:

- Eliminate refcounting
- Move stream destruction to shutdown
- Allow for efficient stream tracing
- Keep the same interface

These per-device pools could consist of the default stream, 32 low priority streams, and 32 high priority streams.

Even with the same interface, a stream pool will cause some behavior changes:

- Users who are profiling networks that use many streams (like 33 non-default low priority streams) will see their profiles change to reflect only the actual 32 streams in the pool.
- Streams X and X + 32 will actually use the same cudaStream and will not run concurrently. 

While any change may sound worrying, I don't think either will be a problem in practice. When profiles involve so many streams reducing the number that appear may even be a perk, and if a network requires a long-lived stream then it can use the default stream or a high priority stream to avoid the latter issue. As long as streams are created and used as needed (something that a pool will make incredibly fast), the latter issue will not occur, and if a user needs even more control for some reason then they can easily implement their own user-level stream pool.

I think a stream pool is a good way to get the benefits of allocating resources upfront and destroying them after while working in a dynamic environment as it will let us use streams freely with no performance concerns. 

I am creating this issue at the recommendation of @colesbury for public review.

Doing `import tensorflow.contrib` take 7.5 seconds on my machine when doing it with Python 3.6.2. With Python 2.7.13 it takes 3.2 seconds.

Keras by default imports tensorflow.contrib when the Tensorflow backend is used. Therefore Keras is slow to import when using Python 3: https://github.com/fchollet/keras/issues/7408

There is a stackoverflow question referencing this issue: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45093653/import-tensorflow-contrib-module-is-slow-in-tensorflow-1-2-1

        tf_example = get_tf_example(random_numbers, without_an_element)

    filename_queue = tf.train.string_input_producer(['data.tfrecord'])
    reader = tf.TFRecordReader()

    features = tf.parse_single_example(
        serialized_example,
        features={
            'inputs': tf.FixedLenFeature(10, dtype=tf.int64),

    images, labels = tf.train.shuffle_batch([features['inputs'], features['outputs']], batch_size=100, capacity=200,

    threads = tf.train.start_queue_runners(sess=sess, coord=coord)

    for i in range(10000):

        if (i+1) % 100 == 0:

    coord.request_stop()
    coord.join(threads)


if __name__ == '__main__':

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python
import tensorflow as tf
import numpy as np
from .config import Params, CONST
from typing import Tuple


def data_loader(csv_filename: str, params: Params, batch_size: int = 128, data_augmentation: bool = False,
                num_epochs: int = None, image_summaries: bool = False):
    def input_fn():
        # Choose case one csv file or list of csv files
        if not isinstance(csv_filename, list):
            filename_queue = tf.train.string_input_producer([csv_filename], num_epochs=num_epochs,
                                                            name='filename_queue')
        elif isinstance(csv_filename, list):
            filename_queue = tf.train.string_input_producer(csv_filename, num_epochs=num_epochs, name='filename_queue')

        # Skip lines that have already been processed
        reader = tf.TextLineReader(name='CSV_Reader', skip_header_lines=0)
        key, value = reader.read(filename_queue, name='file_reading_op')

        default_line = [['None'], ['None']]
        path, label = tf.decode_csv(value, record_defaults=default_line, field_delim=params.csv_delimiter,
                                    name='csv_reading_op')

        image, img_width = image_reading(path, resized_size=params.input_shape, params=params,
                                         data_augmentation=data_augmentation, padding=True)

        to_batch = {'images': image, 'images_widths': img_width, 'filenames': path, 'labels': label}
        prepared_batch = tf.train.shuffle_batch(to_batch,
                                                batch_size=batch_size,
                                                min_after_dequeue=500,
                                                num_threads=15, capacity=4000,
                                                allow_smaller_final_batch=False,
                                                name='prepared_batch_queue')

        if image_summaries:
            tf.summary.image('input/image', prepared_batch.get('images'), max_outputs=1)
        tf.summary.text('input/labels', prepared_batch.get('labels')[:10])
        tf.summary.text('input/widths', tf.as_string(prepared_batch.get('images_widths')))

        return prepared_batch, prepared_batch.get('labels')

    return input_fn


def image_reading(path: str, params: Params, resized_size: Tuple[int, int] = None, data_augmentation: bool = False,
                  padding: bool = False) -> Tuple[tf.Tensor, tf.Tensor]:
    # Read image
    image_content = tf.read_file(path, name='image_reader')
    image = tf.cond(tf.equal(tf.string_split([path], '.').values[1], tf.constant('jpg', dtype=tf.string)),
                    true_fn=lambda: tf.image.decode_jpeg(image_content, channels=params.image_channels,
                                                         try_recover_truncated=True),  # TODO channels = 3 ?
                    false_fn=lambda: tf.image.decode_png(image_content, channels=params.image_channels),
                    name='image_decoding')

    # Data augmentation
    if data_augmentation:
        image = augment_data(image)

    # Padding
    if padding:
        with tf.name_scope('padding'):
            image, img_width = padding_inputs_width(image, resized_size, increment=CONST.DIMENSION_REDUCTION_W_POOLING)
    # Resize
    else:
        image = tf.image.resize_images(image, size=resized_size)
        img_width = tf.shape(image)[1]

    with tf.control_dependencies([tf.assert_equal(image.shape[:2], resized_size)]):
        return image, img_width


def random_rotation(img: tf.Tensor, max_rotation: float = 0.1, crop: bool = True) -> tf.Tensor:  # from SeguinBe
    with tf.name_scope('RandomRotation'):
        rotation = tf.random_uniform([], -max_rotation, max_rotation)
        rotated_image = tf.contrib.image.rotate(img, rotation, interpolation='BILINEAR')
        if crop:
            rotation = tf.abs(rotation)
            original_shape = tf.shape(rotated_image)[:2]
            h, w = original_shape[0], original_shape[1]
            # see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/16702966/rotate-image-and-crop-out-black-borders for formulae
            old_l, old_s = tf.cond(h > w, lambda: [h, w], lambda: [w, h])
            old_l, old_s = tf.cast(old_l, tf.float32), tf.cast(old_s, tf.float32)
            new_l = (old_l * tf.cos(rotation) - old_s * tf.sin(rotation)) / tf.cos(2 * rotation)
            new_s = (old_s - tf.sin(rotation) * new_l) / tf.cos(rotation)
            new_h, new_w = tf.cond(h > w, lambda: [new_l, new_s], lambda: [new_s, new_l])
            new_h, new_w = tf.cast(new_h, tf.int32), tf.cast(new_w, tf.int32)
            bb_begin = tf.cast(tf.ceil((h - new_h) / 2), tf.int32), tf.cast(tf.ceil((w - new_w) / 2), tf.int32)
            rotated_image_crop = rotated_image[bb_begin[0]:h - bb_begin[0], bb_begin[1]:w - bb_begin[1], :]

            # If crop removes the entire image, keep the original image
            rotated_image = tf.cond(tf.equal(tf.size(rotated_image_crop), 0),
                                    true_fn=lambda: img,
                                    false_fn=lambda: rotated_image_crop)

        return rotated_image


def random_padding(image: tf.Tensor, max_pad_w: int = 5, max_pad_h: int = 10) -> tf.Tensor:
    w_pad = list(np.random.randint(0, max_pad_w, size=[2]))
    h_pad = list(np.random.randint(0, max_pad_h, size=[2]))
    paddings = [h_pad, w_pad, [0, 0]]

    return tf.pad(image, paddings, mode='REFLECT', name='random_padding')


def augment_data(image: tf.Tensor) -> tf.Tensor:
    with tf.name_scope('DataAugmentation'):
        # Random padding
        image = random_padding(image)

        image = tf.image.random_brightness(image, max_delta=0.1)
        image = tf.image.random_contrast(image, 0.5, 1.5)
        image = random_rotation(image, 0.05, crop=True)

        if image.shape[-1] >= 3:
            image = tf.image.random_hue(image, 0.2)
            image = tf.image.random_saturation(image, 0.5, 1.5)

        return image


def padding_inputs_width(image: tf.Tensor, target_shape: Tuple[int, int], increment: int) -> Tuple[
    tf.Tensor, tf.Tensor]:
    target_ratio = target_shape[1] / target_shape[0]
    # Compute ratio to keep the same ratio in new image and get the size of padding
    # necessary to have the final desired shape
    shape = tf.shape(image)
    # 计算宽高比
    ratio = tf.divide(shape[1], shape[0], name='ratio')

    new_h = target_shape[0]
    new_w = tf.cast(tf.round((ratio * new_h) / increment) * increment, tf.int32)
    f1 = lambda: (new_w, ratio)
    f2 = lambda: (new_h, tf.constant(1.0, dtype=tf.float64))
    new_w, ratio = tf.case({tf.greater(new_w, 0): f1,
                            tf.less_equal(new_w, 0): f2},
                           default=f1, exclusive=True)
    target_w = target_shape[1]

    # Definitions for cases
    def pad_fn():
        with tf.name_scope('mirror_padding'):
            pad = tf.subtract(target_w, new_w)

            img_resized = tf.image.resize_images(image, [new_h, new_w])

            # Padding to have the desired width
            paddings = [[0, 0], [0, pad], [0, 0]]
            pad_image = tf.pad(img_resized, paddings, mode='SYMMETRIC', name=None)

            # Set manually the shape
            pad_image.set_shape([target_shape[0], target_shape[1], img_resized.get_shape()[2]])

            return pad_image, (new_h, new_w)

    def replicate_fn():
        with tf.name_scope('replication_padding'):
            img_resized = tf.image.resize_images(image, [new_h, new_w])

            # If one symmetry is not enough to have a full width
            # Count number of replications needed
            n_replication = tf.cast(tf.ceil(target_shape[1] / new_w), tf.int32)
            img_replicated = tf.tile(img_resized, tf.stack([1, n_replication, 1]))
            pad_image = tf.image.crop_to_bounding_box(image=img_replicated, offset_height=0, offset_width=0,
                                                      target_height=target_shape[0], target_width=target_shape[1])

            # Set manually the shape
            pad_image.set_shape([target_shape[0], target_shape[1], img_resized.get_shape()[2]])

            return pad_image, (new_h, new_w)

    def simple_resize():
        with tf.name_scope('simple_resize'):
            img_resized = tf.image.resize_images(image, target_shape)

            img_resized.set_shape([target_shape[0], target_shape[1], img_resized.get_shape()[2]])

            return img_resized, target_shape

    # 3 cases
    pad_image, (new_h, new_w) = tf.case(
        {  # case 1 : new_w >= target_w
            tf.logical_and(tf.greater_equal(ratio, target_ratio),
                           tf.greater_equal(new_w, target_w)): simple_resize,
            # case 2 : new_w >= target_w/2 & new_w < target_w & ratio < target_ratio
            tf.logical_and(tf.less(ratio, target_ratio),
                           tf.logical_and(tf.greater_equal(new_w, tf.cast(tf.divide(target_w, 2), tf.int32)),
                                          tf.less(new_w, target_w))): pad_fn,
            # case 3 : new_w < target_w/2 & new_w < target_w & ratio < target_ratio
            tf.logical_and(tf.less(ratio, target_ratio),
                           tf.logical_and(tf.less(new_w, target_w),
                                          tf.less(new_w, tf.cast(tf.divide(target_w, 2), tf.int32)))): replicate_fn
        },
        default=simple_resize, exclusive=True)

    return pad_image, new_w  # new_w = image width used for computing sequence lengths


def preprocess_image_for_prediction(fixed_height: int = 32, min_width: int = 8):
    """
    Input function to use when exporting the model for making predictions (see estimator.export_savedmodel)
    :param fixed_height: height of the input image after resizing
    :param min_width: minimum width of image after resizing
    :return:
    """

    def serving_input_fn():
        # define placeholder for input image
        image = tf.placeholder(dtype=tf.float32, shape=[None, None, 1])

        shape = tf.shape(image)
        # Assert shape is h x w x c with c = 1

        ratio = tf.divide(shape[1], shape[0])
        increment = CONST.DIMENSION_REDUCTION_W_POOLING
        new_width = tf.cast(tf.round((ratio * fixed_height) / increment) * increment, tf.int32)

        resized_image = tf.cond(new_width < tf.constant(min_width, dtype=tf.int32),
                                true_fn=lambda: tf.image.resize_images(image, size=(fixed_height, min_width)),
                                false_fn=lambda: tf.image.resize_images(image, size=(fixed_height, new_width))
                                )

        # Features to serve
        features = {'images': resized_image[None],  # cast to 1 x h x w x c
                    'images_widths': new_width[None]  # cast to tensor
                    }

        # Inputs received
        receiver_inputs = {'images': image}

        return tf.estimator.export.ServingInputReceiver(features, receiver_inputs)

    return serving_input_fn
